statement: The product manager's core job is to discover a product that is valuable, usable, and feasible.
A strong engineering team produces no value unless it is given something worthwhile to build.
Product discovery should be a collaboration between the product manager, the interaction designer, and the software architect.
User experience design is more important than engineering and is usually harder.
Engineers are typically poor at user experience design because they think in implementation models while users think in conceptual models.
Functionality (product requirements) and user experience design are inherently intertwined and cannot be defined in isolation from each other.
Product ideas must be tested on real target users early and often to arrive at a product that is valuable and usable.
Use a high-fidelity prototype to test product ideas quickly and frequently on real users with a realistic user experience.
Identify the minimal product that still meets the objectives of valuable, usable, and feasible, minimizing time to market and user complexity.
A minimal successful product that has been discovered and validated cannot be further stripped down and still deliver the same results.
Everything starts with the people on the product team, but process is what lets those people consistently produce successful products.
How roles are defined and who staffs the team is a determining factor in a product's success or failure.
The product manager has two core responsibilities: assessing product opportunities and defining the product to be built.
Every product idea should be assessed for whether it is worth pursuing before work begins, and the product manager owns this opportunity assessment.
The product spec should describe the functionality and behavior of the product to be built, not how it will be implemented.
Prefer a lightweight, prototype-based product spec over a heavy paper requirements document.
The interaction designer must develop a deep understanding of each target persona and design the tasks, navigation, and flow to be usable and productive.
Assign a dedicated, skilled project manager for significant projects.
condition: the project is significant or large, such as more than five engineers

statement: In Scrum organizations, the product manager typically serves as the Product Owner and the project manager typically serves as the ScrumMaster.
condition: the team uses Scrum

statement: For Internet services, site operations demands specialized skills and is too important to be a secondary responsibility of the engineering team.
condition: the product is an Internet or hosted service

statement: Provide a single accountable product manager for every product, responsible for the product definition of product requirements plus user experience design.
As a guideline, roughly one product manager is needed for every five to ten engineers.
Do not combine the product management and product marketing roles in one person, because the two require very different skills and the model does not scale.
exception: the product is among the simplest, or the rare individual genuinely excels at both roles

statement: Splitting product definition into high-level and low-level requirements owned by two different people leaves no one truly owning the product and reduces product managers to a spec-generation service that stifles innovation.
Routing a marketing owner's market requirements straight to engineering, bypassing detailed product requirements and user experience design, usually leaves the product in trouble from the start.
Industry pundits claim that as many as nine out of ten product releases fail to meet their objectives.
Wasted release cycles most often trace back to a poorly defined product-manager role and inadequate training of the people in it.
Behind every great product there is an individual accountable for that product's definition.
Product marketing is genuinely valuable and important, and emphasizing product management does not diminish it.
Having product managers also cover project management came from the shipped-software world and does not migrate well to Internet services.
condition: the product is an Internet service

statement: These product methods target commercial software and Internet product teams and may not be effective for non-software products or non-product custom software efforts.
exception: the work is a non-software product or a custom, non-product software project

statement: Internet-service projects usually span more than one release interval, which forces parallel development and the software release-train model.
condition: the product is an Internet service

statement: A release train requires strong project management tied to the whole release rather than to individual projects.
condition: the team uses a release-train model

statement: When project managers are dedicated to release trains, product managers generally do not also need to cover project management.
condition: a release-train model with dedicated release project managers is in use

statement: For Internet-service companies, keep product management and project management as separate roles, or release management will thrash and releases will be chronically delayed.
condition: the product is an Internet service

statement: Separate product management, which discovers a valuable, usable, and feasible product, from project management, which executes to deliver it, even for shipped software.
Strong project-management skill benefits a product manager, but the product-manager and project-manager roles should still be kept separate.
Great project managers share seven traits: a sense of urgency, the ability to frame problems, clear thinking, data-driven decisions, decisiveness, good judgment, and a problem-solving attitude.
Great project managers insist on data to inform decisions rather than shooting from the hip, especially under time pressure.
A good product requires a good user experience, and a good user experience requires close collaboration between product management and user experience design.
Four user-experience roles are essential to a good user experience: interaction design, visual design, rapid prototyping, and usability testing.
Visual design does more than set layout, color, and fonts; it communicates and evokes emotion, which matters more than most teams expect.
Treat prototype code as throw-away and never reuse it in the production product.
Large products, especially consumer Internet services, need all four user-experience roles represented, while smaller products can combine roles across fewer people.
exception: the product is small enough that roles can be doubled up

statement: A good user experience is one of the easiest ways for an enterprise product to differentiate from competitors, because most enterprise products are weak in user experience.
condition: the product is an enterprise product

statement: Do not outsource the interaction designer role, because deep user understanding takes several projects to build and is lost with contractors, the role must be on hand throughout the project, and the user experience is too core to the company.
Visual design, user research, and usability testing can be outsourced, visual design especially when a strong interaction designer is on staff.
Have a software architect review progress and prototypes to ensure the product is feasible.
A great product combines a real customer need with a solution that is just now becoming possible.
The product manager defines the right product and engineering builds the product right; they are peers, with neither role subordinate to the other.

Involve engineers, or at least a lead engineer or architect, from the very beginning of product discovery to get early cost assessments and better solutions, rather than defining the product and throwing it over the wall to engineering.
Get engineers in front of real users and customers so they see problems firsthand and generate better solutions.
Enlist engineers to explore what is becoming technically possible as technology develops.
Keep the focus on minimal product: define the smallest product that meets the goals, not the ultimate product.
Minimize churn, meaning changing requirements and product definition, once engineering has begun development; some churn is unavoidable, but active development is not the time to try out new ideas.
During implementation, answer engineering's questions as fast as possible while keeping the focus on minimal product and minimizing churn.
The farther away and more communication-challenged a remote engineering team is, the more thorough the product spec must be.
condition: the engineering team is remote

statement: Use a high-fidelity prototype as the primary communication mechanism with remote teams, for both the spec and its changes.
condition: the engineering team is remote

statement: Designate a single local person to whom the remote engineering team is clearly accountable and who coordinates with them.
condition: the engineering team is remote

statement: Establish periodic face-to-face contact with a remote engineering team; the product manager should spend quality in-person time with them at least quarterly.
condition: the engineering team is remote

statement: Outsource to assemble the right people for the product, not to save costs.
Team caliber matters most: productivity can differ by as much as twenty times within the same job class, which can dwarf perceived cost savings.
When engineering demands a full stop-and-rewrite, the root cause is usually years of product management pushing for maximum features while neglecting infrastructure.

Allocate a fixed share of engineering capacity, about twenty percent and more if the codebase is in bad shape, as headroom for engineering to re-architect, refactor, and improve scale and performance, to avoid ever needing a full rewrite.
Rewrite time estimates are often wildly optimistic because few teams have real rewrite experience, so scrutinize every line item of a rewrite schedule.
condition: the work is a full rewrite

statement: If a rewrite is unavoidable, break it into incremental chunks and keep delivering user-visible functionality, even at twenty-five to fifty percent capacity, so the product stays relevant.
condition: a rewrite is unavoidable

statement: Some traits are very hard to teach and should form the foundation of a product-manager search, while most skills can be learned afterward.
Hire product managers with genuine product passion; probe it by asking candidates about their favorite and worst products and what they would improve.

A product manager must be able to empathize with the target market, which likely differs from the manager in values, priorities, and tolerances; empathy matters more than personally belonging to that market.
Product management depends on insight and judgment, which require a sharp mind, so hard work alone is not sufficient.
Assess a candidate's intelligence by testing problem-solving on unfamiliar problems, observing how they reason when they do not know the answer, rather than testing knowledge recall.
The product-manager role demands high commitment; if you have to tell a product manager to show up at a critical moment, you have the wrong person.
Because a product manager leads by influence rather than authority, integrity is essential, since the trust and respect that enable collaboration depend on it.
Confidence is a critical trait because the team, executives, and sales look to the product manager to persuade them the vision will succeed.
The successful product manager acts as the CEO of the product: taking full responsibility, making no excuses, taking the blame when things go wrong, and giving the team credit when they go well.
A product manager must be comfortable enough with technology to understand it and see its potential applications, without needing to invent or build it.
Keep relentless focus on the key problem and resist creeping featurism and the loud voices of a few, because focus reduces cluttering features, build time, and cost.
Most products carry features that do not materially affect sales or satisfaction, and removing them often makes the product better because more users can comprehend and appreciate it.
Learn to distinguish the important from the merely urgent and protect time for the truly important work, or the product will fail.
Product managers influence by persuasion rather than authority, so strong writing and speaking skills are required from the start.
Only write a document if people will actually read it, and when they will, make it do its job of describing, educating, or persuading.
Effective presentations use a minimal number of slides, state the main points and the ask unambiguously, provide supporting data, and finish on time.
An accent or minor non-native grammar does not constitute poor communication; what matters is being clear enough to be understood and persuasive enough to move the reader.
A product manager must be bilingual across audiences: able to discuss technology with engineers and cost structures, margins, market share, and positioning with executives and marketers.
Recruiting a product manager solely from marketing or for an MBA credential is a recipe for failure today, because MBA programs almost never teach product management.
The best source of product managers is people with the right traits developed through training and mentoring, and such people can be found anywhere in the company.
Product managers are rare and among the most critical hires, so interview rigorously for the required traits and set the bar high.
For most products, deep prior domain expertise is not required, because strong product managers can come up to speed on a new domain quickly, typically in one to three months.
exception: a few products, such as medical devices, where domain expertise is genuinely essential

statement: Too much domain expertise can be dangerous, because domain experts often wrongly believe they can speak for the customer, so product managers must keep revisiting their assumptions about the domain and its customers.
Understanding your product domain in depth is essential even though deep prior expertise is not a prerequisite for the role.
About eighty percent of a product manager's skills transfer across product types, while the remainder differ by type such as enterprise, infrastructure, consumer services, and consumer electronics.
The most valuable experience is not domain or technology knowledge, which dates quickly, but what you have learned about the process of creating great products, leading a team, and managing growth.
For high-tech products, what matters most is how quickly a product manager can learn new technologies and envision applying them to the problem at hand.
Innate intelligence and product passion are not a function of age, and outstanding product leaders exist across the age spectrum.
Hiring biases based on a mental image of a great product leader, such as preferring native-English speakers, cause companies to overlook outstanding product talent.
The head of product management has two essential responsibilities: build a strong team of product managers and own the company's overall product strategy and portfolio.
An inadequate product manager is almost certain to fail and waste product cycles, because most products have only a single product manager and no one else to pick up the slack.
When a product manager is not up to the task, correct the situation immediately; some people will never fit the role regardless of training, but many can significantly improve.

Every new product manager needs roughly three months of hard learning, immersing with users and customers, learning the relevant technologies, and studying the market and competition, before being entrusted to guide a product, and this applies even to experienced hires.
When you hire a product manager, establish a structured program that gives them the needed exposure to users and technologies.
If a product manager is unable or unwilling to do the job, it is the manager's responsibility to replace them promptly.
Once product managers are capable and properly equipped, step back and let them do their job, because micromanaging capable people stops them from taking ownership.
Do not empower people until you are sure they are strong, because empowering the incapable and then micromanaging them means doing their job for them.
condition: the people are not yet proven capable

statement: Always hire people you believe are smarter than yourself and then do everything you can to help them succeed.
The head of product management is most accountable for the company's suite of products, deciding what products to pursue and reviewing each product's strategy and progress.
The head of product management must ensure the product strategy directly supports the company's business strategy, which requires a deep and current understanding of that business strategy.
The head of product leads the product vision and, with the team, establishes the product principles and ensures products adhere to them.
Even with an excellent team, cross-product conflicts arise as each product manager optimizes their own product, so the head of product must identify and resolve these conflicts.
The head of product must keep a trusting, transparent, and accessible relationship with executives, especially the CEO, while remaining able to push back on conflicting or vacillating priorities.
The only true measure of a product manager is the success of their product, even though defining product success with a single metric is difficult.

Net Promoter Score, the percentage of promoters who rate nine or ten minus the percentage of detractors who rate zero to six on likelihood to recommend, is a useful single metric because it focuses the company on creating happy customers.

Distinguish good revenue from bad revenue: revenue that harms the customer experience slows growth and is reflected in a lower Net Promoter Score, while revenue earned without hurting the experience supports growth.

Specials, meaning explicitly defined custom work done for a specific customer in exchange for their purchase, are dangerous because they represent bad revenue and hurt the ability to create happy users.
Do not house product management inside marketing, because it rests on the misconception that products come from asking customers and it tends to conflate product management with product marketing.
You will not find successful products merely by asking your customers what they want.

Housing product management inside engineering is also problematic, because engineering is optimized to build the product right through execution rather than to discover the right product through discovery.

Raise the product organization to be on par with engineering and marketing, ideally including design and with a seat at the executive table, so the product is driven neither solely by technology nor solely by sales and marketing.

In large companies with centralized engineering and decentralized business units where business-unit managers play a major product role, integrate product management and design into the business units.
condition: the company is large with centralized engineering and decentralized business units

statement: Organizational structure matters less than the people and their skills; any structure can succeed if you develop the product team's skills and demonstrate their value across the company.
Tell people what to do, not how to do it, so they can apply their own ingenuity to the solution.

Customers and users tend to tell you how the product should work rather than what it should do; focus on the problem to be solved, because customers cannot design the solution and do not know what is possible.
The product manager should tell designers and engineers what the product must do, not how to design or build it, giving them the latitude to find solutions customers will love.
Designers are most valuable early, when the team is understanding the market and forming the solution, not pulled in as needed after the spec is complete.
Seek out the smartest people across the company as sources of product ideas, because they can be hidden anywhere, including engineering, sales, support, the executive team, or the board.
Great ideas more often come from others than from yourself, so recognizing a great idea and making it real matters more than being its originator; do not let ego limit your sources of ideas.

Find hidden product minds by asking people at all levels who the great minds are, managing by wandering around, listening in meetings, keeping your door open, sharing the problems you struggle with, and spending time with people at all levels.
Measure and plan for churn, the rework and plan changes that consume time; expect some churn, track how much time goes to forward progress, and schedule for it.
Adapt your communication style and frequency to your manager's preference, even when it differs from your own.
Hold the real meeting before the official meeting by pre-briefing key influencers and stakeholders individually, so the group meeting is quick and free of surprises.
Bring managers recommendations, ideally with alternatives and rationale, rather than merely stating the problem.
Use your manager as a resource to get access and support you cannot obtain yourself.
Do your homework and understand the issues thoroughly before presenting to managers, who can quickly spot holes in thinking.
Keep emails to managers short and to the point, shorter the more senior the recipient, offering additional material rather than forcing it on them.
Make decisions and recommendations from data and facts rather than opinions.
Evangelize the product across the organization, because effective evangelism makes cooperation with other groups much easier.
Managers value low-maintenance employees, so be thoughtful with your manager's time and find a mentor outside your direct management chain rather than using your manager as one.
Product opportunities exist in every market, even mature ones, because what is technically possible is always changing.
The product manager must be able to quickly evaluate opportunities to decide which are worth pursuing and which should be rejected.
Do not decide whether to build a product by intuition or because a large customer offers to fund a special.

Market Requirements Documents, like Product Requirements Documents, often take too long, go unread, and fail to answer the key questions, yet jumping straight into building with no assessment is also wrong; look before you leap in a quick, lightweight way.
Do a lightweight product opportunity assessment to either shelve poor opportunities or focus the team on good ones and define what success requires.

A product opportunity assessment should answer ten questions: the problem or value proposition, the target market, the market size, how success is measured, the competitive alternatives, why you are best suited, why now, the go-to-market strategy, the critical success factors, and the go or no-go recommendation.
The opportunity assessment must address only the problem to be solved, not the particular solution.
Do not conflate the problem with a single solution, because abandoning a good opportunity when one solution fails is throwing the baby out with the bathwater.

The hardest opportunity-assessment question is usually the value proposition, stating the exact problem crisply, even though it sounds easiest, because most product managers answer with a list of features instead.
Size an opportunity conservatively and remember that not every opportunity needs to be a billion-dollar market.
Present the opportunity-assessment results to senior management and make a clear go or no-go decision before proceeding.

Choosing the right set of products to pursue is among the most important decisions a company makes, and rejecting bad ideas early, before significant time and money is lost, is as important as pursuing the good ones.
Even when the CEO mandates a product, still do a quick opportunity assessment, because you will be far better informed and may even change the CEO's opinion.
condition: the product has been mandated from above

statement: Treat all projects, whether new products or enhancements, as product investments and invest in the best opportunities rather than trying to hit a fixed new-versus-existing ratio.

Often the biggest return comes from improving existing under-performing products, such as raising a low conversion rate, and these opportunities are frequently the most straightforward to solve with prototyping and user testing.
Improving a product's usability can significantly cut customer-service costs and, more importantly, raise customer satisfaction and Net Promoter Score.

Companies often wrongly assume a product is already as good as it can be and that further investment will not help, when usually the product is simply weak and under-invested in design and user experience.
Building a new product instead of improving a weak one, without changing how the product is produced, just yields another under-performing product.

Product managers, especially those from a technical background, usually understand only shallowly how their product makes money, so learn the economics: the revenue model, total costs, cost of acquiring each customer, customer lifetime value, and the return the product generates.
Make a friend in the finance department, who can help you understand your product's economics, learn more about your customers, and build the business case.
Software projects have two distinct stages: product discovery, which figures out what to build, and execution, which builds the product right.

When engineering begins building, the product manager must shift from a discovery mindset to an execution mindset, keeping everyone focused and resolving issues immediately, or the product manager becomes the source of churn and delay.
Talking to users, building prototypes, and testing are worthless if you do not change course based on what you learn.

Keep two versions of the product going in parallel: as one release enters execution, start discovery for the next, so new requirements are explored in the next release's discovery rather than disrupting the current build.
exception: this parallel work detracts from execution of the current release

statement: Product discovery cannot be reliably scheduled as a sequential, predictable phase, because product invention is fundamentally a creative process, more art than science.

Product discovery has two goals: discover whether real users want the product by validating the market opportunity, and discover a solution that is valuable, usable, and feasible by validating it with customers and engineers.
Market discovery is usually not the hard part; discovering the solution is often the challenge, and some worthwhile problems are simply hard.

Most companies run discovery anyway, but with the full engineering team over full release cycles using live customers as unwitting test subjects, which is why it typically takes three or more releases over one to two years to reach something profitable.

Startups especially must run a faster product-discovery process before scaling engineering, using the engineers they already have to participate in discovery, because most lack the funding to spend two years before gaining traction.
condition: the company is a startup

statement: Help management understand discovery by consistently emphasizing your obligation to ensure engineering builds something valuable and usable, and by enlisting engineers to help discover the solution.
Define a set of product principles, a declaration of the team's beliefs and intentions, as a complement to product strategy that speeds discovery and aligns the team.
Product principles are not a list of features and are not tied to a single product version; they align with a product-line strategy or a startup's mission.
Prioritize your product principles, because when principles conflict, such as ease of use versus security, what matters is which one takes precedence.
Avoid two common product-principle mistakes: stating principles so generic they are useless, and confusing product principles with design principles.
Because the product team does not report to the product manager and the manager has little power to coerce, the product manager must persuade the team rather than dictate to it.

Escalating a deadlocked product decision to a senior manager is a bad outcome; you want the debate but everyone on board at the end, because a forced call from above breeds resentment and the product suffers most.
Constructive debate and argument is an essential ingredient of a great product, and the discovery process cannot be made painless.
To make a product decision well, first frame it and get everyone aligned on the exact problem, the specific persona, the goals, and the relative priority of each goal.
Most strong disagreement within a product team is not about the facts but about differing interpretations or weightings of the goals and priorities.
Take prioritization seriously by getting the team to agree on a specific ordering of goals from most to least important, rather than vague buckets like critical and very important.
Be completely transparent in your decision-making process and reasoning, so every team member can see the goals, their priority, how each option was assessed, and how the decision was reached.
Every product company needs a mechanism to bring key stakeholders and decision-makers together to make timely, informed product decisions, and a product council is an effective one.
The product council sets strategic product direction, allocates product resources and investments, and oversees product efforts, without designing products or setting the company's business strategy.
The product council should give management visibility and oversight without micromanaging or designing the products, which would disempower the team.
Keep the product council cross-functional but small, about ten members or fewer, with clear representation so that absent stakeholders know who represents their views.

Review each product effort at four milestones: select the opportunities to investigate, issue a go or no-go to begin discovering a solution after the opportunity assessment, issue a go or no-go to begin engineering after prototypes and user testing and cost estimates, and issue a go or no-go to launch after the final product, QA, and launch plans.
The product council is not a design session; if there are product issues, the team fixes them and returns, and minor updates should use an expedited process rather than the council.

Give a preliminary cost estimate at opportunity-assessment time and a detailed, high-confidence estimate with the final product spec, because management needs cost information early while engineering cannot estimate accurately until the solution is defined.
At opportunity-assessment time, limit cost estimates to small, medium, or large, because there is no solution yet and anything more precise is unfair to engineering.
condition: the estimate is made at opportunity-assessment time before a solution exists

statement: Include an engineer during solution definition to evaluate options and estimate the costs of alternatives, so the product can be adjusted before the team commits.
Having a solid set of reference customers at launch dramatically reduces the perceived risk for prospects and makes sales and marketing far easier.

Launching with no reference customers is a red flag that usually means the product is bad or not ready, and having only one or a few references suggests you have built a special or custom solution that will not be generally useful.

Use a charter user program to gain deep customer insight and secure reference customers, aiming to end with at least six happy, live, referenceable customers from the target market, which usually means starting with about eight to ten.
Charter users must not pay in advance, because prepayment turns the relationship into custom development; take their money only after you deliver a product they love.
Keep the charter user program to about ten customers or fewer, because you cannot work closely enough with more than that.
If you struggle to recruit charter users, it is a strong sign the problem is not important enough and the product will be hard to sell, which is an early reality check.
Ensure charter users come from your true target market rather than just early adopters, or you will build a product that only early adopters want.

Treat charter users as development partners and colleagues, be clear that you are building a general product rather than a custom solution, and release to them before the general release so they are live and happy references at launch.

If your company forbids the product manager from talking to users, try hard to change the policy, and if you cannot, leave, because you cannot build products users love without deep, direct understanding of those users.
The product manager should personally attend every user interview, site visit, usability test, and charter-user meeting that pertains to the product.

Surveys, focus-group reports, and second-hand summaries are useful inputs but are no substitute for the product manager's direct interaction with users, because real insight comes from digging into users' underlying needs rather than surface-level dialog.

Take advantage of market-research tools while understanding what each can and cannot answer, because some teams miss out by ignoring them and others go astray by using them to answer questions the tools cannot address.
Customer surveys are cheap and valuable, but writing unbiased survey questions is an art, and survey data is one input rather than the answer itself.
Instrument your product and put site analytics in place early, then continually watch, learn, and adjust.
There is no substitute for site visits that observe users in their native environment, though you must pick them carefully because of cost and time.
Recognize that there is no single user, and deeply understand the major user types, both current and future, using personas.
Do not write off competitors as clueless, because every product does some things well; learn from competitors' successes and mistakes.
Market research does not answer the fundamental question of what product to build, and steering your product with market research puts you in trouble.
No winning product is created by market research; winning products come from a deep understanding of user needs combined with an equally deep understanding of what is just now possible.
Asking customers what they want yields at best incremental improvements or a random collection of band-aid features, not the dramatically better solution you are seeking.
Market research and talking to existing customers is valuable for refining an existing product, not for conceiving a new one.
Focus groups can put you in front of target users but will not reveal great products, because customers do not know what is possible and cannot envision a solution they have not seen.

Focus-group dynamics let the most vocal attendees skew the input, and useful product feedback requires customers to see and interact with the product, which is usually not possible at focus-group stage.
If you must run focus groups, the product manager should attend every one, delegating logistics and facilitation but never the interpretation and analysis of the data.
condition: the team decides it must run focus groups

statement: Product management is fundamentally about choices, and while you will never get them all right, you must get most of them right for the product to succeed.
Use personas, which are archetype descriptions of plausible users capturing their behaviors, attitudes, and goals, to make hard product decisions.
The product manager must be deeply involved in creating and prioritizing personas and the underlying user interviews rather than delegating the task, and it should be done as early as possible.
Personas help you prioritize by deciding who a release is for and, just as importantly, who it is not for, because trying to please everyone ends up pleasing no one.
Focus each release on a single primary persona; the release can still be valuable and usable to others, but the goal is to do a great job for one type of target user.
Do not build personas from assumptions and stereotypes; verify them with real users, because creating a persona is not a substitute for talking to and testing with real target users.
For prototype testing, recruit a range of users rather than only the primary persona, because real usage will not be limited to that persona.
condition: the activity is prototype testing

statement: Most paper specs take too long to write, are seldom read, lack necessary detail, and dangerously create a false impression that everything is proceeding fine.

A good product spec must describe the full user experience including interaction and visual design, accurately represent software behavior, serve all its consumers such as engineering, QA, support, marketing, operations, sales, and executives, and have a single master representation.
The high-fidelity prototype is the best form of product spec, because words and pictures cannot adequately represent software behavior.
Prototype virtually everything, all screens and major use cases, because the benefit of a high-fidelity representation the whole team can interact with dwarfs the incremental cost.
It is fine for a prototype to simulate backend processing and data, as long as the user experience is plausible.

Supplement the prototype with the material it cannot represent, such as business logic, release and quality requirements, and key use cases, kept in a single shared place like a wiki so the team always finds the latest answers.

The decisive advantage of a high-fidelity prototype over a paper spec is that it can be tested with real users for usability and value, and you do not have a spec worth giving engineering until the prototype passes both tests.

Specifying via a tested high-fidelity prototype typically reduces total time to market, because a poor untested spec pushes the hard questions into engineering, causing churn or bad assumptions and rework.
Requirements and user experience design are intertwined and should be done together, not handed off in a waterfall from a product manager writing requirements to designers doing design.
Do not do user experience design and implementation in parallel; the user experience design must be completed before implementation begins.
exception: the engineering team has substantial backend infrastructure work that can proceed while the user experience is being defined

statement: Once implementation begins, fundamental user-experience changes become much harder for technical, psychological, and practical reasons, so design changes must happen before then.
User experience design requires trying many ideas early and often, dozens in days, so waiting for a beta or a two-to-four-week sprint to test an idea is an order of magnitude too slow.
Prototype software must be truly disposable and changeable in hours, which is fundamentally different from production software, so do not treat a beta or sprint output as the prototype.
A user experience often cannot be designed in pieces and must make holistic sense to the user at each release, even though implementation can be broken into iterations.
For Agile teams, use a sprint-zero concept to keep the product manager and designers a step or two ahead of engineers, designing in the smallest increments possible.
condition: the team uses Agile methods

statement: Even when doing requirements and design before implementation, have someone from engineering review the design from the start to assess feasibility and cost.
Produce a high-fidelity prototype with the minimal functionality needed to meet the business objectives, in order to minimize implementation time and user complexity.

Have an architect or lead engineer participate from the start of design so trade-offs of what is in and out are made collaboratively, and by the time the prototype is ready engineering has a detailed, committable estimate.

Validate the minimal prototype with real target users before committing the full team, because believing the definition is good is not enough; you must test it just as you would test code before shipping.
Once you have identified and validated the minimal product, you cannot later cut more features and assume it still works, because if you could, you had not really found the minimal product.
When a feature takes longer to build than estimated, respond with a schedule slip rather than a feature cut, because the cutting was already done when the minimal product was defined.
condition: a feature runs longer than its estimate after the minimal product was already defined

statement: Once engineering is underway, do not keep adding requirements, because most spec-change requests stem from not thinking the requirements through, which a high-fidelity prototype surfaces earlier.
Deliver the final spec as a single whole product with the priority tags removed, making clear it describes one complete product.
Product validation means gathering evidence that the spec describes a successful product without actually building and deploying it, which effective prototypes and simulations now make inexpensive.
A common and costly mistake is having far more confidence in the product spec than warranted and planning to fix it after beta feedback, because beta is far too late for major changes.
Perform three types of validation before handing a final spec to engineering: feasibility, usability, and value.

For feasibility testing, have engineers and architects investigate whether the product is buildable within the available technology, time, and funds, and surface insurmountable obstacles early rather than after time and money are lost.

Usability testing often uncovers missing product requirements and reveals requirements that are less necessary than originally thought, so plan on multiple iterations before reaching a successful user experience.
There is no substitute for putting the prototype in front of real people from the target customer base.

Value testing determines whether users actually find the product valuable and want it, which is distinct from usability testing of whether they can use it, and it can be combined with usability testing using the same prototypes.
The high-fidelity versus low-fidelity prototype debate is now moot, because high-fidelity prototypes are inexpensive and yield much higher-quality feedback.
Validate your ideas before building, because surprises are inevitable and far cheaper to discover early, and once engineering begins a special inertia sets in that makes significant change costly.
Testing your ideas with real users is arguably the single most important activity in the product manager's job.
You do not need a professional usability team, a lab, or a big budget to test, because you can do useful testing yourself and still identify the serious issues.

Recruit test subjects from a range of sources such as charter users, trade shows, online ads, a cautious friends-and-family network, user email lists, and on-site volunteers, and always screen them to avoid a sample skewed toward early adopters.
Give scheduled test subjects a personal phone call the day before to cut the high no-show rate, which can reach thirty percent, down to five to ten percent, because email does not work as well.
Define the tasks to test in advance, concentrating on the primary tasks users perform most often.

Use your one-time first-impression opportunity with each user to learn how they think about the problem today before seeing your product, and whether they can tell from your landing page what you do and its value, before jumping into tasks.
After the tasks, interview the user about how they solve this problem today and how much better yours is, and ask the Net Promoter Score question to gauge value.
Structure value questions on a numeric scale, such as zero to ten or willingness to pay, so you can track whether average perceived value rises or falls as you change the prototype.
You do not need a complete prototype to start testing; test the main tasks, and at dead ends ask the user what they would expect to happen.
You do not need a formal lab, since even a coffee-shop table works and can make users more candid, and the customer's own office also works well.
Remote testing is useful but not a substitute for face-to-face testing, where you can read the user's eyes and body language.
The product manager must attend every single test and not delegate it, because first-hand observation of hesitations and confusion yields insights that a proctor's summary misses.
Good product managers and designers can test their own product objectively, because they expect to get it wrong initially and know that learning from tests is the fastest path to a great product.
Ideally have one person administer the test and another take notes, so you can debrief afterward and confirm you both saw the same things.
Get to the prototype fast, because chatting beforehand gives away clues and taints the first impression; if five minutes pass without the user starting, you are talking too much.
Tell the subject that this is just a prototype, that they will not hurt your feelings, and that you are testing the prototype and not them, because only the prototype can pass or fail.

Keep users in use mode rather than critique mode, because what matters is whether they can do the tasks and value the product, not their opinions on aesthetics; watch what they do more than what they say.
Learn to keep quiet during testing by suppressing the urge to help, getting comfortable with silence, and avoiding leading the witness.
Note three outcomes per task: the user got through with no problem, struggled but eventually succeeded, or gave up, where a true give-up is when the user would leave for a competitor.
Act like a parrot by narrating or playing back the user's own words and questions instead of giving leading answers, to avoid leading and to gather their intent.
Fundamentally you are finding where the model your software presents is inconsistent with how users think about the problem, and these counterintuitive spots are usually easy to fix and a big win.

You can respond to feedback and fix a problem after only two or three users rather than freezing a full round, and you are done when about six consecutive users understand, value, and complete the key tasks.

If you cannot get people interested in the problem or make the product clear and usable, shelving the idea is a success, because it saves the cost of building and shipping a losing product and the opportunity cost of what engineering could build instead.
Product improvement is not about adding features; most product organizations are feature factories, and added features often make the situation worse rather than better.
Improve an existing product by relentlessly pursuing the metrics that matter, such as raising a completion rate, and justify any new feature by how much it moves those metrics.
Gain improvement insight from site analytics and testing on real users, plus Net Promoter Score tracking, customer service, the sales force, and win/loss analysis, and act on what the data shows.
When improving a product, do not chase subjective feedback, customer-specific requirements, surveys, or focus groups; focus on what actually moves the metrics by studying live use.

Avoid user abuse, meaning releasing changes users do not appreciate, because as a rule users dislike change even when they clamor for new functionality, since learning a new way to do something carries a cost.
The solution to user abuse is not to prevent change but to be smart about how you deploy it.

Deploy changes gently: communicate them in advance while knowing many users will not read, redouble QA whenever reliability, scale, or performance is in doubt to avoid rollbacks, and contain risk for significant changes through parallel or incremental opt-in deployment.
Large-scale consumer Internet services must weigh community impact in everything they do, because in the Internet era a bad release that is not corrected quickly triggers serious community backlash.
condition: the product is a large-scale consumer Internet service

statement: For gentle deployment, let users opt in to try a new version and make it their default when they like it, then default it with an opt-out period, giving notice before discontinuing the old version, and for large communities expect this to take months.
condition: the product has a large user community and a significant change

statement: Other gentle-deployment approaches are regional rollout, trying the new version in a limited area before expanding, and incremental deployment, introducing changes in bite-size pieces over time.
Goodwill from users who like your product is a finite reserve, so do not waste it through user abuse; save it for when you really need it.
Do not confuse product launch with success, and keep resources on the product after launch, because that is when the opportunity to learn and correct is greatest.
Schedule a rapid-response phase that begins at launch and lasts a few days to a week to respond quickly to what you learn once live, because no phase offers a better return on investment.

Expect issues that can only be discovered once the product is live, even after thorough prototyping, validation, and QA, so the question is not whether issues will arise but how quickly you address them.
Define a clear, prioritized set of business metrics before launch, and decide in advance which results count as success and which count as a problem.

For enterprise software, send product-team members to the customer site to be present during installation and go-live, because issues get identified and resolved much faster when a team member owns being there until the customer is live.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Once issues are identified, the cross-functional product team should meet at least daily, prioritize the issues, and respond quickly, for example with hot fixes or explanatory content.

In Agile, the product manager is the product owner representing the customer and must be deeply involved, driving the backlog and answering questions, because Agile does not make the product manager's job easier.
condition: the team uses Agile methods

statement: Agile is not an excuse for a lack of product planning; you still need to know your goals and how you will measure success, though the planning horizon can be shorter and rolling using a lightweight opportunity assessment.
condition: the team uses Agile methods

statement: In Agile, the product manager and designers should stay one or two sprints ahead of the team so difficult features are validated before implementation, and designers must not do their design work during the sprint.
condition: the team uses Agile methods

statement: Break design work into small, independent chunks but not too small, keeping the emphasis on the minimal product possible.
condition: the team uses Agile methods

statement: Reassemble sprint results in a staging area until there is enough functionality to warrant a release, rather than launching every sprint, because constant change upsets customers.
condition: the team uses Agile methods in a product-software environment

statement: The product manager and interaction designer should attend every daily standup, treating it as the beginning of the communication process rather than the end.
condition: the team uses Agile methods

statement: Demo the current state of the product and the next sprint's prototype at the end of each sprint, to validate the team's work and keep evangelism going.
condition: the team uses Agile methods

statement: Get Agile training for the whole team and hire a transition consultant with proven product-software experience who understands the difference from IT or custom software.
condition: the team is adopting Agile methods

statement: Do not treat early sprints as the working prototype in product software, because a sprint is too long to test an idea that is likely wrong, engineering time is too valuable to spend on discovery, and changing direction after committing to an architecture is hard.

Agile methods originated in the custom-software world, which is why many Agile resources omit product managers and user experience designers, so adapt Agile for product software and hire transition help that understands the difference.
Agile's assumption that implementations can be cheaply re-factored or re-architected is naive for large-scale product software such as consumer Internet services supporting millions of users.
condition: the system is large-scale product software

statement: Waterfall's phased development with phase-gate reviews persists mainly because management values its perceived predictability and the reassurance of thorough documents, even though you cannot execute paper to test whether that confidence is justified.

Waterfall's most costly flaw is that validation occurs too late, because there is no working software until near the end, so there is little visibility into whether the product is useful until after most of the investment is made.

In a waterfall process, the product manager must prototype and test the product with real users before the expensive design and implementation phases, and must resolve major technical-feasibility risks first.
condition: the team uses a waterfall process

statement: In waterfall, changes are costly and disruptive, so when weighing whether to defer a change, include the cost of the follow-on release, since it is often cheaper to course-correct sooner than later.
condition: the team uses a waterfall process

statement: Waterfall assumes people can fully anticipate the issues and understand the requirements up front, which is realistic only for very small projects and rarely true for product software.
The common startup model of taking seed funding and immediately hiring engineers to build in stealth while the founder figures out requirements on the fly wastes money and often fails.

A startup should line up three functions, product management, interaction design, and prototyping, and run rapid product discovery, building a high-fidelity prototype of the eventual experience and validating it with real target users before hiring an engineering team.
condition: the company is a startup or a new product effort

statement: Rapid startup discovery normally produces dozens of prototype versions evolving daily over a few weeks to a few months, ending with a validated product, a living-spec prototype, and clear understanding of what is needed.
condition: the company is a startup

statement: Figure out the right product before burning through seed funding, because everything starts with the right product, and this discovery-first model applies to large companies too, which can afford the iterations startups often cannot.
Innovation can happen in large companies, not only in startups, even though it is harder there.
As organizations grow they become more conservative and risk-averse, because they have more to lose and get good at protecting what they have.
The two biggest factors in your ability to innovate in a large company are the corporate culture and your manager.
condition: the company is large

statement: The best product ideas often come from the bottom up rather than from executive strategy, and a twenty-percent rule that gives people time for self-chosen projects lets many ideas be tried with ownership-driven passion; apply it to product managers and designers, not only engineers.

Skunk works, meaning pursuing an idea under the radar and proving it before asking permission, works because once an idea is proven it is remarkably easy to get funded, and it is easier to beg forgiveness than to ask permission in large companies.
condition: the company is large and bureaucratic

statement: Innovate through observation by watching real target users, not early adopters and not your own people, struggle with your product or a competitor's to spot patterns of frustration and opportunity.
Innovation is rarely about solving an entirely new problem; more often it is solving an existing problem in a new way.
Innovate through user experience design by relaxing technical constraints and considering the ideal experience, eliminating tasks rather than just making them more efficient.
Frustration arises when a product reflects its implementation model instead of the user's conceptual model, so spotting these incongruences reveals opportunities for innovation and improvement.
Acquisition can be a legitimate innovation technique, especially in high-risk areas, letting startups test the waters and acquiring the survivors for their technology and their people.
Large organizations are generally risk-averse because they have more to lose, so you must deal head-on with the mechanisms they use to protect what they have accumulated.
condition: the company is large

statement: Learn how decisions are really made in your organization and who must buy off on them, and do not try to change the culture; embrace it.
condition: the company is large

statement: Build relationships before you need them, across everyone you will depend on to get your product designed, built, and launched.
Show a working prototype rather than a slide proposal, because a proven idea attracts a large company's resources far faster than talking about it.
condition: the company is large

statement: Be willing to do whatever it takes, including stepping in to produce deliverables yourself, when the resources you need are not available.
Pick your battles by fighting only for outcomes that truly matter, fighting for your product rather than against a person, and not backing adversaries into a corner.
Build consensus one-on-one before important decision meetings, because once someone publicly opposes you it is hard for them to switch, and the meeting's real value is public confirmation of support.
Triage meetings ruthlessly and protect time for the work that matters most: product strategy, the roadmap, the current prototype, competitive understanding, and talking to real users.
Share information freely rather than hoarding it, because you gain more by sharing and others will reciprocate.
Put your manager to work by leveraging their relationships and standing, doing your homework, and giving them what they need to make your case.
In a large company, the need to evangelize the product internally never stops.
condition: the company is large

statement: Apple's success rests on three nested principles: the hardware serves the software, the software serves the user experience, and the user experience serves the emotion.
Every hardware technology should exist for a purpose, to enable what the software needs, rather than the software serving the hardware.
Beyond the early adopters, users do not care about the underlying hardware and software technology; they care about the user experience.
Emotion drives consumers to crave, buy, and love a product, so understanding the role of emotion is a decisive product advantage.
Copycats usually copy only the functionality and miss what really matters, which is the user experience and the emotion it evokes.

A special is building exactly what a specific customer or partner demands in exchange for their check, and one of the surest ways to derail a product company is to confuse customer requirements with product requirements.

Specials are dangerous because a product company must serve a broad range of customers and stay nimble, and contractual obligations to one customer's way of doing things slow adaptation while every version must still be built, tested, maintained, and supported.
condition: the company is a commercial product company rather than a custom software shop

statement: To avoid specials, work with the customer to tease out the core underlying problem, since they usually prefer your mainstream product over a custom version, and keep the product general-purpose while allowing tailoring by the customer or a solution-provider partner.
Requirements-management tools rarely help and make it easy to confuse customer requirements with product requirements, institutionalizing bad practice, whereas a simple wiki usually works better.
The next big thing is more often a dramatically better incarnation of something old, done better, faster, or cheaper so that it redefines the category, than an entirely new market.

To win in a mature market, understand your target market and where current products fall short, using usability testing including on competitors' products, and exploit what has newly become possible with technology.
condition: the market is mature

statement: Great product managers combine what is desirable to users with what is just now possible, and product opportunities exist in virtually every market.
Product opportunities never run out, because as long as products frustrate users there is room to do better, what is possible keeps changing, and today's applications become tomorrow's foundations.
People buy and use products largely for emotional reasons, so the best product people ensure their products speak to those emotions.
Enterprise buying is generally driven by fear or greed, while consumer buying is driven by more personal emotions such as belonging, love, greed, or pride.

Apply an emotional lens to your product by identifying and prioritizing the dominant buying emotions, then ask where else users could get that emotional need met, because that is your real competition and it is often an offline alternative.
Different user types bring different emotional needs, so segment the driving emotions by user type.
During prototype testing, after checking usability, probe what emotion drives the user and how well your product meets that emotional need.
Focus product attention on the users' most miserable and frustrating problems, because solving genuine anger and frustration changes behavior and drives the biggest product wins.
High latent customer frustration, such as with telecoms, banks, and airlines, marks the best opportunities for innovation.

Early adopters, the Irrationals, feel the general population's emotions more intensely and will spend irrationally to address them, and they teach you the true value of your product and carry it across the chasm.
Technology enthusiasts, the Lovers, buy for the technology itself and mislead product managers because they do not buy for the reasons the mainstream will, so do not confuse Irrationals with Lovers.

The deeper the human need you tap, toward the base of Maslow's hierarchy, the stronger the driving emotion and the better positioned your product, whereas a product without a strong driving emotion faces a huge chasm to cross.
Emotional user groups are not demographics, so identify the core emotions for each product rather than assuming a demographic profile.
Interaction design and visual design are different disciplines requiring different skills, so you need both on the team to deliver a user experience that is both usable and appealing.
Do not assume that one hired designer can do both interaction and visual design, because most cannot.

Visual design is not superficial fluff; it plays a direct role in creating the emotion that inspires a product, and the same functionality shown as wireframes versus with good visual design produces dramatically different responses.
For consumer Internet services, usability is paramount and performance is part of usability, because a slow-loading page reads as broken and drives users away.
condition: the product is a consumer Internet service

statement: Segment your users into the most important personas and evaluate how each persona values and responds to every feature.

Build for scalability continuously from day one, allocating a significant ongoing share of engineering and operations resources, about twenty percent, to scaling rather than waiting until everything breaks.
condition: the product is a large-scale service

statement: Design in high availability from the start, just as with scalability, because a consumer Internet service must run at all times.
condition: the product is a consumer Internet service

statement: Design and build the product to minimize customer-support costs, while remembering that the goal is a great customer experience, not merely controlling support costs.
condition: the product is a consumer service

statement: Put privacy and data-protection safeguards in place early to protect sensitive customer data, including protecting that data from your own employees.
Facilitate viral marketing by building in ways for happy users to invite others, because word-of-mouth is the most powerful and cost-effective form of marketing.
Design for localization from the start, because it is far cheaper and faster than rewriting a single-country product for another market later.
Treat community management as a top priority from the CEO down by engaging, appreciating, and learning from your user community, because for consumer services the community can make or break you.
condition: the product is a consumer Internet service

statement: Good product management can substantially improve enterprise software, a space where good products are rarer than in any other.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Enterprise usability is badly neglected because the people who use the software often are not the ones who buy it, so invest in interaction design, visual design, and usability testing to differentiate.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Enterprise products must actually work as promised, because too many ship with serious defects that require heavy customization and workarounds.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Avoid specials in enterprise software, because you cannot get product requirements by agreeing to a customer's demanded feature list, and doing so turns you into a custom shop with no generally useful product.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Meet with and listen to many customers to determine real requirements, but do not expect any single customer to dictate them, and use a charter program aiming for at least six live, happy reference customers at release.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Design the product around the needs of the sales and distribution channel, providing value all along the chain, for example not cutting out system integrators or overwhelming value-added resellers.
condition: the product is sold through a sales or distribution channel

statement: Distinguish the customer who buys from the users who use, because enterprise products designed only around the buyer's needs miss the several other user types such as end-users, administrators, and management.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Make enterprise product installation simple and robust rather than dependent on a dedicated administrator performing days of custom setup, because reliance on a single administrator is fragile when that person leaves or is overloaded.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Much enterprise professional-services cost stems from poor product design, and vendors can do much to make their products easier to configure, customize, and integrate.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Invest in making enterprise software updates and upgrades easy and well-tested, because customers do not want to spend their resources on painful upgrades or complex data migration.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Because the Internet has changed how customers research and evaluate software, make your product easy to try and buy rather than relying on sales-rep relationships.
condition: the product is enterprise software

statement: Software earns the status of a product only when people pay for it, it works across multiple customer installations rather than being a special, the channel can sell it, the company stands behind it, and customers know how to install and configure it.

A solutions product additionally solves a business-level problem, often for specific industry verticals, through pre-integrated components, speaking to the business need rather than the underlying technology.
Customers care much less about the underlying technology than about whether you solve their business problem.
exception: the customers are early adopters who value the technology itself

statement: A platform serves three distinct constituencies, the application providers, the developers, and the end-users, and you cannot succeed as a platform without meeting the key needs of all three.
condition: the product is a platform

statement: Do not call something a platform unless it is programmable through an API and has multiple commercial products or services built on it.
The biggest platform mistake is optimizing for developers over end-users; prioritize the end-user, because the delivered application is what matters most.
condition: the product is a platform

statement: Platforms are high-leverage but hard, and done well a platform creates a thriving ecosystem in which the provider and its application partners succeed together.
condition: the product is a platform

statement: Do not cobble together a fake solution from components or field scripts, because customers can easily tell a true solutions product from a fake once a competitor offers the real thing.
If a product team does only one thing, it should be direct, intense interaction with real users and customers, because that one practice ensures several other things get done right.

A strong product manager continually works through a worry list, asking whether the product is compelling to the target customer, as easy to use as possible, able to beat the competition, truly differentiated, going to actually work, a whole product consistent with how it is sold, and worth its price.
You should be able to explain your product's differentiation to a company executive in two minutes, a smart customer in one minute, and an industry analyst in thirty seconds.
Judge your product against the competition that will exist at the time you ship, not today's competition.
Discovery (the work of deciding what to build) and delivery (the work of building and shipping) are fundamentally different kinds of work, even though they can overlap.
Many companies over-emphasize delivery (shipping on time and on budget) while under-investing in discovery, so they fail to assess whether they built the right thing.
Teams should correct the delivery-over-discovery imbalance by deliberately investing in discovery work.
Discovery is not a one-time upfront activity; a digital product is never done and should keep evolving as the market, customer needs, and technology change.
Continuous discovery is defined as, at minimum, weekly touchpoints with customers, by the team building the product, conducting small research activities, in pursuit of a desired outcome.
If a team only engages customers monthly, it makes a month's worth of product decisions without customer input.
Teams should infuse their daily product decisions with as much customer input as possible.

Most successful digital products are built by a cross-functional product trio: a product manager (business viability), a designer (usability and interaction), and a software engineer (technical feasibility and reliability).
The product trio should make product decisions together, leveraging each role's expertise, rather than handing off deliverables through stage gates.
Including more people in each decision improves buy-in and inclusiveness but slows the decision, so teams must balance speed of decision-making against inclusiveness.
condition: when adding members beyond the core trio to a decision

statement: Adopting continuous discovery habits requires changing mindset, not only tactics; tools and frameworks alone will not deliver product success.
An outcome-oriented mindset defines success as the value the shipped code creates for customers and the business (the outcome), not the code or features shipped (the output).
A customer-centric mindset elevates customer needs to be on par with business needs, treating creating customer value as a peer goal to creating business value.
A visual mindset externalizes thinking by drawing and mapping what the team knows, tapping the human capacity for spatial reasoning.
An experimental mindset means thinking like a scientist: identifying assumptions and gathering evidence to test them.
A continuous mindset infuses discovery throughout the development process rather than treating it as something done only at the start of a project.

The Agile manifesto advocated shorter delivery cycles with more frequent customer feedback, a sustainable continuous pace, flexibility to adapt to feedback, and simplicity by ruthlessly limiting what is built.
More frequent releases and better instrumentation let teams measure the impact of what they build sooner, revealing when a shipped feature is unused or moves no metric.

Rather than only validating ideas at the end of discovery, teams should co-create with customers from the beginning, combining the team's knowledge of what is technically possible with the customer's knowledge of their own needs and pain points.
Continuous discovery gives a team the confidence to act while remaining prepared to be wrong, balancing action with doubt so the team can start without being blindsided.
An outcome target pursued without a paired customer-centric mindset can incentivize behavior that harms customers, as when Wells Fargo's push to grow accounts per customer led to fraudulent accounts.

How a problem is framed strongly affects how it will be solved; framing an outcome as grow accounts at all costs invites cheating, whereas framing it as create customers who want to open more accounts does not.
A business needs profit to survive, but profit should not come at the cost of serving the customer; serving customer needs is how a company generates profit.
Starting with outcomes rather than outputs is what lays the foundation for product success.

Tasking a product trio with an outcome (rather than dictating outputs) communicates the value the team should create for the business while giving the team latitude to explore the best solutions for the customer.

Customer value cannot be taken for granted when a trio pursues an outcome, because the trio can reach the outcome either by understanding customers and creating customer value or by taking shortcuts that create business value at the customer's expense.
Talking to customers weekly is a good start but not sufficient; those touchpoints must conduct small research in pursuit of a desired outcome, not research for its own sake.
condition: customer touchpoints must be tied to a desired outcome

statement: Finding the best path to a desired outcome is an ill-structured (wicked) problem: it has many possible solutions with no right or wrong answers, only better or worse ones, and much of the work is framing the problem itself.
Good problem-solvers do not settle on a single framing; they try out many framings of an ill-structured problem and explore how each affects the solution space.

Customer needs, pain points, and desires are collectively called opportunities, and the opportunity space spans both problems to solve and desires to satisfy; the opportunity framing is broader and more inclusive than problems to solve.

Two of the most important steps toward a desired outcome are mapping and structuring the opportunity space and then selecting which opportunities to pursue; many trios skip these steps and jump straight from an outcome to generating ideas.

Discovery has an underlying structure: start by defining a clear outcome that scopes discovery, then discover and map the opportunity space, then discover the solutions that address those opportunities and thus drive the outcome.

An opportunity solution tree visually represents the paths to a desired outcome, with the outcome as the root, the opportunity space below it, the solution space below that, and assumption tests at the bottom.

An opportunity solution tree resolves the tension between business and customer needs by filtering the opportunity space to only those customer opportunities that have the potential to drive the business outcome.

People instinctively jump to solve the first problem they hear and fall in love with the first solution, forgetting to question the framing or ask how else the problem might be solved; visualizing options counters this and builds shared understanding across the trio.

A continuous mindset requires delivering customer value every sprint by addressing unmet needs, resolving pain points, and satisfying desires; carving a six-month waterfall project into two-week sprints is neither Agile nor continuous.

An opportunity solution tree lets a team break large, project-sized opportunities into a series of smaller opportunities and focus on solving one opportunity at a time, so that small continuous solutions add up to address the bigger opportunity.

The four villains of decision-making that lead to poor decisions are looking too narrowly at the problem, confirmation bias (seeking only evidence that confirms our beliefs), letting short-term emotions drive the decision, and overconfidence.

Avoid whether-or-not decisions (should we do this or not) and instead adopt a compare-and-contrast mindset, asking which of several options is most important to address now and what else could be built.

Good discovery reduces the chance of failure but does not prevent it; trios must act on what they know today while being prepared to be wrong, balancing confidence in what they know with doubt about it.
Most discovery decisions are reversible, so a team that tests its decisions can course-correct quickly and should move fast rather than succumb to analysis paralysis.
condition: the decision is reversible and can be tested

statement: The best designers evolve the problem space and the solution space together rather than fully defining the problem before designing a solution; exploring solutions teaches more about the problem, and understanding the problem reveals new solutions.

When a tested idea fails, do not simply move to the next idea; reflect on what was misunderstood about the customer and revise the opportunity-space understanding before generating new solutions, or the next attempt is just guessing again.

Do not use organizational roles to sever the problem space from the solution space (for example, product manager owns the problem while designer and engineer own the solution); the product trio should be jointly responsible for both.

When sharing discovery work with stakeholders, show your work: summarize learnings, highlight key decision points and the options considered, and invite feedback; avoid both dumping raw un-synthesized data and sharing only cherry-picked conclusions.
An outcome is a change in human behavior that drives business results.
