Product outcomes are metrics the product team can directly influence, while business outcomes are the metrics that drive the business; teams often must do discovery to identify how a product outcome connects to a business outcome.

Lagging indicators such as 90-day retention make it hard to measure the impact of fast weekly experiment cycles, so teams seek a shorter-term leading indicator, but must check that the chosen short-term metric actually predicts the long-term outcome.
condition: when experiment cycles are faster than the outcome metric's measurement window

statement: Managing by outcomes gives teams the autonomy, responsibility, and ownership to find the best solution and leaves room for doubt, whereas a fixed feature roadmap communicates false certainty about which features are right.
Managing by outcomes is only as effective as the outcomes chosen; the wrong outcomes still produce the wrong results.

Distinguish three types of outcomes: a business outcome measures how well the business is progressing, a product outcome measures how well the product moves the business forward, and a traction metric measures usage of a specific feature or workflow.

Many business outcomes are lagging indicators that measure something after it has happened, which puts a team in react mode; teams should identify leading indicators that predict the direction of the lagging indicator.
Assigning a team a leading indicator is always better than assigning a lagging indicator.

Product trios generally make more progress on a product outcome than on a business outcome, because a product outcome is within the trio's span of control whereas business outcomes usually require coordination across many business functions.
Increase each team's accountability by assigning it a metric relevant to its own span of control; when multiple teams are assigned the same outcome, it is easy to shift blame for lack of progress.
Assigning product outcomes (rather than business outcomes) to product trios increases their sense of responsibility and ownership, because the trio alone is then responsible for driving results.
Assigning a traction metric as a trio's outcome risks painting the team into a corner, because it fixates them on a specific output and removes the latitude to explore alternative solutions.

Assign traction metrics only when optimizing a known solution, not when discovering new solutions; the two appropriate cases are giving a junior trio an optimization challenge to build experience, and handing a mature product's known-critical traction metric to a dedicated optimization team.
exception: the broader discovery questions have already been answered and the intent is optimization, not discovery

statement: Setting a team's outcome should be a two-way negotiation between the product leader and the product trio, not a top-down assignment.

In outcome-setting the product leader brings the across-the-business view and communicates strategic intent by identifying an appropriate product outcome, but should not dictate solutions nor narrow the scope so far that it becomes a traction metric.

In outcome-setting the product trio brings customer and technology knowledge and should communicate how much it can move the metric in the given period (usually a quarter), without being required to commit up front to the solutions it will build.

More ambitious outcomes carry more risk, because hitting them requires bigger bets that typically come with a higher chance of failure; leaders and trios can negotiate ambition against added resources or removed competing backlog work.
A stable product trio focused on the same outcome over time is critical, because every time the team is reshuffled or the outcome is changed the team pays a learning tax getting up to speed.
Teams who participate in setting their own outcomes take more initiative and perform better than colleagues who are not involved in setting their outcomes.
Teams that set specific, challenging goals outperform teams that do not, but only when the team believes it can achieve the goal, is committed to it, and receives continuous feedback on its progress.
condition: the team believes the goal is achievable, is committed to it, and gets continuous feedback

statement: For complex tasks like those product trios face, a specific challenging goal can decrease performance when the team lacks strategies to achieve it; telling teams to do their best, and setting an initial learning goal, outperforms a performance goal until appropriate strategies are found.
condition: the task is complex and the team has not yet identified strategies to achieve the goal

statement: When a product trio faces a new outcome, it should start with a learning goal (discover the opportunities or strategies that might move the metric) before being tasked with a challenging performance goal.
condition: the outcome is new to the team

statement: SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound) performance goals fit trios that already have experience with their product outcome, but are not one-size-fits-all; it is fine to start with a learning goal and work toward a SMART performance goal.

Anti-pattern: pursuing too many outcomes at once spreads a trio too thin, yielding at best incremental progress on some outcomes and rarely big impact on any; most teams have more impact focusing on one outcome at a time.

Anti-pattern: ping-ponging from one outcome to another each quarter forfeits the learning-curve benefit, since it takes time to learn how to impact a new outcome; instead set an outcome and focus on it for a few quarters.

Anti-pattern: setting individual outcomes for each trio member (common when outcomes tie to compensation) pulls the trio in different directions and prevents collaboration; set a single team outcome instead.

Anti-pattern: choosing an output as an outcome; to keep an outcome from being a disguised output, ensure it represents a number and question what impact it will actually have (for example, prefer increase course views that include reviews over increase the number of reviews).

Anti-pattern: focusing on one outcome to the detriment of all else; pair a primary outcome with health metrics (for example, pair customer acquisition with customer satisfaction) so the team drives the outcome without causing detrimental side effects elsewhere.
Because the opportunity space is infinite, a trio should first take inventory of what it already knows by mapping the customer's experience as it exists today before diving in.

Set the scope of an experience map from the desired outcome: scope narrowly for an optimization outcome and more broadly for an open-ended outcome; there is no single right scope, so the team should discuss a scope that allows room to explore while staying focused on the outcome.

To avoid groupthink, each trio member should first develop their own perspective (for example, draw their own experience map) individually before the trio merges them into a shared one, even though duplicating work feels inefficient.
condition: multiple perspectives matter for the decision

statement: Groups tend to perform at the level of their least-capable member, and some members contribute less or hesitate to speak up, so a trio must actively work to counter groupthink to leverage each member's knowledge.

Experience maps should be visual rather than verbal, because drawing externalizes thinking and makes it easier to see gaps, catch what is missing, and correct what is wrong; the goal is to examine thinking, not to make art, so drawing skill does not matter.
When mapping the customer experience, draw it as the customer perceives it (where they get stuck, how they course-correct, where they abandon), not as a screen-by-screen wireflow of your product.
When drawing an experience map, draw the customer's broader experience from the customer's perspective, not a screen-by-screen flow of your own product.

Externalize thinking by drawing (boxes, arrows, stick figures) rather than describing context in words, because language is vague and drawing forces you to be concrete and reveals gaps in your thinking.
Co-create a shared experience map by synthesizing the trio's individual maps together rather than picking the single 'best' drawing to move forward with.

Build a shared experience map by turning individual maps into nodes (moments/actions/events) and links (relationships), combining all nodes, collapsing similar nodes, determining links, and adding context.
When collapsing similar nodes on an experience map, avoid generalizing so much that you lose key detail.
condition: when collapsing similar nodes together

statement: Map the non-happy paths of the customer journey too—where steps are redone, where people give up out of frustration, and where steps loop back—not just the happy path.
Treat the experience map as a first-draft hypothesis of what you think you know about the customer, to be tested in interviews, not as established truth.
Continuously refine and evolve the experience map as a team as you learn, or individual perspectives will diverge even when working from the same source data.
When the trio gets bogged down debating minute details, draw the differences instead of debating them; forcing specifics often reveals hidden agreement or pinpoints exactly where the disagreement is.
The purpose of a customer interview is to discover and explore opportunities (customer needs, pain points, and desires), not to ask customers what you should build.
Customers cannot reliably tell you what they want or need; inventing the solution is the product team's job, not the customer's.
Interview participants struggle to answer direct, factual questions accurately because recalling facts without context is prone to cognitive biases.
When asked direct questions, people report their ideal or perceived behavior and construct coherent but not necessarily true stories, rather than reporting their actual behavior.
To learn about customers' actual behavior, ask them to share specific stories about recent concrete instances rather than asking direct or generalized questions.
Memories about recent specific instances are more reliable than a person's generalizations about their own behavior.
Distinguish research questions (what you are trying to learn) from interview questions (what you actually ask the participant).
Because you interview customers weekly, focus each interview on what you need to learn at this moment rather than trying to ask everything via a multi-page discussion guide.
condition: when interviewing customers on a continuous/weekly cadence

statement: The primary research question in any interview should be: what needs, pain points, and desires matter most to this customer.
Let the participant set the direction of the interview—what matters most to the customer trumps what you need to learn (the golden rule of interviewing).
Translate research questions into story-eliciting interview questions (e.g., 'Tell me about the last time you...') instead of direct questions (e.g., 'What criteria do you use...').

Tailor the scope of the story prompt to what you need to learn: a narrow scope optimizes the existing product, broader questions uncover new opportunities, and the broadest questions can uncover new markets.

Reset the conversational 50/50 back-and-forth norm by telling the participant up front that you want their full story with as many details as possible and that you'll ask for missing details at the end.

Use temporal prompts ('What happened first?', 'What happened next?', 'What happened before that?') and story elements (location, characters, challenges, helpers) to excavate the participant's full story.
When a participant drifts into generalizing about their behavior ('I usually...'), gently guide them back to the specific instance.
When a participant will not cooperate or has no relevant story, capture what value they are willing to share but do not force it; respect what the participant cares about most.
Continuous (weekly) interviewing lowers the cost of a single disappointing interview because you will be interviewing another customer soon.
condition: when interviewing continuously

statement: Synthesize as you go rather than waiting for a stopping point, because continuous interviewing has no clear point at which to stop and synthesize.

Use an interview snapshot—a one-page synthesis per interview—to turn copious notes into actionable insights and to index the customer knowledge you accumulate, because interviews blur together and memory is unreliable.
Make the interview snapshot visual—include a photo of the participant (with permission)—so the team can remember the stories weeks or months later.
exception: when corporate guidelines require anonymized data or the topic is sensitive, skip the photo and use a memory-triggering visual instead

statement: Capture a memorable, verbatim quote from the participant at the top of the snapshot to act as a key that unlocks memory of their specific story; record vivid language in their exact words.
Capture quick facts about the customer (segment and behavioral traits) on the snapshot to situate the interview's stories relative to other customers.
Represent opportunities as customer needs, pain points, or desires—never as solutions or features.

When a participant requests a feature or solution, ask why (e.g., 'If you had that, what would that do for you?') and capture the underlying need instead of the solution, because a need opens up more of the solution space than a specific feature does.
Frame each opportunity using the customer's own words so it is captured from the customer's perspective, not the company's.
Capture interesting insights that are not yet needs, pain points, or desires, because over time insights often turn into opportunities.
Be thorough and capture even behaviors that seem unique to one participant, because an opportunity that seems unique often recurs as a common pattern across several interviews.

Capture each participant's unique story as an experience map (nodes and links) on the interview snapshot, because drawing the story's structure aids memory, understanding, and later pattern-finding across stories.
Interview at least one customer every week; weekly interviewing is foundational to a strong discovery practice.
The opportunity space is never finite or complete and continually evolves, because customer needs change, new products disrupt markets, and competitors change the landscape.
Do not pause interviewing after choosing a target opportunity; if you must change course after having stopped, you will have to ramp up from scratch and delay your next steps.
It is easier to maintain a weekly interviewing habit than to start and stop it, and every week you skip increases the chance you stop interviewing altogether.
Automate the recruiting process so an interview is scheduled each week without manual effort, so the habit survives the weeks when something unexpectedly goes wrong.
Recruit participants while they are using your product or service by integrating a single recruiting question into the product flow.
condition: works best for high-traffic sites; low-traffic services should ask the visitor to schedule an interview, and new products can drive traffic to a landing page via ads

statement: Enlist customer-facing colleagues (sales, account management, customer success, support) to recruit interview participants, using clearly defined triggers and a simple script.
For hard-to-reach customers or small markets, set up a customer advisory board and interview its members in recurring monthly one-on-ones with an ongoing incentive.
condition: when the audience is extremely hard to reach (e.g., doctors, CEOs) or the market is small

statement: Pair advisory-board interviewing with one or two other recruiting methods to avoid designing your product for a small subset of customers that may not reflect the broader market.
Teams dramatically underestimate how much customers want to help; most customers will be eager to help improve a product that solves a real need for them.
The whole product trio should interview together rather than designating one role as the 'voice of the customer,' because that role would then trump all others in team decisions.
The more diverse the interviewing team, the more value you get from each interview, because what each person hears is shaped by their prior knowledge and role.
An interview can be as short as five minutes, so everyone on the team has time to spend a few minutes each week with a customer.
Do not rely on one person to recruit and interview; ensure everyone on the team is well-versed in recruiting and interviewing so the habit survives absences.

Ditch long who/what/why/how discussion guides—they overwhelm participants and yield unreliable data; instead generate research questions and ask one or two story-based interview questions ('Tell me about a specific time when...').
Share what you learn using interview snapshots rather than sending raw pages of notes or full recordings, because colleagues cannot invest the same effort in your discovery work as you do.

Address only the customer opportunities that drive your desired outcome, not every need you hear, because that is how you create business value alongside customer value and keep the product viable long-term.
Because you can never fully satisfy all customer desires, prioritize the opportunities with the biggest impact on your outcome first.
Structure (map) the opportunity space before diving into solutions, because finding the best path to a desired outcome is an ill-structured problem that must be framed before it can be solved.
Expect to restructure the opportunity space repeatedly—reframing, regrouping, re-parenting, and rephrasing opportunities as you keep learning—because structure gets done, undone, and redone.
A flat opportunity backlog is hard to prioritize because opportunities come in different shapes and sizes—some interrelated, some subsets of others.
Use an opportunity solution tree instead of a flat backlog to visualize and manage the complexity of the opportunity space.
In an opportunity solution tree, parent-child links represent subset relationships: a child opportunity is a subset of its parent opportunity.
Sibling opportunities in the tree should each be a subset of the same parent yet be independently addressable—you can address one without addressing another.
Search systematically and deliberately for the highest-impact opportunity, comparing and contrasting options, rather than jumping to the first need you could address.
Thinking in a tree structure lets a team deconstruct a large, intractable opportunity into a series of smaller, more solvable sub-opportunities (children of a parent opportunity).
Break a big opportunity into smaller sub-opportunities and completely solve a smaller one first, delivering value iteratively over time rather than waiting to solve the whole problem.
Every opportunity on the tree must be distinct from every other; when opportunities overlap you cannot work on one at a time and are forced to address them all at once.

Uncover the tree's structure by organizing opportunities around distinct moments in time, derived either from the steps of the experience map or from key moments identified in interview story drawings.
Map each node of the customer experience map to a top-level opportunity on the tree.

When the team lacks a strong understanding of the customer experience, build the experience map first by labeling the key moments across interview story drawings and stitching the most common recurring nodes together.
condition: the team is not starting from a strong understanding of the customer experience

statement: Ensure there is no overlap between the moments in time chosen as top-level branches, because overlap prevents working on one opportunity at a time.

Do not add every opportunity heard to the tree; add one only if it is framed as a customer need, pain point, or desire (not a solution), recurs across more than one interview, and would drive the desired outcome if addressed.
If an opportunity could belong under more than one branch, reframe it to be more specific or split it into multiple opportunities, one for each moment in time in which it occurs.

Reframe an overly broad opportunity into specific ones tied to where the pain surfaced in the customer's story, because specific opportunities are easier to solve and each lives in a single spot on the tree.
Add structure one branch at a time: group similar opportunities as siblings under a shared parent, and merge opportunities that are the same need worded differently into one.
It is acceptable to add a parent opportunity that is implied by its children even though it was never explicitly stated in an interview.
Iterate grouping siblings into mini-trees and clustering their parents under shared parents until every opportunity ladders up to a single top-level opportunity representing a key moment.

Opportunity mapping looks deceptively simple but demands substantial critical thinking; a tree finished in 30 minutes usually reflects too little thought, while churning for hours chasing a perfect tree is the opposite mistake.
The opportunity solution tree is not a one-and-done artifact; revisit and reframe it often as you learn what the opportunities really mean, capturing just enough structure for now.
Anti-pattern: opportunities framed from the company's perspective instead of the customer's; reframe every opportunity in the customer's voice and verify it was actually heard in interviews.

Anti-pattern: vertical opportunities (a parent with a single child chained to a single child) signal either duplicate opportunities worded differently, which should be reframed into one and the rest removed, or missing sibling opportunities, which should be identified and filled in.
Anti-pattern: an opportunity that ladders up to more than one parent is framed too broadly; make it specific by defining one opportunity for each moment in time in which the need occurs.
Anti-pattern: opportunities that represent themes, design guidelines, or sentiment are not specific enough; rewrite them as concrete needs, pains, or desires.

Anti-pattern: solutions in disguise; if there is only one way to address a stated opportunity it is actually a solution request, so uncover the implied opportunity, which should admit more than one potential solution.
Anti-pattern: capturing a feeling (e.g. 'I'm frustrated') as an opportunity; treat the feeling as a signpost and capture its underlying cause instead, because feelings cannot be fixed directly.
The build trap is when an organization measures success by outputs (features shipped) rather than by the outcomes and value those features actually produce.
A solution-first mindset is good at producing output but rarely produces outcomes, because customers do not care about the majority of feature releases.

Product strategy happens in the opportunity space and emerges from the decisions about which outcomes to pursue, which customers to serve, and which opportunities to address, not from prioritizing features in the solution space.
Focus on one target opportunity at a time; spreading effort across many opportunities reverts the team to a waterfall mindset of delivering too much all at once.
Focusing on one opportunity at a time lets the trio explore and compare multiple competing solutions, consistent with the kanban practice of limiting work in progress.

A University of Oulu literature review found that software teams using kanban see increased quality, more consistent delivery, and fewer customer complaints, with limiting work in progress a key component of that success.

Assess top-level parent opportunities by comparing and contrasting the whole set against each other rather than asking 'should we pursue this?' in isolation, because whether-or-not questions invite confirmation bias and ignore opportunity cost.
Once the highest-priority parent branch is chosen, you can ignore all other branches for the rest of the assessment because the highest-impact opportunity lives under that branch.
condition: the opportunity space is well structured

statement: Recurse the compare-and-contrast assessment down through the children of the chosen branch until you reach a target opportunity that has no children (a leaf node), because leaf nodes enable iterative delivery.
Choosing a leaf-node target opportunity does not imply it is easy to address; it only means no contributing sub-opportunities have been identified yet.
Assess a set of opportunities along four lenses: opportunity sizing, market factors, company factors, and customer factors.

Size opportunities only roughly and relatively by comparing a set of siblings on how many customers are affected and how often, distinguishing how-many from how-often, rather than precisely sizing each one.
Prioritize opportunities that are important to customers and where satisfaction with existing solutions is low over opportunities that are less important or already well satisfied.
Do not score opportunities numerically and stack-rank them like features; keep prioritization a messy, subjective, relative comparison of siblings, and accept that there may be no clear winner.

Turning a subjective, ill-structured prioritization into a quantitative math formula falsely implies there is one right answer and stops the team from thinking, so leave room for doubt to enable later course-correction.

Classify a decision as one-way-door (hard to reverse, Bezos's Level 1) and decide slowly, cautiously, and data-driven, versus two-way-door (easy to reverse, Level 2) and decide fast without waiting for perfect data, learning more by acting and observing the consequences.

Choosing a target opportunity is a reversible two-way-door decision: you commit only to exploring it further in discovery for the next days or weeks, not to shipping it, so if you learn it was the wrong choice you simply pick another target.

Studies by Lottie Bullens and colleagues found that when people view a decision as reversible they keep critically evaluating it afterward (noticing their choice's negatives and the alternatives' positives), whereas framing it as irreversible makes them notice only their choice's positives; frame prioritization decisions as reversible to stay open to being wrong and avoid confirmation bias.

Anti-pattern: delaying a decision to gather more data; prevent analysis paralysis by time-boxing the prioritization decision to an hour or two (at most a day or two), deciding on what you know today, and course-correcting later.

Anti-pattern: over-relying on one set of factors at the cost of the others; the four factor sets (opportunity sizing, market, company, and customer factors) are lenses on the same decision and should all be used.
Anti-pattern: working backwards from an expected conclusion, using the lenses to justify a foregone decision rather than to explore; enter the assessment with an open mind.
Your first idea is rarely your best idea; keep the ideation loop open longer to push past obvious first ideas into the realm of more diverse and original ideas.

Creativity is measured by fluency (number of ideas), flexibility (diversity of ideas), and originality (novelty); research shows fluency correlates with both flexibility and originality, so generating more ideas increases their diversity and novelty.
The most original ideas tend to be generated toward the end of an ideation session rather than at the start.

Not every opportunity needs an innovative solution, but for strategic opportunities where you want to differentiate from competitors you should take the time to generate several ideas to uncover the best ones.
condition: the opportunity is a strategic one where you want to differentiate from competitors
exception: routine, non-differentiating workflows such as a forgot-password flow

statement: Osborn's four brainstorming rules are: focus on quantity, defer judgment (separate idea generation from evaluation), welcome unusual ideas, and combine and improve ideas.

Decades of studies comparing brainstorming groups against the same number of individuals ideating alone found that the individuals working alone generated more ideas, more diverse ideas, and more original ideas.

Four factors make group brainstorming underperform individuals: social loafing, group conformity, production blocking, and downward norm setting (the group's output tends toward the lowest-performing member).

Nijstad and colleagues identified an 'illusion of group productivity': brainstorming groups overestimate their performance and report high satisfaction despite lower output, because group sharing reduces cognitive failures (moments a participant is stuck), making the work feel easier.

Korde and Paulus found that alternating individual ideation with group sharing improves the quality of ideas generated in subsequent individual sessions, because exposure to others' ideas inspires new ones while individuals still ideate on their own.
Do not try to ideate in one long block; take frequent breaks, spread idea generation across the day, and experiment with different times of day to find when you are most creative.

Take advantage of incubation, the brain's continued work on a problem after you stop consciously thinking about it, by sleeping on a problem when you are stuck; incubation is especially helpful after hearing other people's ideas.
To get unstuck, draw inspiration from analogous products: start with competitors, then look wider to unrelated industries that solve a problem analogous to your target opportunity.

When stuck, consider what extreme users need (power users, first-time users, people with disabilities, remote or urban locations, different ages) to generate ideas that may end up working for everyone.
Do not be afraid to consider wild ideas even though they are rarely pursued, because they can improve more feasible ideas when solutions are mixed and matched.

Run ideation as: review and align on the target opportunity (distinct, appropriately sized leaf node), generate ideas alone, share ideas across the team, then repeat the alone-then-share cycle until you have 15 to 20 ideas for the target opportunity.
Begin evaluating ideas by removing any that do not solve the target opportunity (partial solutions are acceptable), since idea generation naturally produces some ideas that do not address it.

Dot-vote as a team to narrow many ideas down to three, giving each member three votes and judging only on how well an idea addresses the target opportunity, not on how novel, easy, or impossible it is.
Research shows individuals are better at generating ideas while groups are better at evaluating them, because a group brings a wider breadth of experience to evaluation.
Do not dot-vote all the way down to a single idea; keep three ideas to set up a compare-and-contrast decision that later prototyping and assumption testing will resolve down to one.

After selecting three ideas, confirm every team member is excited about at least one and that each idea has a strong advocate; full consensus on all three is not required, but if that condition is not met, dot-vote again.

Ideation anti-pattern: not including diverse perspectives; ideate with the whole team and consider inviting key stakeholders, because more diversity in the group produces more diverse ideas, but first set the target-opportunity and customer context.

Ideation anti-pattern: generating too many variations of the same idea; deliberately seek categorically different ideas, using analogous products from industries far from your own to surface diverse options.
Ideation anti-pattern: limiting ideation to a single session; spread idea generation over time to exploit the brain's ability to incubate the problem.
Ideation anti-pattern: keeping ideas that do not address the target opportunity; remove them before dot-voting so a shiny but irrelevant idea does not undo the strategic target-opportunity decision.

Teams build the wrong product when they make untested assumptions about what customers want; in the Portland affordable-housing project, the city and developer assumed one- and two-bedroom units would help the most families, but most displaced families had four or more members, so the units went unsold.

Two cognitive biases drive building the wrong product: confirmation bias (seeking and remembering confirming evidence over disconfirming evidence) and escalation of commitment (the more you invest in an idea, the more committed to it you become).

Product teams are especially susceptible to confirmation bias and escalation of commitment because they fall in love with their ideas and must defend them to stakeholders, which further entrenches commitment and produces overconfidence.

To avoid overconfidence, be prepared to be wrong: work with a set of ideas that could each solve the same target opportunity and compare and contrast them, which counters confirmation bias and escalation of commitment.

You cannot build three ideas for the same target opportunity and A/B test them to pick a winner because it takes too long; instead test the ideas quickly through fast iterations that probe their underlying assumptions.

The best product teams complete a dozen or more discovery iterations per week, which is possible only by shifting from testing whole ideas to testing the specific assumptions that must be true for an idea to succeed.
Explicitly enumerate the assumptions behind each idea, then look for both confirming and disconfirming evidence to support or refute each one.

Assumption testing is generally quicker than idea testing, and its faster pace guards against the escalation of commitment because the less time you invest in an idea the less likely you are to fall in love with it.
The biggest barrier to testing assumptions is becoming aware of the assumptions you are making in the first place.

Product trios should examine five categories of assumption behind a solution: desirability (does anyone want it), viability (should the business build it), feasibility (can we build it, technically and organizationally), usability (can customers understand and use it), and ethical (is there potential harm).

A viability assumption holds when a solution creates enough return for the business (typically more revenue than the cost to build, service, and maintain it), except for deliberate loss leaders that must still contribute enough value to another business goal to be worth the effort.
exception: the idea is a deliberate loss leader contributing to another business goal

statement: Every product introduces some potential for harm; a trio need not mitigate every possible harm but should be aware of its product's impact and ask how to reduce the potential harm, an area most teams underdevelop.

Story-map your ideas to align the trio on what each idea actually means and to surface its assumptions, because after ideation ideas are vague concepts and each person interprets them differently, making their private assumptions untestable.
When story mapping an idea, assume the solution already exists and map what end-users do to get value from it, not what it would take to implement it.

Identify the key actors in a story map: every end-user who must interact for anyone to get value, including multiple user types in marketplaces, and the software or interface itself (e.g. a chatbot) when it acts.
Map the specific steps each actor must take for anyone to get value, sequenced horizontally in the order they happen, mapping the successful path (or multiple successful paths sequentially).

You have to make assumptions before you can test them, so story-map the best solution you can based on what you know today as a starting point, and refine it as you test rather than trying to get everything right first.

Walk step by step through the story map to generate assumptions: every expected end-user action yields desirability, usability, and feasibility assumptions, so even a five-step map can produce around twenty assumptions.
Assumptions are not bad; when discovery homework is done most assumptions are true enough and will never be tested, but generating many assumptions raises the likelihood of uncovering the risky ones.

Conduct a pre-mortem to generate assumptions: at the start of the project, imagine it is months in the future, the product launched and completely failed, and list the reasons it failed; each reason exposes an assumption the idea depends on.

A pre-mortem's success hinges on phrasing the outcome as certain (the product did fail, not might fail); Mitchell, Russo, and Pennington found prospective hindsight generated better explanations only when paired with a certain outcome.

Generate assumptions (especially viability) by walking the lines of the opportunity solution tree backward from solution to outcome using starters like 'This solution will address the target opportunity because...' and 'Addressing the opportunity will drive the outcome because...', and when the outcome is a product outcome also connect it to the business outcome; each logical inference is a testable assumption.

Uncover ethical assumptions by asking 'What is the potential harm in offering this solution?', probing data practices (what is collected, whether customers understand its collection and use, third-party sharing) and broader harms such as addiction, exclusion of under-represented users, inequality, loss of anonymity, damaged relationships, and abuse.

Use the front-page-news test to surface ethical assumptions: ask whether a major news outlet running a front-page story that exposed your internal conversations, the data you collected and how you used it, and who benefited would be a good thing, and if not, why not.

You do not need to use every assumption-generation method for every idea every time; choose the methods that shore up your team's specific blind spots, since most teams are biased toward one or two assumption categories and most forget ethical assumptions entirely.

Prioritize assumptions with assumption mapping (David J. Bland): plot each assumption on two dimensions, how much evidence you already have that it is true or false (x-axis) and how important it is to the idea's success (y-axis).

An assumption's importance is set by how hard it is to work around if it turns out to be false: assumptions that are easy to work around are less important, and those that are hard to work around are more important.

Place assumptions relative to each other rather than precisely, and go fast (no more than about ten minutes per idea), because teams do just as well mapping quickly as when they deliberate over every placement.

Start testing with the two or three assumptions in the top-most, right-most corner of the map, the most important assumptions with the weakest evidence (Bland's 'leap of faith' assumptions), rather than testing the entire top-right quadrant.
Story map, generate assumptions, and assumption map separately for each of the three ideas so they can later be compared and contrasted against each other.

Anti-pattern: not generating enough assumptions; assumption generation is a divergent exercise, so aim for as many as you can (often twenty to thirty even for a simple idea), because the mapping exercise can only surface risky assumptions you actually wrote down.

Anti-pattern: phrasing an assumption so that you need it to be false; always phrase assumptions so that you need them to be true (e.g. 'Customers will remember their passwords'), which also makes them easier to test.
Anti-pattern: assumptions that are not specific enough to test (e.g. 'Customers will have time'); make each assumption concrete about who does exactly what in what context.
Anti-pattern: favoring one assumption category at the cost of others; a usable product is not necessarily desirable, so use all five categories to catch your team's blind spots.

Test assumptions drawn from the whole set of ideas rather than one idea at a time, because testing a single idea invites confirmation bias (noticing confirming, missing disconfirming evidence) and the escalation of commitment.
Systematically collect evidence about the assumptions underlying all three ideas so you can compare and contrast them and identify a clear front runner.

Do not rush into experimenting; rushed experiments throw variations at the wall, test the whole idea instead of the leap-of-faith assumption, skip defining success upfront, test the wrong audience, or chase interesting-but-meaningless data, all of which yield ambiguous results.
Before running an assumption test, clearly define what you are trying to learn and what success looks like, or the results will be ambiguous.
Collect data about what people actually do in a specific context, not what they think or say they do in general, to get reliable evidence for an assumption.

A strong assumption test simulates an experience that gives the participant the chance to behave either in accordance with the assumption or not, and that observed behavior is what lets you evaluate the assumption.
Simulate only the minimal right moment needed to test an assumption, no more than necessary, so you can iterate quickly through several assumption tests.

Ideas often share assumptions, so a single assumption test can evaluate a whole set of ideas rather than give a go/no-go on one idea; if a shared assumption core to the target opportunity is false, you can abandon the entire set of ideas, which is part of why assumption testing is faster than idea testing.
Define how you will evaluate the observed behavior by stating what success looks like before running the test: if the assumption is true, what exactly would you expect the participant to do?

Make evaluation criteria specific by defining both how many people you will test with and how many must exhibit the expected behavior (e.g. 'at least 3 of 10 choose sports'), instead of vague words like 'some' that different team members interpret differently.

Define success criteria upfront, before seeing the results, to align the team on how to interpret them and to guard against confirmation bias, which otherwise leads the team to see supporting evidence and miss refuting evidence.

Choosing the specific numbers is a subjective team decision balancing speed of testing against an actionable outcome: test with as few people as possible while still getting enough information for the team to act on the data.

You are not trying to prove an assumption true, because the burden of truth is too high; you are only reducing risk by collecting enough evidence to move the assumption from weak-evidence (right) toward more-known (left) on the assumption map.
When a simulation is less than optimal, adjust the success threshold (lower or raise it) to account for its shortcomings rather than demanding a perfect simulation.
Agree as a team on the smallest assumption test you can design that still produces results the team will feel comfortable acting on.

Start with small tests that yield early signals rather than large-scale experiments (surveys of hundreds, production A/B tests, representative samples), because you should not invest heavy time and effort until you have an early signal that you are on the right track.

Iterate to bigger, more reliable tests only after each prior round shows continued investment is worthwhile; escalate to a next-level experiment (such as a smoke-screen test) when the assumption remains the riskiest and its risk still exceeds what the organization can bear.

Most learning in assumption testing comes from failed tests, because that is when you discover something you thought was true might not be; small tests let you fail sooner, and failing faster lets you move on to the next assumption, idea, or opportunity.
Stop testing an assumption when you have removed enough risk, or when the effort to run the next test is so great that it makes more sense to simply build the idea.

Testing with small numbers produces false negatives (the test fails even though the larger population would exhibit the behavior) and false positives (the test passes even though the assumption is false).

Reduce the risk of false negatives by selecting participants for variation (geographic location, demographics, relevant behavior) instead of a homogeneous group, though variation alone cannot eliminate them without a representative sample and larger numbers.

False negatives are usually not costly: opportunity-level assumptions get corroborated by tests across the whole set of ideas, solution-level assumptions are typically designed around, and a needlessly abandoned idea or opportunity is cheap because ideas and opportunities are abundant.

Triangulate an assumption by using a mix of research methods and multiple data points (e.g. past-behavior questions, a mockup choice, a simulated moment) rather than accepting or rejecting it based on a single data point.

False positives are less risky in practice than they sound because you never make a go/no-go decision from one test; a genuinely faulty idea's false positive is usually caught in the next, bigger round of testing, costing only the effort of that next test rather than the far larger cost of building the wrong solution.

Product teams are not scientists seeking truth; their research findings are not truths but confirming or disconfirming evidence that supports or refutes a point of view, and the goal is to mitigate risk rather than to validate or invalidate anything.
Do just enough research to mitigate the risk that your company cannot bear, and no more, to balance sound methods against the pace needed to get products to customers.

Two tools belong in every product team's toolbox for fast assumption tests: unmoderated user testing (post a stimulus and tasks, participants complete on their own time, you receive videos) and one-question surveys, which cut what used to take weeks of recruiting and scheduling down to a day or two.

For unmoderated testing, recruit thoughtfully: screen for the right audience (e.g. your own subscribers) and for variation, and use tools that let you upload your own participant list when testing with niche audiences.
When asking about past behavior in a survey, ask about specific recent instances (the last week, the last month), not what people do 'in general'.

Avoid asking about future behavior because it yields unreliable data; to test a willingness assumption, simulate the behavior (e.g. ask 'What are your favorite sports teams?' and measure the share who answer versus skip) rather than asking 'Are you willing to tell us?'

You can also test an assumption by mining data already in your own database, but define your evaluation criteria upfront (sample size, threshold, and the rule for classifying a data point) to guard against confirmation bias.
Anti-pattern: overly complex simulations; design first-round tests to be completed in a day or two, or a week at most, to keep your discovery iteration count high.

Anti-pattern: using percentages instead of specific numbers for evaluation criteria; '70%' is ambiguous with small samples and cannot be assumed to hold as sample size grows, so state the actual count and sample size (e.g. 7 of 10).

Anti-pattern: not defining enough evaluation criteria; at minimum define how many people to test with and how many must exhibit the desired behavior, and use multiple measurements for complex actions (e.g. email opens, then clicks, then the target action).

Anti-pattern: testing with the wrong audience; ensure participants actually experience the need, pain point, or desire of the target opportunity, and recruit for variation rather than the easiest-to-reach or most vocal audience.

Anti-pattern: designing for less than the best-case scenario; when testing with small numbers design tests likely to pass with the most-likely audience first, because a failure in the best case is less ambiguous and a pass lets you expand to tougher audiences.

Stop asking customers questions they cannot answer; at AfterCollege, college seniors could not say what job type or location they wanted, so the team switched to questions students could answer (school, field of study, graduation date) and used proprietary behavioral and employer data to recommend jobs.

Build a crude manual approximation of a risky idea to test it before investing in the real technology; AfterCollege hand-crafted saved searches per field of study instead of building a machine-learning matching algorithm.
Start testing a risky idea by diverting a small percentage of real traffic to a working prototype and watching what happens, which AfterCollege got live in a few days.

Evaluate a change across the whole funnel rather than a single step: AfterCollege's new interface raised search starts from 36% to 83%, and although searchers who then viewed and applied dropped slightly, the far larger number of searchers made overall performance better, justifying continued investment.

Measure not only what you need to evaluate your assumption tests but also what you need to measure impact on your desired outcome, because a successful assumption test does not guarantee the idea drives the outcome, and an outcome-focused trio must stay focused on the end goal.
You are never done with discovery; discovery and delivery are not two distinct phases but feed each other continuously, and you cannot have one without the other.

Testing in your production environment is a natural progression of discovery and also where delivery begins; instrument your delivery work so that delivery feeds discovery as well as discovery feeding delivery.

Do not try to measure everything from the start when instrumenting a product; you cannot know the right setup upfront and will waste weeks debating events, naming, and ownership, so start small and experiment your way to the best instrumentation.
Instrument first exactly what you need to evaluate this week's assumption tests, measuring only what supports your evaluation criteria and little beyond that.

Decide whether to count people or count actions by asking 'if one person did many actions, does that create as much value as many people doing one action?'; count people when you need many people to act (revealing how many customers succeed) and count actions when the number of actors does not matter (revealing how hard each customer had to work).
Over time move beyond leading indicators to measure the desired outcome itself, so you can track progress week over week and quarter over quarter.

Do not be afraid to measure hard things; an easy proxy metric can be gamed and does not equal real value (job applications can be inflated without increasing hires), so measure the outcome that reflects real customer value even when it is difficult.

To measure an outcome that happens off your platform, find a way to incentivize customers to report it (AfterCollege emailed students 21 days after applying and grew responses from 5% to 37% over time); an imperfect measure with a low response rate is still worth having for visibility, and you should keep iterating to improve it.

You do not need the full solution to evaluate its impact on your outcomes; run a small slice in production (e.g. stream a single sporting event through one partner) to test outcome impact before committing to the full build, new partnerships, and long-term contracts.

Track the long-term connection between your product outcome and your business outcome, and if driving the product outcome does not drive the business outcome over time, find a new product outcome that does.

Anti-pattern: turning product instrumentation into a massive waterfall project by trying to define all needs upfront; instead start by instrumenting this week's assumption tests, then measure impact on the product outcome, then strengthen the connection between product and business outcomes.

Anti-pattern: hyperfocusing on assumption tests and forgetting to walk the opportunity solution tree; desirability is not enough, because the job is to satisfy customer needs while creating business value, and viability is the key to long-term success.
Anti-pattern: forgetting to test the connection between your product outcome and your business outcome; that connection is a theory that must be tested rather than assumed.

Discovery is a messy, winding path rather than a linear process, and most of the work is not following the process but managing the cycles, looping back to an earlier habit when a surprise appears while relying on the same core discovery habits to find the way.

Assumption testing can overturn strong prior evidence: at Simply Business, despite interviews, market research, and government data all flagging late payments as a top pain, tests showed customers did not want third-party help (fearing harm to client relationships), so it was not the highest-impact opportunity to tackle next, even though the need was real.

A strong habit of weekly customer interviews lets a team kill an opportunity and choose a new target without starting from scratch, because the opportunity solution tree keeps evolving; such fast course-corrections should be celebrated, since the fruit of discovery is often the time saved by deciding not to build something.

Do not blindly copy a competitor's feature; at CarMax, copying competitors who highlighted cosmetic dings would have conflicted with CarMax's value proposition of fixing those defects during reconditioning, so the team tested how to communicate their own value proposition instead.

Test whether customers' stated priorities are real with a trade-off test rather than taking their words at face value; CarMax showed two wireframe versions of the same car (one $1,000 cheaper with minor cosmetic issues versus one $1,000 more with none) and learned people would pay more for cosmetic reconditioning, confirming the value proposition mattered.

Pursue the quickest path to customer value first before larger efforts, and set a high test threshold for content placed in a high-visibility, highly-engaged area to ensure it genuinely solves the opportunity; CarMax tried general reconditioning messaging before larger vehicle-specific solutions.

Opportunity selection is temporal (now, next, future): some opportunities are a better fit to tackle now and others must be deferred; when quick-win attempts fail to meet test thresholds, defer the opportunity, choose a new short-term target to keep making progress, and use the discovery work to make the case for the larger future investment.

Watch for solutions that threaten an existing relationship or value proposition customers care about; at FCSAmerica, moving to self-service digital tools risked the trusted financial-officer relationship customers valued, so the team looked for a digitally-addressable opportunity ('What can I afford?') that customers were already pursuing online.

The human touch may matter at some stages of a customer's process but not others, so test where in the journey it is actually needed; at FCSAmerica, customers did not want to talk to a person during the 'what can I afford?' calculation stage but valued that relationship later in the process.

Iteratively tackling small sub-opportunities one at a time compounds into a large impact on an outcome, because addressing sub-opportunities over time eventually addresses their parent opportunities, which is the path to consistently driving product outcomes.

To understand a big, poorly-understood problem, immerse yourself directly in the customer's context; at Snagajob the team went on 'walkabouts' to local businesses and acted as unpaid hiring assistants for about 30 days to uncover the sub-opportunities behind why hiring managers could not reach candidates.

Test stated preferences against observed behavior rather than trusting what people say; at Snagajob, even candidates who said they preferred phone calls rarely answered a hiring manager's call, revealing a mobile-first persona that preferred texting, so switching to texting immediately improved response rates.

A solution in a two-sided marketplace must work for both sides; Snagajob's texting solution failed when it required hiring managers to use personal devices, so they adopted a mobile-first, web-accessible tool that worked for both candidates and managers.
condition: the product is a two-sided marketplace

statement: Anti-pattern: overcommitting to an opportunity; you will uncover opportunities important to customers that you cannot deliver on right now, and the hardest challenge is picking the right opportunity for right now, so run a quick round of assumption tests to assess fit rather than overinvesting in the best tests.

Anti-pattern: avoiding hard opportunities; do not confuse quick testing and iterative delivery with delivering only easy solutions, because you can find a quick test of a hard solution (as AfterCollege prototyped a crude approximation before building machine learning) and can lay the groundwork for a hard solution while working another opportunity in parallel.

Anti-pattern: drawing conclusions from shallow learnings; discovery requires strong critical thinking, so when a surface finding suggests abandoning a strategy, ask the harder reconciling question and dig for the depth and nuance behind it, as FCSAmerica did when customers valued their loan officer yet were also willing to research online.

Anti-pattern: giving up before small changes have time to add up; do not expect a large step-function result from every change, because it often takes a series of changes over time to move the needle on an outcome.

What customers (or a sales team relaying prospects) ask for is not always what they need; rather than simply building the feature competitors offer, use your discovery habits to learn the underlying opportunity, as Airship did in discovering existing journey builders were too complex and building a differentiated solution instead.

Doing good discovery is not enough if you cannot bring your stakeholders along with you; strong discovery work is wasted unless the sales team and other business stakeholders are on board with the solution.

Do not open a stakeholder conversation with your conclusions (roadmap, release plan, prioritized backlog); anchoring in the solution space invites stakeholders to share ungrounded preferences and turns the meeting into an opinion battle the most senior person wins (the HiPPO), a situation the product trio creates itself by framing the conversation around outputs.

Slow down and show your work by walking stakeholders through the opportunity solution tree: start at the desired outcome and confirm nothing has changed, then share the opportunity space, your prioritization decisions, the target opportunity, the solutions, the assumptions, the assumption map, and the tests, asking for their input at each step.

Make sure a stakeholder fully understands the target opportunity before you share any solutions, using interview snapshots to build empathy, because understanding the opportunity sets the context for evaluating solutions and moves the conversation away from opinions and preferences.

Invite stakeholders to co-create by sharing your work and asking them to assess your thinking and add their own opportunities, ideas, and assumptions, which leverages their expertise to catch your blind spots and can generate more diverse ideas than the team produces alone.

Manage stakeholders continuously by sharing your work along the way rather than all at the end, adapting the cadence and level of detail to each stakeholder's needs, and showing the work behind your outputs even when a stakeholder asks only for outputs.

Frame a stakeholder meeting as generating and evaluating options (the potential paths to the outcome) rather than presenting a finished conclusion, because inviting stakeholders to help choose the path leads to much more buy-in and long-term success.

Anti-pattern: telling instead of showing; the curse of knowledge makes your own conclusions feel obvious once you hold the discovery work, so slow down, start at the beginning, walk stakeholders through what you learned and decided, and give them time to reach the same conclusion themselves.

Anti-pattern: overwhelming stakeholders with every messy detail; act as a smart filter tailored to each stakeholder, giving even a busy CEO a compressed show-your-work narrative that moves from the desired outcome to the top two or three opportunities, why you chose the one you did, the top solutions, and one or two supporting assumption-test results.

Anti-pattern: arguing with stakeholders about why their ideas will not work; shooting down ideas discourages stakeholders who do not share your assumption-testing building blocks, so instead use the discovery framework to show where their idea fits (a different outcome or opportunity), and capture it on your tree or idea backlog rather than your development backlog.

When a stakeholder proposes a solution for your target opportunity that rests on a faulty assumption, do not just call it out; story-map the idea and generate its assumptions together so the stakeholder sees the assumptions and reaches the conclusion themselves from what you have learned in past assumption tests.

Anti-pattern: turning stakeholder disagreement into an ideological battle; if a more senior stakeholder overrides your process, do not argue that this is the way it is supposed to be done, but focus on the specific decision and the best outcome given the constraints, and choose your battles rather than fighting ones you cannot win.

You get to choose how you do your own work even if your company operates differently (e.g. throwing designs over the wall); you can start practicing continuous discovery habits yourself regardless of the surrounding process.

When you lack direct access to your end-users, use every proxy you can find to stay close to them: join client meetings from the start, attend their conferences, talk to intermediaries, read your product's forums, mine feedback channels, and build feedback loops directly into the product.

You have more agency than you think: you can improve how you do your own work and get results without first changing how your whole company operates or getting senior-leadership support for modern discovery.
Instead of asking for permission or waiting for someone to show you how, start small and iterate from there when adopting continuous discovery habits.

Do not work alone; the continuous discovery habits are designed for a cross-functional trio, so a product manager should partner with a designer and an engineer and consult them on key build decisions even if the company culture does not formally support the trio model.

If your company does not hire designers, partner with a design-minded person instead: look for someone good at simplifying complex concepts, with firsthand experience of your customers and abundant empathy for their challenges.
condition: your company does not employ designers

statement: Make your ask small when building a trio: rather than asking someone to partner on all your discovery decisions, ask them to weigh in on one small decision and iterate from there, and if the first person is not interested, find someone who is.
Use the guiding principle of including all three disciplines (product, design, engineering) in as many discovery decisions as you can, aiming to make next week look better than last week.
A keystone habit (Charles Duhigg) starts a process that over time transforms everything, because adopting it drives the adoption of other habits by building motivation for them.

Continuous interviewing (a weekly customer touchpoint) is the keystone habit of continuous discovery and the single best place to start, because teams that interview weekly also start prototyping and testing assumptions more often and better connect their research to their product decisions.

When access to customers is hard, take a continuous-improvement approach: start by finding a single customer to talk to, or if you cannot, talk with someone similar to your customers, and use each conversation to get introduced to the next person, making next week better than last.

When you are told what to build in a feature-team model, work backward to build discovery habits: ask 'if our customers had this solution, what would it do for them?' to uncover the implied opportunity, and 'if we shipped this feature, what value would it create for our business?' refined to a clear metric to uncover the implied outcome, which together form your first opportunity solution tree.

Story map the solutions you are asked to build and use the maps to identify hidden assumptions; even without infrastructure to prototype or test, being aware of your assumptions helps you notice the evidence around you that supports or refutes them.

Agree with stakeholders on the impact they expect a feature to have and document it, instrument what you need to measure against that expected impact, and run post-release impact reviews comparing the expected impact to the actual impact.

The best time to advocate for discovery is when a feature falls short of expectations; gently suggest how the gap could have been found earlier as a collaborative problem solver rather than with an 'I told you so' attitude, read the room, and if stakeholders push back, let up.

Use retrospectives to reflect on and improve your discovery process by asking 'What did we learn during this sprint that surprised us?', then for each surprise asking 'How could we have learned that sooner?' to trace it back to a missed assumption, a misprioritized leap-of-faith assumption, or a category blind spot.
Be kind to yourselves in discovery retrospectives, because no matter how good you get you will still encounter surprises, and those surprises are what help you improve.

Anti-pattern: focusing on why a strategy will not work ('that would never work here') instead of on what is within your control; the habits have been adopted across many industries and company sizes, though they must always be adapted to your unique organizational context.

Anti-pattern: being the annoying champion for the one 'right way' of doing discovery; there is no single right way, the habits are templates to adapt to your team's needs rather than recipes to follow exactly, so do not let perfect be the enemy of good and instead adopt a continuous-improvement mindset.

Anti-pattern: waiting for permission to talk to customers; many teams who believe they are not allowed to interview customers regularly engage with people like their customers outside work, so get started by talking to anyone who is like your customers and iterate from there.
A live prototype is a prototype you build and test in your production environment, which lets you test with real customer data in an actual situation rather than in a simulated one.

Whether you categorize legal, security, and compliance concerns as feasibility assumptions or viability assumptions does not matter; what matters is that you enumerate them, question them, and, when needed, test them.
The build trap is the state in which an organization measures its success by outputs (features shipped) rather than by outcomes (the value those features produce for customers and the business).
Organizations caught in the build trap over-focus on shipping and developing features and neglect whether those features actually create value.
When a company stops producing real value for its users it begins to lose market share and becomes vulnerable to being disrupted by competitors.
An organization escapes the build trap by deliberately building intentional and robust product-management practices rather than by simply shipping more.
With robust product-management practice in place, product managers can identify the opportunities that maximize both business value and customer value.

Becoming a product-led organization requires four components together: a product-manager role with the right responsibilities and structure; a strategy that enables good decision-making; a process for determining what to build through experimentation and optimization; and organizational policies, culture, and rewards that let product management thrive.
Persistent product problems are usually systemic (rooted in process, strategy, and organizational structure) rather than merely a deficit of individual product-manager skill.
Teaching product managers better techniques does not produce lasting change when the surrounding organization keeps rewarding the old output-focused behavior; the managers revert to old habits.
condition: when organizational incentives, deadlines, and strategy still reward shipping features over delivering outcomes

statement: Tying individual bonuses and incentives to the features that get shipped pushes product managers back toward output-focused work and undermines outcome-focused practice.
Staffing a large, multi-team initiative with only a single (often junior) product manager and one development team sets that team up to fail.
Running an organization in too many directions at once (for example dozens of simultaneous major projects) prevents the strategic focus needed to deliver any of them well.
Committing feature deadlines to customers in contracts before validating whether the features should be built strips the team of the ability to question or reprioritize that work.
Setting delivery deadlines before a strategy exists handicaps teams regardless of how skilled their product managers are.

Companies fall into the build trap when they misunderstand value, associating value with the quantity of things they produce instead of with the outcomes those things create for customers and the business.

Shipping many features is not evidence of value; features that achieve no customer or business goal produce none (Marquetly shipped ten features in a month that hit no goal, and a data platform had thirty features of which customers consistently used only about two percent).
A product or service is not inherently valuable; the value lies in what it does for the customer, such as solving a problem or fulfilling a need, done repeatedly and reliably.
Business value is whatever fuels the business (money, data, knowledge capital, or promotion), and every feature built or initiative taken should tie back to a business outcome.
When a company does not understand its customers problems, it substitutes an easy-to-measure proxy, and the number of features delivered becomes the primary metric of success.

Rewarding people by output proxies (developers for volume of code, designers for pixel-perfect interactions, product managers for long specs or large backlogs, teams for shipping quantity) is detrimental yet pervasive.

Outputs are the easily quantified things a team produces (features, releases, development velocity); outcomes are the results that occur when delivered features solve customer problems, and true value is realized only in outcomes.
To make people operate strategically, stop judging teams by the quantity of features shipped; instead define and measure value and reward teams for delivering business and customer outcomes.
Rushing many poorly-tested features out at once can break the product and overwhelm users, driving customers away.
A product is a vehicle of value that delivers value to customers repeatedly without the company having to build something new each time.
A project is a discrete, deadline-bound scope of work with specific outputs; projects are essential to product development, but a mentality of thinking only in projects causes damage.

A product must be nurtured and grown to maturity over a long time; a shipped feature is a project that contributes to the product, but the work continues by scoping further projects toward the overall outcome.
Companies stuck in the build trap commonly mistake project-management frameworks (such as PRINCE2 and PMBOK) for a product-management framework.
Organize the company around products rather than projects; companies that optimize their products to achieve value are product-led organizations.
Product-led companies treat the success of their products as the primary driver of company growth and value, and they prioritize, organize, and strategize around product success.

Sales-led companies let contracts and customer promises define their product strategy without aligning to an overall strategy, which does not scale once a company has roughly fifty to a hundred or more customers.
exception: unless the company intends to operate as a bespoke agency that builds uniquely for each client

statement: Operating sales-led can be acceptable for an early startup that must close its first big clients, but persisting in it too long lets the sales process outrun product strategy and forces perpetual catch-up.
condition: only in the early startup stage while securing initial revenue

statement: Visionary-led companies depend on a single visionary; this can be powerful with the right person but is not sustainable, because product direction tends to crumble when that visionary leaves.
exception: unless innovation is built into the system so that no single person is the single point of failure

statement: Innovation must be built into the organizational system so that no single person is the weakest link or single point of failure.

Technology must not drive product strategy; technology-led companies that chase the latest technology often produce many cool things with no buyers because they lack a market-facing, value-led strategy, so product strategy must lead.
Product strategy is what connects the business, the market, and the technology so they work in harmony, and a company must lead with a value proposition for users or it will not make money.

Becoming product-led is not technically difficult and requires neither a whole new team nor scrapping existing products; the hard and essential part is a sustained mindset shift practiced consistently.
Becoming product-led requires focusing on outcomes and adopting an experimental mindset to reduce the uncertainty that what is being built will actually reach the goals.

Product managers identify the features and products that solve customer problems while achieving business goals, sitting between the business and technical sides and translating needs into products; they are the key to becoming product-led, yet many companies place people without these capabilities into the role or give them the wrong responsibilities.

Product development is inherently uncertain, so teams should separate what they know to be true (known knowns) from the assumptions and questions they must still test (known unknowns), using discovery and experimentation to turn known unknowns into facts before building.
Intuition from experience (an unknown known) should be listened to but always checked with experiments, because intuition is a common place for bias to thrive.
Product management is a career and a discipline, not merely a role someone plays on a team.

A product manager deeply understands both the business and the customer, synthesizes user analytics, customer feedback, market research, and stakeholder opinions, and decides which direction the team should move.
The product manager keeps the team focused on the why: why are we building this product and what outcome will it produce.
Companies should create a standardized product-management career path to attract the right talent, provide growth opportunities, and remain competitive.
Over-detailed specification documents are largely wasteful; much of the work behind a long spec can be accomplished with a few conversations with good developers and a fraction of the documentation.

Agile improves collaboration and the speed of building software but largely ignores how to do effective product management, because it assumed someone else was generating and validating ideas at the front of the funnel.
Adopting Agile is not a silver bullet for creating value; many product managers in Agile organizations still operate with a Waterfall, stakeholder-order-taking mindset.

Going through the motions of product management without active thinking produces useless features; the thinking is rarely taught or measured, while writing detailed specs and shipping on time are praised.
Product managers are not mini-CEOs: they lack authority over people and cannot unilaterally hire, fire, or change direction, so they must lead through influence rather than command.
The mini-CEO myth breeds an arrogant product manager who dismisses the team ideas, demotivates the team, and ends up building things no one adopts.
A product manager job is to produce value, not to push their own ideas; humility and listening to the team come before building products people love.
Product managers should listen to their team and customers, focus on customer problems rather than their own solutions, and validate ideas with concrete data and evidence rather than opinion.
Listening to everyone opinions does not mean a product manager should implement every suggestion.
The waiter archetype is an order-taking product manager who turns stakeholder or customer wants into a build list with no goal, no vision, and no decision-making.
Without a goal to provide context for trade-offs, prioritization degenerates into a popularity contest in which the most important requester gets their features built.

Implementing customer-requested solutions without validating them leads to the product death cycle, a form of the build trap; it is the product manager job, not the customer job, to understand problems and determine the best solutions.
Pushing back on requested solutions and digging into the underlying problem is an essential part of the product manager job, not an optional extra.

Product managers are not project managers: project managers own the when (deadlines and on-track delivery) while product managers own the why (value and goals), and a former project manager promoted into product often lacks the required strategic mindset.

The real role of the product manager is to work with a team to create the right product that balances business needs with solving user problems, which demands understanding of the market, the business, the company vision, and deep empathy for users.
Product managers own the why (the goal and the direction to build toward) while the team collectively owns the what (the product itself).

A product manager should be at the helm of the team experiments and continually surface known unknowns, which early in development concern the problem and customer behavior and later shift to what will solve that problem.

A product manager must be humble enough to treat their beliefs as assumptions to validate with a scientific mindset, aiming to reduce risk by focusing on learning, and must accept that not all good ideas are their own.

The lone-wolf mentality, believing the product manager is solely responsible for product success, is one of the worst traits; great product managers get further by leveraging the skills and expertise of their team.

Product management is broader than UX design: it means looking at the whole system (requirements, features, value proposition, user experience, business model, pricing, and integrations) and figuring out how the product produces revenue.

Hiring a product manager by looking for a pure technical expert or a pure market expert is a mistake; product managers are experts in product management and need only enough domain knowledge to make informed trade-off decisions.
