A product manager should be tech literate rather than tech fluent, able to discuss technology, ask engineers the right questions, and make trade-offs without necessarily being able to code.
exception: unless the product is highly technical and deep technical understanding is essential to the decisions

statement: Effective product-management practice starts from the department vision, sets a business goal aligned to that vision together with leadership, and then uses that goal as the lens for deciding which customer pain points to solve.

Anchor on the problem before jumping to solutions: use data to find what drives a metric, talk to the affected customers, bring the whole team to user-research sessions, and confirm the problem prevalence with a wider survey before generating solutions.

Validate candidate solutions with short experiments (including manual or concierge tests) before building the full solution; a manual document-verification test showed online verification raised application completion sharply before any investment in the full build.
Work backward from a validated experiment to a first version by prioritizing value against effort, ship an incremental improvement, and keep iterating toward the long-term vision.

Product managers should start by asking why before creating solutions: why do this project, what result do we want, what does success look like, what happens if it fails, and how are we mitigating that risk.
Diving into building solutions without first thinking through the associated risks is a common product-management failure.

When organizations hand product managers solutions or features to build (for example features committed during annual budgeting), they invite failure from bias and typically skip setting success metrics and goals.
All solution ideas are subject to bias, whether organizational or personal, and the only reliable way to fight that bias is to learn from users and to experiment.
When a solution is dictated without goals or success metrics, the product manager is left with no space to detect a failing direction or to correct it.

Product ownership is only one piece of product management; the Scrum product-owner responsibilities (defining, grooming, prioritizing the backlog and accepting stories) leave unanswered the key value questions of how to determine value, measure market success, ensure the right thing is built, price and package, go to market, decide build-versus-buy, and integrate.
Product owner is a role played on a Scrum team, whereas product manager is a career; product management is not dependent on Scrum and should exist under any framework or process.
Without a product-management background a person can go through the motions of the Scrum product-owner role but can never ensure that the team is building the right thing.

Most organizations do not give their people the time to do product vision and research work, instead holding them responsible for a steady stream of outputs such as stacking backlogs and writing stories.

Product managers succeed in large part when the organization sets them up for success: a goal defined jointly with their manager, the space and support to pursue it, and, crucially, permission to talk directly to users.
A core product-management skill is marrying business goals with customer goals, achieving business outcomes by creating or optimizing products aimed at solving real customer problems.
Companies that dismiss the need for product management (believing the CEO or leadership can handle everything) rarely sustain long-term value and are disrupted or slowly fizzle out.

A product manager responsibilities shift with context, product stage, and seniority: more strategy and validation on small or undefined products, more execution alongside a Scrum team, and more strategy and coaching as a manager of product managers.

The Scaled Agile Framework split, in which external-facing product managers hand requirements down to internal-facing product owners, tends to fail in practice because the product owners are disconnected from users, the product managers waterfall requirements down, and no one does validation work.

One person writing user stories roughly forty hours a week is a sign of being in the build trap; it should prompt asking whether those stories are valuable and what they are being prioritized against.

With a good strategy framework and ruthless prioritization around a few key goals, one person can talk to customers, understand their problems, and help define solutions with the team; the mix of external and internal work shifts with product maturity, but it should never all be done at once.

Do not hand a product manager a large Scrum team backlog to maintain while the product is still in discovery mode; they will keep the backlog filled and be torn between feeding developers and validating direction, so neither gets done well.
Keep team size flexible by product stage: validate the direction with a small team first, then form larger Scrum teams around the validated people and directions to build out solutions.
People may play the product-owner role on a Scrum team most days, but they must think like product managers in order to validate that the team is building the right things.

As companies scale, product teams must scale and specialize into levels defined by the mix of tactical, strategic, and operational work; as a product manager grows more senior, the work shifts away from tactical toward strategic and operational.

Tactical work is the short-term building and shipping of features and daily scoping and data work; strategic work positions the product and company to win in the market and reach its future state; operational work ties strategy back to tactics through a roadmap that aligns the teams.
Product management must be developed through experience and practice, like any specialty and often by pairing with senior practitioners, and cannot be learned in a two-day course.

Companies must grow their own product managers by setting up associate or junior product-management programs that pair juniors with senior product managers, because experienced product people are scarce on the market.

The danger for a product manager is becoming one hundred percent operational, focused only on shipping, and falling behind on the strategy and visioning work; push as much project-management effort as possible back to the team and trust them to deliver.

The industry should drop product owner as a separate title and call everyone in the role a product manager, because a product-owner-only tactical framing severs vision from day-to-day work and leaves people without the strategy experience needed to advance.

A VP of product must be fundamentally strategic and hire people to take over tactical and operational work in order to scale the organization and grow toward chief product officer, and in enterprises is accountable for the product line financial success, not just feature delivery.

A company should add a chief product officer when it develops a second product, expands into a new geography, or merges with another company; the CPO owns the entire portfolio, drives its economic success, ensures strategic alignment and resourcing, and holds a seat at the executive table.

A chief product officer must translate product and technology decisions into financial terms the board understands; beyond skill in product, technology, and finance, the best CPOs inspire confidence, empathize, and are relentless and resilient.
Having a strong product leader in the C-suite is a critical step toward becoming a product-led organization.

How you structure and organize product teams around the work is critical to product-development success, and companies tend to organize in three main ways: around value streams, around features, or around technical components.

Organizing teams around technical components (a Scrum team over every component) promotes poor product management by creating make-work: teams keep filling backlogs for stable, functional components that do not need further work to hit company goals.

Organizing teams around specific features gives coverage but promotes an output-oriented mindset, so instead of saying no to work that does not advance a goal, teams look for more things to build on their slice of the product.
When features are stable, teams should monitor them but move on to the more important work needed to support the strategy.
To organize teams effectively, balance the coverage and scope of teams against the goals you are trying to achieve.

Small companies can organize teams around the strategic goals they are trying to reach, giving each team ownership of a goal, judging it by its outcomes, and allowing it to work across products to reach that goal.
Having fewer teams forces ruthless prioritization around the most important initiatives and eliminates useless work.
A goal-based team structure creates knowledge redundancy so that critical product knowledge is not trapped in one person head, reducing risk when someone leaves or is busy.

A value stream is all of the activities needed to deliver value to the customer, from discovering the problem, setting goals, and conceiving the idea to delivering the product or service; every organization should optimize this flow to get value out to customers faster.
To organize around a value stream, start from the customer and the value you provide them, then work backward through their touchpoints to optimize and streamline that journey.

A product is a vehicle for value, so an app, interface, or feature that does not add value on its own is only a piece of the whole product and must be managed within the larger division that holds the true value.

Keep strategy and value execution together by setting strategy at the division level while the product manager executes initiatives tied to their product, which makes each team work evaluable against the strategy.

As a company scales to more products it needs more management levels, but it should minimize the number of layers and give product managers more scope over their product areas to create a structure that supports the product strategy.
You cannot build an organizational structure without a product vision, because without the vision the value streams are not apparent.
Restructuring around whole value delivered instead of around components often reveals that you need fewer teams and people than a component-based structure required.

A small team that ruthlessly prioritizes can achieve outsized results, as when Pandora scaled to seventy million monthly users with about forty engineers by prioritizing quarterly; staying small forced focus on the most important work.
Product managers need the scope to manage toward an entire outcome-oriented goal, aligned around value and given room to make measurable impact.
When an organization lacks a coherent product strategy that is ruthlessly prioritized around a few key goals, it spreads itself thin, with many teams optimizing components instead of the whole.

A strong VP of product who is good at the tactical and strategic work of a single product cannot necessarily manage a portfolio of products or interface with the board on revenue growth, so a scaling company needs an experienced chief product officer.
A good strategy is not a detailed plan; it is a framework that helps you make decisions.

Product strategy connects the company vision and economic outcomes down to the product portfolio, individual product initiatives, and the teams solution options, and strategies are created at each level and then deployed across the organization.

Do not commit to a vision or a lofty feature set without validation; paying a consultancy millions does not guarantee its suggested features are right, so ask how you know something is the right thing to build before locking into a plan.

Thinking of strategy as a plan is what gets companies into the build trap, because they keep adding features to a list with no way to evaluate whether those features are right in the holistic context of the company.
Strategy is a deployable decision-making framework that enables action to achieve desired outcomes, constrained by current capabilities and coherently aligned to the existing context.

A good strategy transcends the iterations of features, focuses on higher-level goals and vision, and should sustain an organization for years; changing strategy yearly or monthly is a sign of treating it as a plan rather than a framework.
exception: unless data or the market gives a good reason to change the strategy

statement: Committing to outcomes rather than to the specific solutions being built lets a company change tactics or kill ideas, as when Netflix killed the nearly finished Project Griffin because a hardware business did not align with its vision, spun it off as Roku, and instead partnered to run on Xbox.

A strategic framework forces you to think about the whole before zooming in on details; focusing only at the feature level loses track of the outcomes features should produce and lands you in the build trap.
Even a company with an excellent strategy framework can still fall into the build trap when it gets distracted, and the way back out is to execute better on the core mission.
Focus the company around a solid vision that states both why the company exists and the plan for getting there, which aligns the team in the right direction.

When companies approach strategy as a plan they often fail to achieve what they expected, because of the actions taken to fill three gaps between outcomes, plans, and actions (the knowledge gap, the alignment gap, and the effects gap) that create organizational friction.

The knowledge gap is the difference between what management would like to know and what the company actually knows, and organizations wrongly try to fill it by demanding ever more detailed information.

A deluge of information does not help upper management; leaders should communicate and ask for just enough information to make a decision, and should limit their own direction to defining and communicating strategic intent (the business goals and outcomes) that points teams toward outcomes.

When there are too many unknowns, a detailed plan is impossible; the team needs room to experiment and understand why before it can decide how to solve the problem, and leaders demanding ever more detail usually signals a deeper alignment gap between team goals and company strategy.

The alignment gap is the difference between what people do and what management wants them to do; organizations wrongly try to fill it with more detailed instruction, when instead each level of the company should be allowed to define how it will achieve the intent of the level above.

Passing feature requests down to teams instead of expected outcomes and goals severs the connection between team activity and company outcomes, and once those features are committed they are nearly impossible to change.

Basing performance reviews on delivering a predetermined roadmap forces teams to knowingly build the wrong thing even when they know customers do not want it, and the company still misses its goals (a large company committed to a consultancy five-year roadmap missed all of its goals while penalizing teams who delivered it).

Product teams need the freedom to explore solutions and adjust their actions according to the data they receive, and as long as they are aligned with the company strategic intents and vision, management should grant capable teams that autonomy.
Instead of sending down mandates, align every level of the company around the why and give the next layer down the opportunity to figure out the how and report back.
Lack of leadership alignment at the top is the single biggest issue standing in the way of successful product management, because the lack of meaning and focus trickles all the way down to the teams.

The effects gap is the difference between what we expect our actions to achieve and what actually happens; when results fall short, organizations wrongly add more controls, when the thing that actually delivers results is giving teams the freedom to adjust their actions toward their goals.

Knee-jerk control reactions (demanding more information, forcing year-long commitments, prescribing fully-formed solutions) restrict teams from learning and adjusting, whereas the better move is to align a team with a framework of goals and direction and then step back to give it room.

The complaint that product managers will not own the vision and the complaint that leaders must keep prescribing solutions are two symptoms of the same root cause: no strategy framework that enables action, so unaligned teams cannot make decisions.

Autonomy is what allows an organization to scale; the alternative of hiring armies of middle managers who lead by authority becomes incredibly inefficient, costly, and demoralizing as headcount grows.

Leading by authority is a relic of industrial-age management of low-skilled workers; software companies hire expensive, highly skilled people and must give them room to make decisions to get the full benefit of their knowledge and skill.
With coherent alignment and a good strategic framework, an organization can let people make decisions without heavy management oversight.
Objectives and key results framed as outputs (ship the first version, deliver by a date) rather than as business or user outcomes are not tied to value and do not get a company out of the build trap.

An organization can have every part measuring something and still miss its goals year after year if it is not correctly creating and deploying strategy, for example by prioritizing work on what leaders think is right and reacting to the loudest customers.

A company strategy has two parts, an operational framework for keeping day-to-day activities moving and a strategic framework for realizing the vision through product and service development, and getting the strategic framework right is what is essential for great products.

Strong company and product visions aligned to a strategic framework help a company avoid planning and execution swirl, whereas companies that create new visions and strategies every year are thinking too short-term.

Tying budgeting, strategy, and product development to an artificial yearly time cycle creates a lack of focus and follow-through and leaves no room for long-term work; instead companies should continuously evaluate where they are, decide where to act, and fund those decisions.
Treat the major pieces of work you take on as bets informed by data, insights, and beliefs; framing initiatives as bets sets a different type of expectation that supports experimentation.

To maintain innovation, do not mandate what to build from the top; give employees leeway to try their ideas, create an environment where it is safe to try things and fail, and embrace uncertainty so the organization can course-correct quickly.

When strategy is communicated well, product development and management synchronize in a cyclical process where company strategy informs team activities and the execution and data those teams produce inform company direction, communicated up, down, and across.
Strategy deployment is the act of communicating and aligning interconnected narratives about the objective and outcomes, tailored to a specific time frame, throughout the organization.

Strategy should be told as stories at different time scales by level: teams act on two-to-four-week stories, middle management on quarterly or yearly ones, and executives on multi-year ones, because a team cannot act on a five-year story.
Set goals and objectives at the right level for each layer to narrow the playing field so teams can act; direction that is either too prescriptive or too broad lands you in the build trap.

An unconstrained team is the most frightened to act because it faces too many options, while an appropriately constrained team feels safe to make decisions because it can see how its work aligns to the goals and structure of the organization.

Strategy deployment methods such as OKRs at Google, Hoshin Kanri at Toyota, and mission command in the military all share the premise of setting direction for each level so it can act, and understanding what makes a good strategy framework matters more than which framework you choose.
Product strategy deployment has four major levels: vision and strategic intent at the company level, and product initiatives and options at the product level.
Creating a strategy is not a one-day or one-week process, and cramming it fails; for the C-suite, getting strategy right should be the top priority or it sets thousands of employees up for failure.

Strategy is how you move the organization from where it currently is to its vision: first understand the vision, then identify the problems and obstacles in the way and experiment to tackle them, repeating until you reach the vision.

The Improvement Kata and PDCA cycle from Toyota, systematically identifying obstacles to the next target condition, planning, experimenting, checking, and acting, can be adapted to product development as the Product Kata.

Vision should not be set solely top-down; the whole organization should surface information as it learns what reaches goals and feed it back to inform strategy, because executives often lack decision data when teams do not continuously surface it.

The company vision is the linchpin of the strategy architecture that sets direction and gives meaning to everything that follows, and in large multi-product companies strategy starts at the corporate level and flows through business lines to products, which are the vehicles of value the vision gives meaning to.

A mission explains why the company exists and a vision explains where it is going based on that purpose; the best approach combines both into one value-proposition statement that is short, memorable, free of fluffy terms, and gives context on how the company will win, reinforced by leaders who communicate and tell the story behind it.

The vision should remain stable over a long period, but the strategic intents (how you intend to reach the vision) change as the company matures; strategic intents communicate the current areas of focus and usually take one to several years to reach.

Strategic intents must be aligned to the current state of the business, so the C-suite should ask what is the most important thing we can do to reach our vision based on where we are now, and consider how each part of the organization contributes.
Keep the list of strategic intents small, just a few key things rather than a laundry list of desires, in order to focus everyone.

The C-suite should focus on setting high-level strategic intents rather than dictating feature-level solutions down to teams, because dictating features spreads the organization thin (peanut-buttering) instead of making a concerted push in one direction.

Getting the right number of strategic intents matters: about one intent is usually right for a small company and about three is plenty for a large organization, because too many higher-level goals return you to peanut-buttering (one company of five thousand people with eighty intents shipped only one feature per quarter).

Strategic intents are high-level and business-focused (entering new markets, creating new revenue streams, or doubling down in an area) and are about the whole company rather than just a product solution, so they take an army to execute.
Product initiatives translate the business goals into the problems the product will solve; they answer how to reach the business goals by optimizing existing products or building new ones.

Options are the possible solutions (bets) that teams explore to solve a product initiative; sometimes the solution is apparent from best practices or prior work, and other times you must experiment to find it.

Product initiatives set the direction for teams to explore options and tie the company goals back to a solvable user or customer problem, and product managers are responsible for keeping initiatives and options aligned with the product or portfolio vision.

Many otherwise successful companies stall because they have too many products and no coherent product vision, building one-off products for individual requests or entering new markets without reconciling the new products with existing offerings; having a strategy then reveals the deeper need for an overall product vision to tie the value delivery together at the top.

The product vision communicates why you are building something and the value proposition for the customer; Amazon does this with short (one-to-two-page) press-release documents describing the user problem and how the solution solves it.
A product vision emerges from experimentation around solving user problems, and only after validating that the solution is right do you grow it into a scalable, maintainable product.
Do not make the product vision too specific; describe the main capabilities it enables for the user rather than every feature, because over-prescription stifles how you can grow the product later.

The VP of product usually owns the product vision and ensures everyone is aligned to that holistic vision, although the product itself usually emerges from a smaller team experimenting before a larger team is built to grow it.

The chief product officer sets direction for and oversees the product portfolio, answering how all products work as a system, what unique value each line offers, what guidelines govern new solutions, and what to stop doing because it does not serve the vision.
Managing a portfolio means balancing the investments, number of people, and capacity across each area to achieve success across the board, which is also how you find time for innovation.

Leaders do not lack the time to innovate, they fail to make the time (usually because of poor capacity planning and strategy); to create space you must say no to some things and deliberately dedicate teams and portfolio room to innovation, as Amazon did spending years on a dedicated team before launching the Echo.

The best solutions are linked to real problems users want solved, and product managers should use a process like the Product Kata to fall in love with the problem rather than the solution and keep iterating until they reach the outcome.

Break a goal into its component levers using what you know from product metrics before generating solutions; for example, increasing revenue from users decomposes into acquiring new users, retaining existing users better, or creating new revenue streams.

Diagnose the real problem with data and lightweight tools before choosing a solution; at Marquetly an exit-intent survey gathered over a hundred responses in a week and revealed the true drop-off drivers (missing relevant content and no proof of skills), none of which matched the free-trial and discount solutions the team had been debating.

Frame product initiatives as testable hypotheses that tie an action to an expected outcome and a quantified value estimate (for example, we believe that by increasing content we can acquire and retain more users for a given revenue gain per month).

Most processes focus on the act of developing software rather than on building the right software, which is the build trap; you escape it by applying problem-solving and experimentation techniques to find what to focus on.

The Product Kata is a systematic, repeatable process that teaches product managers a problem-solving approach to building products, and practicing it repeatedly ingrains the habit until the thought pattern becomes second nature.

To reach a product initiative, understand the strategic intent, evaluate the current state of that intent in relation to where your products can help, and determine what problems you can solve to further it.

Break the product-initiative success metric into a shorter-time-scale team goal that can be measured after every release; the initiative goal may take six months or more, but the near-term team goal gives feedback that the option is working.

Understand where you are and what is needed at the current stage before jumping into work; one of the biggest product-management mistakes is rushing to apply a tool or practice at the wrong stage, such as experimenting when the problem is not yet known or when a good solution is already understood.

The Product Kata proceeds through six questions (what is the goal, where are we now, what is the biggest obstacle, how do I try to solve it, what do I expect to happen, and what actually happened and what did we learn) that carry the team through problem exploration, solution exploration, and solution optimization, with the tools changing by phase.

Do not overdesign unique solutions for things that are not core to your value proposition; if a best practice already solves the problem, adopt it, gather data to confirm it works in your situation, and iterate, reserving your energy for what makes or breaks your value proposition.
condition: when the problem is not core to your value proposition

statement: When the problem you are solving is core to your value proposition, do not rush into the first solution; use your unique context to differentiate from competitors and experiment with a few solution ideas before committing to one.

All design and development work should be in service of reaching a goal, and not everything you try should ship; killing bad ideas and keeping features few reduces product complexity and avoids customer feature fatigue, because it is about quality, not quantity.

Use the data you already have (current retention and acquisition rates, survey percentages with statistical significance, and churn revenue) to size the upside of solving a problem and to set realistic acquisition and revenue goals.
Quantify a product initiative as a hypothesis that links the proposed action to expected metric changes and a revenue estimate before seeking investment or approval.
Base metric targets on historical trends and reality rather than optimism; approximate what is feasible from analytics and feedback instead of assuming best-case outcomes.
Identify and baseline the leading indicators of the outcome you want before writing an option statement, so you can tell whether the option is moving those indicators.
Product metrics tell you how healthy your product and ultimately your business are, and keeping a pulse on them tells you when and where to act, which is how you set direction.
Avoid vanity metrics such as total users, page views, or logins that always get bigger and look impressive, because they do not help teams make decisions or change behavior and priorities.
Turn a vanity metric into an actionable metric by adding a time component and context, asking whether the number changed versus last period and what you did differently.

Output-oriented metrics such as number of features shipped, story points completed, or user stories worked on are productivity metrics, not product metrics, because they cannot tie the results of product development back to the business.
Pirate Metrics (AARRR) track the user lifecycle through acquisition, activation, retention, referral, and revenue, and you can reorder the stages to match your product flow.
condition: the order depends on the product type, for example a B2B product with a sales team generates revenue before activation

statement: Activation (a user taking the first step toward a great experience) is distinct from acquisition (a user landing and signing up), and activating people well early leads to retention down the line.

HEART metrics (happiness, engagement, adoption, retention, and task success) add measures of user satisfaction and interaction that Pirate Metrics lacks and are usually used for a specific product or feature.
Maintain metrics at every level of strategy, including the product initiative and the option, so you can tell whether you are succeeding along the way.

Guide product decisions with a system of metrics rather than a single one, because a lone focus metric is easy to game; pair a metric with a balancing counter-metric (a mutually destructive pair), such as watching retention while pushing acquisition.

Retention is a lagging indicator that cannot be acted on immediately because solid data takes months, so also measure leading indicators such as activation, happiness, and engagement to know whether you are on track.

Option-level success metrics are usually leading indicators of the outcomes expected at the initiative level and must be commensurate with the length of the bet; measuring at the option level prevents surprises when initiative-level facts arrive later.

Implementing a metrics platform, whether homegrown or third-party, is one of the first things every company should do and is essential for a product-led company because it enables product managers to make well-informed decisions.
You cannot set meaningful success metrics without first investigating the problem, because the metrics you set are relative to the problem you discover and the solution you implement.

Kick off option work with the Product Kata by stating the goal, where you are now relative to it, the biggest obstacle in the way, and one step to better understand that obstacle, then investigate for a bounded time and regroup.
Write user-need problem statements and map the current user journey to mark the troublesome areas before deciding where to experiment.

Product managers are called the voice of the customer, yet too many do not actually talk to customers because it takes effort; since data analysis alone cannot tell the entire story, product people must talk to real users to get at their problems.

Distinguish generative, problem-based research (going to the source of the customer problem to find the problem, its root cause, and its context) from evaluative research or usability testing (which checks whether people can use a solution, not whether it solves a problem).
Do not solve problems before finding their root causes, because without an underlying understanding of the problem you can arrive at the right solution only by luck.
Beware framing the problem as the lack of a feature; probe why the user wants that feature to surface the underlying problems, which often require different solutions than the requested one.

It is easy even for experienced people to become attached to solution ideas; kill bad ideas before they consume team time and before you get hooked, and fall in love with the problem you are solving instead (a chatbot idea that solved no real problem was just a distraction).

Test the riskiest desirability assumption cheaply and early, through interviews and pitching the idea, before building; a women-mentorship app assumption that users would connect with strangers for mentorship was invalidated in interviews, saving expensive development.
The prior success of one product does not validate a new one; understand what customers actually want rather than rushing features out the door for the sake of shipping.
Invalidating a solution does not tell you the right problem; after a solution is invalidated, return to proper problem research through interviews.
Getting into a problem-solving mindset early gives you far more time to build the right thing, because you stop wasting time and money chasing the wrong things.

When it is hard or forbidden to talk to customers, get creative: trace the actual rule back to its real source (which is often less restrictive than assumed), use friends-of-friends in consumer settings, or enlist sales and account managers as research proxies in B2B, because some information is better than none.

In customer research people immediately jump to proposing solutions (I just need a button here), so back up and ask why to understand the underlying need, because it is your job, not the customer job, to ask the right questions.
Use generative solution research to learn what users value in a solution, which is less about proving a hypothesis and more about understanding what would make a good solution to test.
Start a concierge-style test without imposing a template so you can observe what users actually submit or do, then design the template or structure from what you learn.

Trying to solve one problem often uncovers a bigger, real problem; the Marquetly team discovered the true blocker to publishing courses was creating and editing videos, not getting content into the system.
When experiment results contradict your assumptions, follow up with users to find the real problem rather than forcing the data to fit your prior hypothesis.
Confirm the prevalence and scale of a newly discovered problem with a broader survey before committing to solve it.

Frame each next experiment around what you still need to learn (for example, whether solving the discovered problem will move the goal metric), which is what the Product Kata question of what to learn next enforces.
Scope an experiment to your manual capacity and set a clear success metric tied to the outcome you care about before you run it.
Identify both the solution components that matter to users and the experience factors that would make or break the solution before designing a scalable offering.
Distinguish building to learn from building to earn: experimentation exists to prove whether a hypothesis is true or false and to find value, not to produce the final product.
Experiments should be short by nature, and you will eventually scrap whatever you build; only if the solution succeeds do you then build a sustainable, scalable version.

Defining an MVP as whatever gets built in the first release is the build-trap misconception, because using an MVP just to ship a feature faster cuts corners on the experience and sacrifices the learning.
The most important part of an MVP is the learning, so it is best defined as the minimum amount of effort required to learn, which keeps the team anchored on outcomes rather than outputs.
When experimenting to learn, you are not creating stable, robust, scalable products and you often do not know the best solution when you begin, and that uncertainty is the point of doing the work.

Limit customers exposure to experiments and plan in advance how you will close the loop, setting expectations by explaining why you are testing, when and how the experiment ends, and what you will do next, because communication keeps customers happy and mitigates the risk of a failed experiment.

A concierge experiment delivers the end result to the customer manually and openly (the customer knows it is not automated); it requires no coding, is quick to start, and creates tight learning loops through close customer contact.

Concierge experiments suit B2B companies (many of which started by doing the work manually before automating it), because taking on the work yourself teaches you how to build the software correctly the first time and it is faster and cheaper to iterate on a service than on coded features.

Concierge experiments do not scale because they are labor-intensive, so run them with just enough users to stay in close contact and gather feedback, calculate your capacity, and switch to another experiment type when you want to test whether the solution scales.

A Wizard of Oz experiment looks and feels like a finished product to customers while being manual on the backend, which makes it useful for getting feedback at scale (Zappos validated demand for buying shoes online this way before building infrastructure).

A Wizard of Oz test can reveal the real reason behind behavior that raw metrics cannot explain; when subscription cancellations turned out to be about wanting control, switching to monthly reorder-reminder emails made sales skyrocket and saved over a hundred thousand dollars in development.
Do not leave Wizard of Oz experiments running for a long time because they are still manual on the backend; once you know the direction, build the full solution or move on to other experiments.

Use A/B testing to split a portion of traffic to a new idea and see whether it moves a metric versus the current state, but do not use it when you are still very unsure of the solution direction or lack enough traffic for statistically significant results.
exception: avoid A/B testing when the solution direction is still uncertain or when traffic is too low for statistical significance

statement: Concept testing demonstrates or shows a concept (landing page, wireframe, prototype, or video) in the lightest, fastest way to gauge feedback, and it tends to be generative, helping you learn what a user desires in a solution.

To make concept testing evaluative and firmly test a hypothesis, define pass-or-fail criteria and include an ask, a commitment of money, time, or other investment that shows the user is genuinely interested (for example a landing page that asks for an email address).
A concept-test video can validate demand and secure funding when a solution is hard for others to picture, as when a rough demonstration video validated Dropbox path and won its first investment.

You do not always need heavy experimentation; concierge, Wizard of Oz, and concept testing are for high uncertainty and high solution risk, so when you already know both the problem and the solution you should implement it and simply measure the result afterward.
condition: when you already know both the problem and the solution

statement: For cases of moderate uncertainty you should still build to learn rather than rush a complete solution, and prototypes are a popular no-code tool for testing whether a specific user flow or feature solves the user problem.

Prototypes do not help you validate the problem; without heavy user research first you can get stuck making shiny designs for a problem you do not understand, so explore the problem before any solution activity.
condition: prototypes are inappropriate when you still need to validate the problem rather than the solution

statement: Experimenting to learn is possible in any industry, including banks, aviation, and hardware, because making the unknown known reduces risk; even a space shuttle is developed by hypothesizing, testing panels, iterating, and only then building the known component, so there is no excuse for not learning.

Get creative to run experiments within physical or hardware constraints; GiveVision simulated its assistive glasses with an Android phone in 3D-printed frames to learn what sight-impaired users valued most before committing to a months-long manufacturing cycle.
Learning reduces risk and the goal of solution exploration is to get faster feedback, because the opportunity cost of building the wrong thing (wasted time and money) is too high.

Internal tools must be treated the same as any other product (understand the direction, diagnose the problem, research it, experiment to prove value, then build and optimize) even though they are often neglected because customers never see them.
If users cannot figure out how to use a tool, that is the product manager fault, not the users.

Neglecting internal-tool experience harms the business through help-desk load and employee churn; treating internal users like real customers made them happier, reduced churn, increased their output, and lowered operating costs.
When choosing a solution, evaluate build versus partner versus buy explicitly, weighing margin against the risk that a given option will not actually work for users.

Even after selecting a candidate solution (such as buying software), run another experiment to retire the remaining user-side risk by testing whether users can use it on their own, rather than assuming the concierge results transfer.
Track each experiment step in a Product Kata record (current state, what to learn, next step, expected result, and what was learned) so you can assemble an evidence-based business case.

Present a solution to leadership as a business case grounded in experiment data: the size of the problem, the outcome achieved in experiments, the risks already eliminated, the cost, and the expected ROI.

Prefer the option that reaches market sooner with less development effort and acceptable ROI; at Marquetly, buying and integrating existing software beat building from scratch (which would have taken over a year) and licensing for every teacher (which had no ROI).
Experimenting first retires risk so that a large investment decision, even an acquisition, can be made with high confidence in both user desirability and business value.

A product vision is best reached by iterating through experimentation; jumping to dictating features early risks never finding the right solution, because the team would have kept redesigning a workflow that was not the real problem.

Use a North Star document to give the whole team and company shared context (the problem, the proposed solution, the make-or-break solution factors, and the outcomes) and evolve it over time; it is not an action plan and does not describe how the team will build.
Use story mapping to break work down, align the team on what delivers value, and prioritize the first release.
Building shared understanding as a team lets you develop product faster and therefore get value to customers faster.
Always anchor the act of scaling back to a Version 1 on the big-picture North Star, because without that anchor you lead yourself into the build trap.

Prioritization is a top difficulty for product managers, and Cost of Delay (a numeric value combining urgency and value to describe the impact of time on outcomes) is a strong framework for deciding what to ship sooner.

Building the first version is an optimization problem: reduce scope enough to capture the maximum value in the right time, because overscoping loses revenue and cedes the market, while shipping something terrible loses early adopters who are hard to win back.

Use Cost of Delay (urgency times value) to decide what ships first and to end prioritization debates, deferring components of low urgency and value (Marquetly prioritized audio and image splicing and deferred the little-used video splicing).
condition: when you understand the desired outcomes from a strategic perspective

statement: The Agile Definition of Done, framed as finishing the features required to ship, sets the wrong expectation of what a finished feature is.

A feature is done only when it has reached its goals; shipping a first version and moving on without measuring outcomes leads to the build trap, which is why the idea that there will always be a Version 2 is a dangerous lie.

Set success criteria before launch, treat Version 1 as a hypothesis like any other work, and measure and iterate until you reach the criteria, staying willing to roll the feature back and try something else if it does not hit its goals.

Feed launch success criteria into the Product Kata loop (set direction, find the obstacles in the way, and tackle them through experimentation); the process is the same whether you are building a new feature or optimizing one, though timeframes and experiments scale with the size of the feature.

Even after a successful launch, keep diagnosing why metrics fall short of their targets (for example, reaching out to non-adopters to learn why), because optimization is continuous problem-solving and the Product Kata should become a habit of always looking for the next problem to learn about.
Escaping the build trap and building with intent requires not only a solid process and strategy but also a company that actively supports good product management.

A team succeeds at product management only when its environment allows it: it can talk to customers, it is oriented around outcomes, and leadership gives it the space to figure out how to achieve those outcomes, which are the marks of a product-led company.
Process and frameworks take you only so far toward product success; culture, policies, and structure are what truly set a company apart to thrive at product management.

A product-led organization is characterized by a culture that organizes around outcomes over outputs, a company cadence that revolves around evaluating strategy against outcomes, rewards for learning and achieving goals, management that encourages teams to get close to customers, and product management treated as a critical function that furthers the business.

Innovation efforts fail without organizational support: Kodak researched the right disruption but was reactive rather than strategic, waited too long, isolated a small underfunded team in a lab, and could not fund execution until its annual review, so competitors built what it had discovered.

Isolating innovation in a silo cut off from strategy and resources means good discovery work cannot be executed; dedicate enough people and resources to the future of the business and connect innovation to the overall company strategy.

Good roles, strategy, and process are necessary but not sufficient to escape the build trap; without an organization (culture, communication, policies, and rewards) to sustain it, even good customer research is too little, too late.

The main reason companies fail the transition to product-led is lack of leadership buy-in to become outcome-oriented: leaders say they want results but still measure success by features shipped, because seeing things ship feels satisfying.

Executives get antsy and revert to output-thinking when they cannot see meaningful progress, so a cadence of communication that shows progress at every level, tailored to each audience, is essential to keep leaders bought in.
Companies get stuck in the build trap because they are not patient enough to let outcomes emerge, so they fall back on measuring progress by the number of features shipped.

Visibility is key: the more leaders understand where teams are, the more they step back and let teams execute, whereas hiding progress widens the knowledge gap and provokes demands for more information and control, so transparency is what earns autonomy.

Communicate strategy on a cadence that matches the four strategy levels (vision, strategic intent, product initiatives, and options), because each sits on a different time horizon and progress toward it should be communicated accordingly.

Use three core product meetings at different cadences: quarterly business reviews for executives (financial outcomes and strategic intents), product initiative reviews for product-development leaders (options against initiatives, new initiatives and funding), and monthly release reviews (only what is confirmed to ship).
Review meetings should indicate progress and raise red flags rather than make all decisions; the actual decision making usually happens afterward when something needing action surfaces.

Treat a roadmap as an explanation of strategy and the current stage of the product (its goals, themes, and emerging deliverables) rather than a Gantt chart of dated feature promises, and keep it constantly updated as a living roadmap.
Locking dated feature promises into a roadmap and committing them to customers leads to overpromising and underdelivering.
Communicate roadmaps differently depending on the audience, sharing uncertainty internally with the team but sharing sellable features with sales, designing the communication to match the audience.

Align the company on development-stage terminology so everyone understands which activities are happening and what may be sold; a useful set of stages is Experiment, Alpha, Beta, and Generally Available.

In the Experiment stage teams do problem and solution exploration with no production code; Alpha tests desirability in production code for a small set of users who know it may change or be killed; Beta tests technical scalability for a larger subset (the feature is unlikely to be killed unless unstable); and Generally Available means the solution is widely released and sales can sell it freely.

Poorly-constructed roadmaps are a major source of tension between product and sales; since sales still needs something to sell, create working agreements that let sales put Generally Available (and later-stage Beta) items on their sales roadmap.
As product teams scale beyond a few, tracking progress, goals, and processes and deploying strategy becomes too much for product leaders alone and distracts them from growing the product.

Implement a product operations team (led by a chief of staff under the CPO in growth-stage companies, or a VP-led team in large organizations) to streamline operational and process work: automated progress data, reporting translated into financial implications, an analytics platform, standardized processes, running strategy and release meetings, and coaching.

A product operations team should create the criteria and systems for the inputs and outputs of work; it must not dictate how teams build the product or whether they can talk to users, but instead build templates and systems that help teams do those things.

A product operations team should stay small, functioning as an efficiency engine to automate, streamline, and optimize (its success is measured by automating away its own work), and be staffed with a mix of project managers, product people, and a few developers.

The biggest failure in becoming product-led is not re-evaluating reward structures to ensure they incentivize the right behavior; scorecards full of items to deliver rather than goals to hit drive teams to ship anything just to check the box and collect bonuses.

Tying people livelihoods to shipping product at all, rather than to learning or solving customer problems, forces even good product managers into the build trap, makes people afraid to try anything new, and stifles innovation.
Asking people to adopt new ways of working while still judging their success by outdated output-based methods is self-defeating; align incentives with the new behavior you want.

Even without the authority to change incentives, a product manager should push back with data by presenting analysis that a product is the wrong thing to build, which can lead to sunsetting it and even to career reward (one product manager who made this case was reassigned to a more important product with more seniority).

If you lack the seniority to change policy directly, influence the people who can carry the message up the chain: talk to your bosses about what success really means, define your done metrics, and always come with data.

Sales incentives drive behavior too: commission-heavy pay pushes salespeople to oversell the roadmap and target the wrong customers, causing churn, so reducing dependence on commission percentages and tying retention to sales success metrics helps mitigate this.

Leaders should reward people for moving the business forward (achieving outcomes, learning about users, and finding the right business opportunities), because everything else amounts to vanity metrics.

Beyond reward structures, organizational culture matters: teams may not be judged only on outputs and still refuse to try new things if there is not enough safety in the organization to fail and learn.

Product managers need trust and room to explore different options, because if teams are not allowed to explore weird or unexpected paths they will never push the status quo, and the status quo keeps a company from innovating.
Failing is not a success unless you learn from it; learning should be at the core of every product-led organization and be what drives it.

It is better to fail in smaller ways earlier and learn what will succeed than to spend all your time and money failing in a large, public way, which is exactly why problem and solution exploration exist, to de-risk failing in the market.

How a company responds to spectacular failure defines its culture; Netflix rolled back the Qwikster split quickly, explained the choice was not core to its strategy, returned to satisfying customers, and kept innovating, signaling that it is a safe place to push boundaries.
Companies cannot get the innovation they say they want without an understood safety to fail, because without built-in safety product managers will not feel comfortable trying anything new.
Experimentation is the ultimate risk-management strategy, because experimenting early can prevent the failure of something you would otherwise spend far more money on later.
Failing slowly, by releasing products and never measuring whether they produce value while burning cash for years, is more dangerous and costly than allowing smaller failures along the way.
Product managers should act as risk mitigators who ask how to test an idea and become more confident it is the right product before investing money in it.
It is the leader job to give people boundaries within which to operate, such as a spending cap on an experiment, and then let them explore and report back before investing more.

Segment the user base into Alpha and Beta populations: launch first to a small representative group, learn from them, and expand as confidence grows, which reduces the publicity needed for a launch and contains the rollback if the product does not work.

The first experiment is the scariest for everyone, so product managers should have a boundaries conversation with leaders that explains the possible impact, how risk will be mitigated, and how money will be saved.

Demonstrating value in small ways earns organizational trust and the safety to keep working experimentally; a two-day test that showed the original idea would not increase sales, followed by an email approach that tripled sales, saved a quarter of a million dollars and won leadership buy-in.

Annual budgeting drives the output-over-outcome mindset, because teams penalized for not spending their whole budget or not delivering the yearly roadmap will build things anyway, even things that should not be built, and yearly budgets kill the ability to change course during the year.

Fund product development like a venture capitalist: allocate by portfolio distribution and stage of work, give small amounts to explore, more as an opportunity validates, and large sums only to scale a proven product, tying all budgeting to getting the product to its next stage and stopping funding for work that cannot advance.

Being customer-centric, putting yourself in the customer shoes to ask what would make them happy and move the business forward, is required to be truly product-led and is how you determine what products and services fulfill value on the customer side.

Get the people who build the product close to customers; John Deere sends its engineers and product managers to a working farm to understand users and protects customer visits even when economic times are tough.

You can focus on outcomes over outputs, put the right people in the right roles, follow a good strategy-deployment process, and have the right structure and policies, and still not escape the build trap, because escaping it is an entire organizational change rather than following the motions.

Getting out of the build trap takes years, not one year, and requires changing how the whole organization thinks and works, with participation from the C-suite leaders down to the product managers on the teams.

A transformation succeeds when the leader understands that change starts with them; a leader who will not adopt the outcome-oriented, customer-centric, uncertainty-comfortable mindset cannot expect the rest of the organization to.
Transformations fail when leadership delegates the change, thinking it is everyone else job to change rather than their own.

A product manager core role is to be the bad-idea terminator rather than the big-idea generator; humility and the buy-in of the team are what make great products, and data beats any opinion every time.

Personalities and politics can kill a good product even when it is the best idea for the company, so you must understand what motivates senior stakeholders and win them over with information and data.
One of the quickest ways to lose a great employee is to put them in an environment where they cannot succeed, because good product managers tire of fighting policy every day instead of building.

Being product-led is a winning strategy: the best companies build with the intent to deliver customer value rather than reactively building every request or following Agile blindly, and their fundamental criterion for building a product is that it solves a problem for a user.

To diagnose whether a company is product-led, ask who came up with the last feature built: in a healthy organization management sets the goals and the team discovers how to reach them with the product manager leading problem discovery, management-originated ideas are the exception, and a team that cannot even say why it is building something is a red flag.

To diagnose product-led health, ask what the company last decided to kill; an inability to kill products or ideas signals an unhealthy culture, usually caused by ideas already committed to customers, budgets that must be fully spent, or teams that do not feel safe to push back on management.
A healthy organization not only allows but actively encourages product managers to talk with customers regularly and recognizes that dialogue as a core part of the job.

A strong product manager can articulate a clear, outcome-oriented (not output-centric), actionable goal tied to the company vision, and talks more passionately about the problems being solved than the solutions being shipped.

Product management should be respected as a leadership role, neither dictators who throw requirements over the wall to a resentful team nor weak order-takers beaten down by stakeholders and management into having no decision-making power.
Story mapping exists to restore the big-picture view of a whole product that a flat backlog or a pile of individual stories loses.
Splitting requirements into small stories improves visibility into development progress but makes it easy to lose the big picture and assemble an incoherent product.
Stories were intended to spark conversations, not to serve as one-way documentation handed from analysts to developers.
Programmers should understand what users are trying to achieve and collaborate in writing the stories that capture those needs, rather than receiving stories as a one-way handoff.

Building software one feature at a time is a sound construction strategy, but using one-feature-at-a-time as the method for designing a product's behavior and scope yields an incoherent 'Frankenstein' product.
condition: when one-feature-at-a-time is used as a design method, not merely as a build sequence

statement: Designing a product's behavior and building the software are distinct practices, usually performed by different people with different skill sets.
Producing a product people love requires design and development disciplines to collaborate, because neither alone bridges design intent and implementation.
The goal of using stories is not to write better stories.
The goal of product development is not to produce products, but to achieve the outcomes those products enable for users and the business.
Story mapping keeps a team focused on users and their experience, which produces better conversations and ultimately a better product.
To build a story map, tell the product's story by writing each large step users take on sticky notes arranged left-to-right in narrative flow.
After laying out the big steps, break each step into detail notes placed vertically beneath it, producing a grid that reads as a story left-to-right and as details top-to-bottom.
Stories are more misunderstood and misused now than ever, largely because they are treated as a way to write better requirements rather than to organize better conversations.
Building one small thing after another without a shared plan leaves stakeholders unsure when the work will finish or what exactly will be delivered.
Treating 'stories are about conversations' as license to write nothing down leads teams to forget what they discussed and agreed.
Focusing on writing acceptance criteria without first building a shared understanding of what to build leaves teams unable to finish planned work in the planned timeframe.
The objection 'our product has no users, so user stories won't work here' is a misconception; story practices apply even to parts of a product that users never directly see.

Strong product teams draw ideas from KPIs, from observing customers struggle, from product-usage data, and from new technology, rather than gathering requirements from sales, customers, or stakeholders.
Strong product teams rapidly try out product ideas to learn which are worth building, instead of holding meetings to produce prioritized roadmaps.
Strong product teams engage directly with end users and customers every week to understand them and to see responses to their latest ideas.
Handing off written documents and presentations between people works like a game of telephone: each reader reinterprets them differently, so intent gets garbled rather than clarified.
Shared documents are not the same as shared understanding.
Shared understanding exists only when each party understands what the other is imagining and why.
Teams build shared understanding by getting together and talking while externalizing their thinking with sketches, index cards, or sticky notes.
Externalizing ideas with pictures and movable notes lets a group combine and refine everyone's best thinking into a common understanding, which is very hard to reach with words alone.
Stop trying to write the perfect document; instead write something, then use conversations with words and pictures to build shared understanding.
The real goal of using stories is shared understanding, not the written artifact.
Stories get their name from how they should be used (told together with words and pictures), not from what is written down; using stories without talking is doing it wrong.
A document works like a vacation photo: it evokes rich shared meaning only for people who were present at the conversation, so a reader who was not there will not reconstruct the same understanding.
Do not assume a reader who was absent from the conversation truly understands a document even if they say so; get together and use the document to retell the story.
A story-driven process still needs many documents, but they look different from traditional requirements documents.
To help people remember a conversation, photograph the notes and boards and shoot short videos of someone talking through them.
Story work should be interactive and high-energy; having one person type what everyone says into a story-management tool at a conference table is usually doing it wrong.
Your job is not to collect and communicate requirements but to change the world for the people who use what you build.
Use a now-and-later model: study the world as it is now (frustrated users and their current tools), form ideas, deliver, and aim for those people to be better off later.
Requirements are just another name for the ideas we have that would help people.

Output is what you build (and velocity measures output); outcome is what people actually do differently to reach their goals as a result and whether their lives improve, so success is not measured by features delivered or capabilities added.
Good story conversations are about who the work is for and why, not just what will be built.
You must also focus on what helps your organization earn more, protect or expand its market, or operate more efficiently, because an unhealthy company cannot fund helping anyone.
condition: when you work for an organization that must sustain itself financially

statement: A company cannot get what it wants unless its customers and users get something they want.
Impact is the longer-term business benefit (revenue, lower cost, market share) that follows good outcomes; outcomes are observable soon after delivery while impact takes longer.
There is always more to build than you have time or resources to build.
Your job is not to build more software faster; it is to build less — minimize output while maximizing outcome and impact.
Distinguish choosers (who decide to buy) from users (who use the product); they are sometimes the same people and sometimes not, and both must be considered.
Business strategy should guide which customers and users to focus on, because no business has the resources to make everyone happy.
Building software faster is a good thing, but faster output is never by itself the solution.
Declaring that something is simply 'the requirements' tends to shut down the conversation about who the work is for and what problem it solves.
Building only a fraction of what is nominally 'required' can still make people very happy.
Adopting an Agile, story-driven process does not require sacrificing the big picture; a team can keep discussing the whole product while still shipping visible progress every few weeks.
A story card alone gives no indication of its size or effort; you cannot know how long it will take until you talk about it.
Early in a project a story you hoped to finish in one iteration is often too big; developers can carve out a small part to build next, but doing so can lose the big-picture discussion you needed.
condition: on an early pass before the story has been broken down

statement: Story maps are for breaking down big stories into smaller ones as you tell them.
Story mapping is a recurring pattern — what sensible people independently do to make sense of a whole product or feature and break large stories down — not a single inventor's invention.
The common approach of listing stories, prioritizing them, and turning them into software one at a time sounds reasonable but can create big problems by losing the whole.
As you tell stories, write key points on cards or sticky notes so ideas do not vaporize — a practice the author calls 'talk and doc'.
Pointing to a few words on a card helps everyone quickly recall the conversation, and movable cards let a group reorganize ideas and use pointing shorthand, which saves time.

Use a Think-Write-Explain-Place habit: write a few words about an idea right after thinking it, explain it while pointing to the note, then place it in a shared workspace everyone can see, add to, and move.
Writing an emerging idea on a sticky note lets you set it aside and keep listening, instead of losing focus by holding it in your head or interrupting the speaker.
Begin a story map by framing the product idea: discuss the business goals, why you are building it, its benefits, and what problems it solves — seeking the outcomes wanted, not the output to build.
Placing one card above another silently signals priority; deliberately mis-ordering a set of goals prompts people to reach in and correct them, which surfaces their real priorities.
After framing, describe the customers who will buy and the users who will use the product: list the user types, the benefits each gets, and why they would use it.
Because there is always more to build than time and money allow, the goal should never be to build everything; minimize what you build and focus first on thrilling a single chosen user.
Simply naming the user types and what each wants often reveals there is too much to build, letting a team defer building for some user types before discussing any features.

Tell users' stories by imagining the product live and narrating a day in the life of a user, laying the steps left-to-right in a flow; placing one card to the left of another silently signals sequence.
Mapping your story helps you find the holes in your own thinking, no matter how clear you believed your story was.
A product's story usually involves more than one user, so when one user's story connects to another's, tell those connected stories too.
A card placed below another can mean decomposition — the smaller details that make up a bigger thing — not only priority.
Think 'mile wide, inch deep': get to the end of the story (breadth) before diving into the details (depth).
condition: during the initial breadth-first pass of building a map

statement: Once the breadth of the map is in place, explore details and options by stopping at each step and asking what specifically the user would do, what alternatives exist, what would make it great, and what happens when things go wrong.
Write each card as a short verb phrase stating what a specific type of user wants to do, so the cards can be strung into a story with connectors like 'and then' or 'or he might'.
Hang the framing context — the product's goals and information about its customers and users — above and around the map, along with UI sketches and other notes.
Building from a flat prioritized list can lead you to start in the wrong place: in one case a founder had built almost none of the product that mapping revealed as the valuable core.

When multiple teams must release parts of one product together, build a single shared map so teams can visualize dependencies and see where each team's work fits; you cannot plan a release until you can see it all together.
condition: when multiple teams depend on each other and must release together

statement: The flat-backlog trap is when interdependent teams each prepare their own prioritized backlog for what is really one product that must ship together, losing the holistic view.
A map's backbone is the row of big steps across the top (sometimes summarized at a second level); its terminology need not be precise — it is 'just big things and little things'.
Reading the backbone left-to-right gives the narrative flow — the order in which you would tell the story — even though in reality people do many of these things concurrently and out of order.

For a big system whose flow cuts through many users and subsystems, place persona thumbnails above the backbone to track who you are discussing, and it is fine to represent backend services as personas.
Teams that reliably hit unmovable deadlines do so by being smart about building less, not by being faster than everyone else.
condition: when deadlines are genuinely fixed and cannot move

statement: Mapping a product together reveals holes: missing work between the big features and work that each team wrongly assumed another team owned.

After envisioning the whole product, play the 'What-About' game — ask what happens when things go wrong and what about other users — and add sticky notes for the features needed to address each concern.
Teams whose systems connect to each other are especially good at spotting the problems that arise at those connection points, so involve them when mapping.
Scope does not creep; understanding grows — the 'extra' work story mapping surfaces is work you would have hit later, found earlier.
Teams are poor at estimating work they have never done before and tend to be optimistic, so treat long up-front estimates skeptically.
Decide what to build inside the system by focusing on what you hope will happen outside the system — the target outcome.
Slice out a release by stretching horizontal lines across the map and moving cards above or below them to mark what is needed in the first release versus later.
A release slice should contain exactly what users need to be able to do and see when the system is released in order to achieve the target outcome.
Build a release roadmap by labeling each horizontal slice down the left edge of the map with its target outcome, yielding a list of named releases each with a specific target outcome.
A good release roadmap is a list of real-world benefits (target outcomes), not a list of features.
Focusing on specific target outcomes is the secret to prioritizing development work; without knowing your target outcomes, prioritization is nearly impossible.
Do not prioritize features — prioritize outcomes; break a big chunk of output down by focusing on a smaller, specific outcome.

Behind every outcome are specific behavior changes for specific people doing specific activities, so choosing an outcome means choosing whom to serve first and accepting that others stay on the current product for now.

After mapping the 'perfect' product and feeling overwhelmed, distill who the users are and what they must accomplish into a sentence or two, then carve away the rest to reveal a surprisingly small viable solution.
The term MVP is widely misunderstood — different organizations, and even people in the same conversation, mean different things by it.
A minimum viable product is NOT the crappiest product you could release, nor one usable only in the simplest circumstances by someone with a high tolerance for pain.
The minimum viable product (or solution) is the smallest release that successfully achieves its desired outcomes.
'Minimum' is subjective to your customers and users, not to you, so be specific about who they are and what they must accomplish and ask what is minimal to them.
Avoid deciding what is minimal by the HiPPO method — the highest paid person's opinion.

When you slice out a release and call it minimum viable you are really guessing, because outcomes cannot be observed until you ship; guessing too low fails and guessing too high wastes money and risks not finishing.
A third, complementary definition of MVP is the smallest thing you could build or do to prove or disprove an assumption — a Lean Startup experiment.
During story conversations, explicitly discuss your biggest, riskiest assumptions and what you could do to replace those risks with real information.
Treat your product idea as an experiment: your first product, and the next, should be experiments until you have proven you have the right product.
A product owner's job often includes taking ownership of someone else's idea and making it succeed or proving it will not; the best product owners help the whole team take ownership of the product.
Your first story discussion should frame the opportunity: what the big idea is, who the customers and users are, why they would want it, and why you are building it.
Treat a big product idea as a hypothesis and validate that the problems you intend to solve really exist by talking to customers and users directly.
The more you learn by talking to customers, the more the original opportunity tends to change, so do not simply build what you were initially told to build.
Envision your solution cheaply first — as user scenarios, then wireframe sketches, then a higher-fidelity prototype — before building any working software.
A product owner who lacks interaction-design skills should pair with a designer to interview users and envision solutions.
condition: when the product owner does not have design skills

statement: Prototype and test with real users to learn whether your solution is valuable and usable, and celebrate bad news early because the same bad news after building the software is far more costly.

Be wary of what people say they want: showing lots of cool ideas makes people love everything, and their stated preferences are guesses; the real proof is whether they choose to use the product every day.

Build to learn: build something less than minimal — just enough for potential users to do something useful — and show it only to people who genuinely want a solution (development partners), never to marketing, sales, or the market.
exception: do not put this less-than-minimal build in front of marketing, sales, or the broader market
