statement: Instrument the early product with simple metrics to measure whether people actually use it and what they do, because people are polite (may say they like it yet never use it) and heavy complainers may still use it daily.
In a story-mapped backlog the backbone stays fairly consistent across releases while the details beneath it change release to release.
Make the current top release slice thicker than later slices, because the imminent release needs the most detailed What-About discussion, story splitting, and prioritization.
condition: for the imminent (top) release slice

statement: Iterate until viable: grow the product a little each cycle using both subjective feedback and objective data until development partners use it routinely and would recommend it (become reference customers) — only then is it minimum and viable and safe to market.

A useful prioritization model labels each feature as a differentiator, spoiler, cost reducer, or table stakes, then uses voting to converge on the most meaningful outcome-focused set, which surfaces first-time conversations and can reveal large savings before any code is written.

Building a solution part-by-part so that every intermediate release is unusable until the final one is a broken release strategy; instead plan each release to deliver something people can actually use.
Treat every release as an experiment and be explicit about what you want to learn from it.
Always keep your target customers, users, and hoped-for outcomes in mind, because you cannot get the same great outcome for every type of user, so you must focus.
condition: when the product could serve several distinct user types

statement: Apply validated learning: recognize that your problems, customers, users, and solutions are all assumptions, and at each step build or do something with the explicit goal of validating them, moving from problem to solution.

The goal of product discovery is not to get something built but to learn as fast as possible whether you are building the right thing; building something to put in front of customers is one of the best ways to learn that.
If your goal is to learn, build only what you need to learn; if what you build early is already production-ready, you have probably done too much.

You can run early product experiments on simple or throwaway infrastructure (for example an in-memory database) to test ideas with a small subset of customers using real data, deferring costly production work until the solution is validated.
Map only what you need to support your conversation; you do not need to map a whole product to make a small change, and that is no excuse to skip mapping.
Use the map to tell a feature's story step-by-step from the user's perspective so the team can point out problems, possibilities, and technical dependencies and can estimate the work.
Injecting printed screens or prototype images into the map and pointing at details while walking through it helps listeners envision the solution.

The best estimates come from the developers who genuinely understand what they are estimating, and no estimation method works without shared understanding between the builders and those who envisioned the work.
When you have already validated that you need all of a feature and cannot cut scope, plan to build it piece by piece using crosscutting slices rather than delivering a fraction users cannot use.
condition: when scope has been validated and cannot be reduced further

statement: Build a functional walking skeleton first — a thin slice cutting through all the functionality end-to-end — so the team can run real data, test performance and scale, and surface technical risks early.

Expect predictably unpredictable work (unknown unknowns) — overlooked characteristics and performance surprises that emerge as you build up functionality — and plan for it rather than pretending it does not exist.
Internal build slices are milestones for the team to take stock, not releases to customers, so do not ship incomplete slices to users.
exception: do not release incomplete internal slices to customers and users

statement: Think of build slices as buckets with distinct learning goals rather than one slice per sprint, and decide which sprint each goes into when the time comes.
'Accurate estimate' is an oxymoron; measuring how long small built pieces actually took is far more accurate than estimating, and measuring more frequently improves your predictions.
Slicing large things into small things gives more opportunities to measure, and more measurements of similar work yield better delivery predictions.

Treat the team's early estimate as a delivery budget and actively manage it: measure each built piece as spend, and when you are over budget, borrow from other work, trim benefit-neutral scope, or renegotiate expectations.
When slicing a development strategy, tackle the risky things that could blow your budget as early as possible, and rely on whole-team conversations to spot them.

Adding 'Risk Stories' to the map alongside activities, tasks, and details, and mapping more frequently, surfaces uncertainties, makes the map reflect the real work including learning, and improves predictability; a risk burn-down chart helps communicate that progress to stakeholders.

Avoid the naive incremental strategy that assumes your vision is correct and defines parts precisely without seeing them in context; building strictly incrementally works only when every piece is as regular and well-defined as a brick.
condition: purely incremental building is safe only when each piece is regular and well-defined

statement: In product work, 'iterate' means evaluate and change what you have already made, not merely repeat a process; changing software after building it is a necessary result of learning, not a failure or 'scope creep'.
Keep an eye on the calendar and keep incrementally adding, because it is easy to get trapped endlessly iterating without ever shipping.

Combine iterative and incremental thinking: build a simple version first (a sketch), then build it up by adding functionality, arriving at something as good as or better than originally envisioned because it benefits from what you learned.

In the opening game of a release, build just enough of the essential and technically risky features that cross the whole product to see it working end-to-end, skipping optional steps and sophisticated business rules.
In the midgame, fill in and round out features, add optional steps and tough business rules, and begin end-to-end testing for performance, scalability, and usability.
In the endgame, refine and polish the release using real data at scale and user feedback, finding improvements that were hard to see from a prototype.
The team that creates the product is best at identifying where the risks and learning opportunities are, and it feels the strongest ownership over a plan it creates together.

Distinguish the risk of building the wrong product (reduced by putting whole products in front of customers) from technical risk (reduced by building internal slices and sequencing the risky bits first).
Great work is never truly finished, only abandoned: refinement could continue forever, so at some point you must decide to deliver.
Tasks are short verb phrases describing what people do to reach a goal; user tasks — what people do with your software — are the most important building block of a story map.
Different people perform the same activity differently, with different details and in different contexts, so expect users to have different goals, contexts, and task breakdowns.

Use the goal-level (altitude) concept: a sea-level task is one you would complete before intentionally stopping; smaller subtasks sit below it and summary-level tasks above it — use it to aggregate small tasks or decompose large ones.
Organize tasks in a left-to-right narrative flow — the order in which you would tell the story.
Laying the story out in narrative flow makes it easier to spot missing steps, so review the map for steps you skipped.
Explore alternative stories by playing What-About: add tasks for what you did on other days, what you would do when things go wrong, and what an ideal version would look like.
Details, alternatives, variations, and exceptions fill in the body (depth) of a map, and similar alternative tasks can be stacked together in a column.

Adding alternatives usually forces you to reorganize the narrative flow; place things where they feel natural until the flow feels right, after which you can tell many versions of the story by pointing at different cards.

If people argue about the order of tasks it usually means the order does not matter (it is preference); people do not argue about orderings that genuinely matter, so go with what is most common for the group.

Distill the map into a backbone by finding clusters of tasks that go together toward a bigger goal and labeling each cluster with a higher-goal-level card (an activity) written as a short verb phrase.
Activities aggregate tasks done by similar people at similar times to reach a common goal; the row of activities across the top, read left-to-right, is the map's backbone.
To share a large map, start by telling the high-level story — read just the backbone activities with an 'and then they' between each.
Name activities the way your actual customers and users name them, since activities lack a common vocabulary.

Slice the map to find the tasks and details needed to reach a specific outcome: hang the goal on the left, move below the line the tasks you would not do for that goal (keeping the activity headers even if empty), and add tasks specific to that goal.

The core map concepts are tasks (short verb phrases), goal levels, the left-to-right narrative flow, depth for variations and alternatives, activities across the top, activities forming the backbone, and slicing the map to reach a specific outcome.
To teach the basics, run the map-your-morning exercise with a small group; once people have done it they can map almost anything.
A 'now map' describes how people work today, in contrast to a 'later map' that imagines future product use, and the mapping concepts are identical for both.

Enrich a now map to understand users by adding pains (what does not work), joys or rewards, questions (why do they do this?), and ideas (what could remove pain or amplify joy); such maps are also called journey maps.

To learn a domain you do not know, ask real practitioners to recall the last time they did the task and write down everything they did from start to finish; organizing those tasks builds shared understanding of how they work now.
Software professionals find it hard to stop talking about features and screens and start writing short verb phrases about what people are trying to do, so keep practicing.
If you do not know who your user is, what they are trying to accomplish, or how, a map will only expose what you do not know — so go learn about the people, ideally by mapping directly with them.
condition: when you lack knowledge of your users and their goals

statement: A reliable six-step story-mapping process is: frame the problem (who and why); map the big picture breadth-first (mile wide, inch deep); explore depth, other users, alternatives, and failures; slice out a release strategy that reveals minimum solutions; slice out a learning strategy of small MVP experiments against biggest risks; and slice out a development strategy that builds risk-exposing parts earlier.
A map helps you see the big picture (the forest), but you still have to build the product one tree at a time, so the map is only the beginning.

For a team's first user story mapping, involve an experienced coach who sets up the workshop (goals, whom to invite, agenda, inputs); a facilitated one-day workshop plus smaller follow-up sessions is a workable format.
Start a mapping workshop with a product-vision exercise such as an Elevator Pitch or Cover Story to reveal whether the team shares a common direction or needs further research.

For big, multi-team products, define stories in three tiers — high-level usage steps, then finer activities per user role, then concrete user stories — deciding on each tier where to drill into detail and where cross-team dependencies matter.
condition: for large, multi-team products

statement: Put white spots, open questions, dependencies, and gaps directly on the map using different sticky colors or sizes; surfacing these unknowns is one of the most useful parts of mapping.

Prioritize with simple techniques such as dot voting or a simplified Kano model (tagging stories as must-haves, delighters, or satisfiers), sometimes at the activity level for large projects, as a basis for aligning with stakeholders and users.

Rolling a practice out across an organization requires both shared materials (map and persona templates, standard agendas, cheat sheets, tooling) and experienced coaches who train more coaches, supported by communities of practice.

In traditional processes different people read the same requirements document and imagine different things — even signing off while actually disagreeing — and the gap surfaces only later, during or after development.
Blaming 'bad requirements' misdiagnoses the problem: the real issue is a lack of shared understanding, and everyone ends up hating the document while still trying to write a better one.

Documents usually describe what we need but not why, and they often accurately describe the wrong thing; talking with someone who understands the users and their reasons often reveals a more cost-effective way to delight them.
The best solutions come from collaboration between the people who have the problems to solve and the people who can solve them.
Kent Beck's idea was to stop working so hard on the perfect document and instead get together to tell stories, arriving at a solution and building shared understanding along the way.
You know you are telling a story well if you are generating energy, interest, and vision in the listener's mind.
If you are not getting together to have rich discussions about your stories, you are not really using stories.

The story process is captured by the three Cs: Card (write what you want on cards), Conversation (get together for a rich conversation about what to build), and Confirmation (agree how you will confirm the software is done).

A product backlog is the set of cards describing the whole product or all desired changes; index cards are used because they are easy to organize, prioritize, and arrange into a structure such as a story map.

In a story-driven process the shared goal is not to write requirements correctly and understand them correctly, but to work together to understand the problem and arrive at the best solution you both believe helps users.

Confirmation means agreeing what you will check to see the work is done — the acceptance criteria or story tests — and discussing how you will demonstrate it, which often reveals holes and adds criteria.

Story conversations go best with both words and pictures — personas, workflow diagrams, UI sketches, whiteboards — that you mark up and create on the spot, and you should photograph the results before leaving.
Keep the acceptance criteria big and visible during the story conversation.

For people used to the old way, story conversations can fail when they revert to one person pushing a specification and the other punching holes, so use techniques deliberately to keep the conversation collaborative.
Having only a feature's name does not help the team find the right people to talk to or start the right who-and-why discussion.

Use the template 'As a [type of user], I want to [do something], so that I can [get some benefit]' to write story descriptions and start conversations, because it forces you to think about who, what, and why.
exception: if you cannot fill in the who, what, and why, question whether the story should be written at all

statement: The story template is only a conversation starter, not a specification; a good story conversation ends up far richer than the template sentence.

Beware 'template zombies' — letting a template drive the work instead of the thinking needed to deliver — which shows up as forcing ideas into the template, writing from your own perspective instead of the beneficiary's, or believing something is not a story unless written in template form.
A story does not need to be written in a template to count as a story; the real value comes from what you learn when you tell it, not from what is written on the card.
Treat the story template like a skier's snowplow: a best learning practice for your first stories rather than a best practice, useful to start with but not the right choice for difficult cases.
condition: while learning or writing your first stories

statement: Replacing one big everyone-discusses-everything meeting with smaller, tighter-focus conversations (for example a small backlog-grooming group before the full-team session, plus short pair conversations per story) improves story quality, makes story sizes more uniform, and makes planning easier.

Really talk about who: do not just say 'the user' — be specific about which user, discuss the different user types, distinguish customers and choosers (especially enterprise buyers) from users, and include other stakeholders, because there is rarely just one user who matters.

Really talk about what: it is fine to discuss services beneath the interface, the systems that call them, and specific UI components and behavior, as long as you do not lose sight of who cares and why.
Really talk about why, digging into the layered reasons ('poke it with the why stick') for the user, other users, the user's company, and business stakeholders.
Talk about what is going on outside the software — where users are, when and how often they would use it, and who else is present — because those things give clues about a good solution.
Talk about what goes wrong: what happens when things fail or the system is down, how else users could accomplish the goal, and how they meet the need today.

Talk about your questions and assumptions: identify what you do not know, decide how important each is to answer before building, assign someone to get the answers, and question both your user assumptions and your technical assumptions, then plan the work to resolve them.

The biggest win in a story conversation comes when the group discards its original solution assumptions, returns to the problem it is trying to solve, and together arrives at a solution that is more effective and cheaper to build.

Optimize for what, why, and how together: without explicitly discussing how a solution would be implemented you cannot judge its cost, and a solution that is too expensive may not be a good option — but respect others' expertise and do not dictate how they do their work.

Talk about how long: a go or no-go decision needs a price tag (usually time to build); early estimates are rough and best expressed by comparison to past work, and they remain estimates, not commitments.

Record decisions, questions, and assumptions visibly as you talk (vacation photos), note who was in the conversation, and photograph the results to share, so the team remembers and you avoid repeating everything.
Different roles look at the same cards but have different conversations because they have different concerns, so every story involves many kinds of conversations with different people.

Do not expect all of a story's conversations and details to fit on a single card; a story card is like a library card-catalog card — just enough to identify and organize it, a token pointing to a growing body of information that evolves with each conversation.

Make the wall an information radiator: big, visible information on the wall draws people in and generates conversations, whereas information locked in tools becomes an 'icebox'; keep information alive and useful both on the wall and in tools.

The only thing required on a story card is a good, short title; description, number, estimate, value, metrics, dependencies, status, dates, and acceptance criteria are all optional and chosen by the team.
A good, short title is the most valuable part of a story; if people start referring to stories by number it signals the title is poor, so rewrite confusing titles.
You can use the wrong tool for a job or use the right tool the wrong way, so diagnose problems by looking at the job first, not the tool.
Do not use a tracking tool to build shared understanding, and do not struggle to do complex analysis on a whiteboard — use the right tool for the right job.
Nothing beats face-to-face work at a whiteboard with sticky notes for building shared understanding.
For remote collaboration, point a document or web camera at the growing model on the wall rather than at faces, or use a tool that lets everyone see, add to, and reorganize the model concurrently.
Use tools such as a wiki to store pictures, videos, and text that help you retain and remember conversations; photographing or videoing after working together is one of the fastest ways to document.
Use tools to sequence, track, and analyze progress for larger teams across locations and longer-running projects; for a single collocated team on a small project, the wall is fine.
condition: for larger, distributed teams and longer projects; a collocated small team can rely on the wall

statement: Stay lo-fi with index cards and whiteboards and avoid unnecessary tools where you can, remembering that tools are only a means to an end.
When it is time to build, the most important thing is that developers, testers, UI designers, and writers all share the same picture in their heads — the one they built while talking together.

Handing off all a story's details to someone else to build does not work, because the documentation seems clear only to you: your brain fills in the unwritten details, which are your vacation photos, not theirs.

Instead of handing off, build an oral tradition of storytelling: someone who understands the story retells it to the next person using the written notes and pictures, letting the listener ask questions and make the details their own.

Requiring everyone to attend every conversation because anyone might pick up the story is an anti-pattern that produces too many meetings, where 'meeting' is often a euphemism for unproductive collaboration.

Effective discussion and decision-making works best in small groups of two to five people (dinner-conversation sized); beyond about five it becomes hard, so let small groups decide and then share the results with everyone through continued conversations.
After software is done, bring the team back together to inspect the work — go beyond show-and-tell to a short but serious reflection on the quality of what you built.

Evaluate three aspects of quality: user-experience quality (easy and enjoyable to use, looks good, on-brand), functional quality (does what was agreed without bugs), and code quality (meets standards and is maintainable rather than accrued technical debt).
When reviewing finished work, separate two questions: did we build what we agreed to build, and — now that we can see it — should we change it?

You can get good at building exactly what you agreed to, but you can only judge whether it is what users need after seeing it, so being right the first time is a risky strategy and changes should be captured as new story cards.
The people who wrote and built the software are usually not its daily users, so do not assume you nailed it — take the software to real users and test it.
Testing with users is not show-and-tell: watch them use the software to accomplish a real goal they normally need to achieve.
Test with the people who will actually buy, adopt, and use the product on a regular cadence, never letting more than a couple of weeks pass without watching a genuine user interact with the software.

Not everyone needs to attend user tests (a crowd unnerves users), but attending builds empathy you cannot get otherwise, so those who watch should tell stories about what they saw to the rest of the team.

Building software is not assembly-line repetition — each new story is something new — so plan to learn from everything you build and plan on being wrong a fair amount of the time rather than assuming you are always right.
As a rule of thumb, expect roughly two more stories to fix and refine each story you write; if you are not cycling through learning several times per story, you are not learning.
In a traditional process learning is dismissed as scope creep or bad requirements, whereas in an Agile process learning is the whole purpose.

Validated learning means deciding what you want to learn as part of making something and then reflecting on the consequences of what you learned — Kent Beck reframed the Agile value as 'validated learning over working software'.

You do not always need to build software to learn, but you usually need to make or do something; use stories to drive the making of anything — prototypes, user interviews, observation — agreeing who, what, and why first and reflecting on the consequences afterward.

Turning a story into work produces a work plan of development tasks (coding, testing, UI, documentation); the team creates that plan after the story conversation, not during it, by listening, taking notes, and gathering the details it needs.
If a story describes a solution that is too expensive, step back to the problem and desired outcomes and consider a cheaper alternative solution.
condition: when the described solution is too expensive

statement: If a story is affordable but big, still break it into smaller parts so you can measure and see progress sooner and evaluate whether you are on the right track.
condition: when the story is affordable but large

statement: Do not break big things into big plans (weeks of frontend, then weeks of business logic); break big things into small deliverable things with small plans, each one a 'cupcake' you can taste and learn from sooner.

The small deliverable pieces are portions of working software that let users evaluate whether they can complete a task or that expose a technical risk, and unlike cake they combine into one larger working product.
Aim to deliver half a baked cake, not a half-baked cake — a partial but genuine, usable slice rather than an unfinished mess.
There is no single right size for a story; the right size is the one relevant to the conversation you are having.
A right-sized story from the user's perspective is one that fulfills a need.
A right-sized story from the development team's perspective is one that takes just a few days to build and test.

A right-sized story from the business perspective is one that helps the business achieve a business outcome, and businesses should strive to release such outcome-focused bundles smaller and more frequently.
Big stories contain smaller stories which contain smaller stories still, and at every size they are still stories; conversation is one of the best tools for breaking them down.

Keep story-size language intentionally imprecise; over-precise size classification is not worth it, and the deliberate wiggliness gives the flexibility to use stories throughout the development cycle.
An epic is a story you expect to be large and know must be broken down; do not wield the word 'epic' as a stick to reprimand a requester, because it is a bad start to a productive conversation.
A theme is a useful grouping of related stories — by release, feature, or user type — and the same story can belong to more than one theme.
Begin the story journey with an opportunity backlog: name and list opportunities such as new features, whole new products, or problems to solve.

The first opportunity conversation is a high-level who/what/why discussion whose goal is a go-forward-or-trash decision, where go-forward means proceed to deeper discussion (not build), and killing a mediocre opportunity early should be celebrated.

After a go-forward decision, use discovery to find a solution worth building and aggressively minimize it, making it as small and valuable as you can, and celebrate every part you can safely trash or push back to the opportunity backlog.

During discovery, dig deep into who the customers and users are, how they meet the need today, how the world would change for them with your solution, how the solution might look and behave, and how long it might take to build.

Discovery is where you must scrutinize assumptions and do work to validate them: analyze business rules and regulations, spend time directly with customers and users, build and validate solution prototypes, and build technical prototypes to chase out technical risk.
A spike is a bit of development or research done with the explicit goal of learning and may not yield shippable software; use stories to describe spikes.
The small subset of stories you are confident you should build and release is the release backlog.

Hold deep-dive story workshops — last-best conversations with the developers, testers, and others who will build the software — to discuss details, keep breaking stories into the smallest buildable-and-learnable parts, and agree specifically what to build and its acceptance criteria.
Call these sessions workshops rather than meetings, because workshops are for getting work done; hold them as needed (often daily) or during planning or backlog grooming and refinement.
Even the best story workshops will not predict everything you learn once building starts, so plan frequent ad hoc story conversations every day and raise the need for them in the daily standup.

As you build, keep talking: developers should go find someone to talk to when captured details fall short rather than blaming bad requirements, and the people who decided what to build should leave their desks to see progress and give feedback.

When finished pieces are done, the people who described and who built them should pause to inspect quality and reflect on how well they planned and how well the way they work is working, then adjust to get better, more predictable output.

Get working software in front of users and customers to evaluate whether it is right, because seeing and touching something working lets them judge far better than a prototype, wireframe, or written description.

A single small piece is often not enough to test with users; wait until you have enough — usually a whole screen or flow that lets users complete a task or reach a meaningful goal — then test to learn rather than to show off.

Review progress with internal business stakeholders against the bigger plan, focusing on progress toward the minimum viable solution (the smallest releasable value) rather than each small part, and share the results of your user and customer tests.
Release when you have enough to produce the outcome you are after, but do not stop there, because a product's life starts at delivery.
condition: when you have enough to produce the target outcome

statement: After release, use metrics and face-to-face conversations to learn whether your target outcomes were actually met and why people do or do not use the product, instead of assuming your predictions held, and feed improvement ideas back to the start.

Requiring a single product owner to write all stories and attend all story conversations does not work: there are too many conversations (creating a bottleneck) and no one person has the expertise and diverse viewpoints needed to arrive at the best solution.

Avoid design by committee (everyone gets an equal say, producing bad compromises or bloated do-everything products) by holding a product owner responsible for a cohesive product, because design is never democratic.
A good product is valuable to the company and customers, usable by its users, and feasible to build with the available time and tools; the right solution is the intersection of all three.

Finding the valuable-usable-feasible sweet spot takes a small, cross-functional discovery team (ideally two to four people, dinner-conversation-sized) led by a product owner and including someone who understands users and can prototype the UI plus a senior engineer who knows the architecture.
The most innovative solutions often come from an engineer who has been given insight into the business problem and the users' problems.
The core discovery team is often called a 'triad' after the three concerns — valuable, usable, feasible — not three bodies, so it may have two, four, or more people.
A discovery team must also coordinate with the development team, business stakeholders, subject-matter experts, customers, and end users, which demands strong communication and facilitation skills.

In the story workshop use the 'three amigos': a developer who will build it, a tester (who is best at playing What-About and spotting failures), and someone who understands what, who, and why (often a UX designer or business analyst); together they agree acceptance criteria, produce the best estimate, and split stories into one-to-three-day right-sized development stories.

The client-vendor anti-pattern — one side hands over 'requirements' and the other estimates, commits, and delivers — fails because the client understands the problem but not the solution while the technologist who understands the solution is shut out; a central goal of stories is to break this anti-pattern.
Aim for a doctor-patient working relationship rather than a waiter-diner one: do not just take orders, but diagnose the real problem and sometimes tell stakeholders what they do not want to hear.
When acting as product owner for other stakeholders' ideas, take on the role of a music producer who turns their vision into a success, not an order-taker.
condition: when acting as product owner for other stakeholders' ideas, such as a business analyst in IT

statement: Forcing a busy business stakeholder to be the product owner is a potential anti-pattern; it works only if they have plenty of help, an aspiration to learn the role, and dedicated time, because product ownership is not a spare-time job — otherwise give them a producer.
Treat ideas as opportunities to evaluate, not commitments to build, because there is never enough time or people to build everything and customers would be overwhelmed if you did.

In an opportunity conversation, discuss who it is for, what problems you are solving (and how users solve them today), what you are imagining, why it benefits the organization (rough strategic alignment and return, not formal ROI), and a rough size by comparison to past work (days, weeks, or months).
Select opportunities that are aligned with your business strategy and solve compelling customer and user problems, having enough discussion to make a go or no-go decision.
A go-forward decision means moving an opportunity into deeper discovery discussion, not committing to build it, and after all that work you might still decide to kill the idea.

A no-go or trash decision is a great, celebrate-worthy result of an opportunity discussion; if an opportunity does not look promising, trash it now, ideally involving the people who championed it so they reach the same conclusion.
If you lack the information to make a go or no-go decision, list what you need to learn and go get it; if you still cannot decide, put the opportunity back into the backlog for later.

Use a canvas to size up an opportunity, because organizing the information spatially in one big shared view lets a group see all the concerns and their dependencies at once, which a slide or document cannot.

Fill an opportunity canvas collaboratively as a discovery team with stakeholders and experts, using sticky notes so it is easy to change, recording assumptions where you lack answers, and iteratively improving it as you learn; it is a set of topics to discuss, not a form to fill out, and the go/no-go decision ultimately rests with the product owner leveraging the team.

The Opportunity Canvas covers problems and solution ideas, users and customers, how users solve the problem today, user value, user metrics, adoption strategy, the business problem, business metrics, and budget.
It is a bad idea to target 'everyone' with your product; separate users and customers into types based on differences in their goals and how they would use the product.
Start from a clear problem when you can, but you will often be handed a feature or enhancement idea and must work backward to the problem it addresses — start with what you have.

You should not turn every clever idea into software regardless of the requester's job title, and even when the answer is 'go' you should leave the conversation with shared understanding of the problems, for whom, and how the organization benefits.

If the go/no-go decision is not yours, include the decision-makers; if they are unavailable, have the conversation anyway, make explicit who/what/why assumptions, and share them so decision-makers can correct you and start the right conversation.
Do not use a story map to manage opportunities themselves, but do build a simple, high-level 'now' or journey map of your existing product to find opportunities and give them context.
exception: do not use a map to manage the big opportunities themselves

statement: Add opportunities onto a now-map in a distinct color to reveal opportunity 'hot spots' — places in the user flow with a high density of ideas and likely user pain — and also mark existing pains and joys.
Prioritize opportunities that affect high-frequency activities engaged in by critical users, sooner rather than later.

Challenge a journey map's assumptions with rehearsal remapping: assign personas and desired outcomes (not step-by-step instructions), let actors try to reach the goals while observers watch, rebuild the map from what they actually did, then collect pains and gains — building empathy and surfacing unknowns quickly.

Be picky: you help no one by agreeing to take on everything, so aggressively trash opportunities unlikely to create the outcomes you want, working with business stakeholders so they help make those calls.
A good, actionable product backlog does not just materialize from a list of things people want; it is the result of deliberate discovery focused on learning who, what, and why.
Discovery is not about building shippable software but about learning — what problems we are really solving, what would be valuable, what a usable solution looks like, and what is feasible to build.

If the only thing you produce while making sense of a big, ambiguous opportunity is smaller stories, you are probably doing it wrong, because discovery should also produce other simple models that build shared understanding.

Follow four discovery steps: frame the idea from a business perspective, understand customers and users, envision your solution, and minimize and plan to find the smallest viable solution and how to build it.
Use framing discussions to set the bounds of the work: being clear on why you are building something and for whom lets the team shut down discussion of solutions that do not fit.

Build lightweight personas together as a team to create shared understanding and empathy, assembling them from the facts (and honestly labeled assumptions) you have about target users and filtering out the noise.
Do not just shout guesses into a persona; discuss what you know and have observed, involve people with firsthand user experience, bring in any research, and honestly mark what is still a guess.
For products that organizations buy, create organizational profiles ('orgzonas') for the customer organizations, much as you would create personas for users.

Map how users work today as a 'now' or narrative journey map — containing facts, observations, pains, and joys — to understand the problems they solve, spot hot spots, and use it to spring-board or validate solutions.

Words alone are not enough, so visualize the user interface — sketch individual screens and post them above the map like a storyboard — because people imagine very different things from the same words.

Use a Design Studio or collaborative ideation approach to have a group generate many possible ideas, because no single person has the best ideas — the best usually combine several people's ideas rather than the first workable one.
Visualizing your solution will surface things you missed in the map, requiring you to add, change, or reorganize it — and that is a good thing.

A workable Design Studio recipe: invite eight to twelve people whose ideas and buy-in you need; describe the problem (reviewing framing, personas, and now-maps) without over-sharing your own solution so you do not anchor them; optionally show inspiring examples; have everyone sketch individually in a short time-box; share in small groups with feedback; have each group consolidate into one sketch and present it; then have the discovery team merge them into a final sketch.
When sharing ideas in ideation, coach participants to give feedback on how well a solution addresses the problem rather than on how much they like it, and to build on one another's ideas.

Telling the full breadth of users' stories on a map helps you remember the necessary in-between details, because our brains tend to fill in the interesting features while neglecting the connecting steps.

Discuss your solution map with engineers and architects early, because seeing the big picture lets them flag solutions that are infeasible given the current architecture and time budget and suggest more cost-effective alternatives that give users an equivalent experience.
condition: early, before getting too far along in the solution

statement: Play What-About on what lies beneath the user interface — tough business rules, complex data validation, and awkward backend systems and services — adding stories or notes for them, and review with many people to surface 'what about' problems early.
Ideas do not need to be brilliant; ideas that do not shine at first often grow in value as you explore their use in the real context of someone accomplishing something meaningful.
Create a varied range of concrete examples — a simple or obvious one, a complex one, and some in between — to set a range of constraints for exploring journeys.
Beware product arrogance — the gap between what you think people need and what they really need — and close it by building and validating one journey at a time.

The biggest problem in discovery is agreeing on a fabulous solution full of bells and whistles because you focused on making everyone happy instead of on small, specific target outcomes, producing a solution far bigger than it needs to be.
If you are not cutting away more ideas than you keep, you are probably not doing discovery work right.
Viable means successful for a specific business strategy and a specific set of target customers and users — the intersection of valuable, usable, and feasible for that target.

The secret to prioritization is that specific business outcomes drive focus on specific users and their goals, which in turn drives focus on the specific features they need, so prioritize business goals, customers, and users before prioritizing features.
The common prioritization error is trying to prioritize features first; 'prioritize by business value' is empty until you fill in the specific value you have chosen.

Choose from a menu of discovery activities and artifacts (named business problems and metrics, user lists, personas, orgzonas, now/journey maps, story maps, use cases and scenarios, UI sketches, storyboards, and prototypes), but do not do all of them and do not just sit in a room writing stories.

The core purpose of discovery is building shared understanding, because the team and its collaborators often already hold the answers and could have foreseen the problems they hit if they had gotten on the same page.
A minimum viable solution identified in discovery is just a guess until you ship and observe what customers and users actually do; discovery yields a good starting guess, not a validated product.
One of the biggest mistakes teams make is actually believing their minimum viable solution will be successful.

Most of what teams build delivers little value — the author estimates only about 20 percent has real impact, roughly 20 percent is a genuine failure, and about 60 percent is neither — and industry research reports that a large majority of features are rarely or never used.

Talk directly to customers and users and experience the challenges you are helping with firsthand (design thinking's 'empathize' step), because hands-off quantitative research yields data but not empathy.
After empathizing, define and focus: make sense of what you learned through collaboration (stories, personas, now-maps of pains and rewards) and choose one or a few specific problems to focus on.

Ideate by deliberately generating multiple possible solutions and thinking past the obvious first one, using a story map that shows pains and joys as a backdrop and injecting solution ideas where they are most relevant.

Prototype with simple, often paper, prototypes to think through and experience your best solutions and filter out ideas that will not work, advancing fidelity only enough for users to evaluate whether it solves their problem.

Test by putting the prototype in front of real potential users to learn whether it solves their problem — using it for a real task, not bug-checking, selling, or show-and-tell — and expect to iterate.
exception: testing here means learning whether it solves the problem, not bug-checking, selling, or show-and-tell

statement: A design process done well beats working on gut alone, but do not confuse process with skill: design processes fail in predictable ways, and blaming the process rather than execution or skill is itself a mistake.

Avoid the common ways to wreck a design process: starting without framing business needs and target customer, doing endless un-time-boxed research, not talking to users at all, failing to focus on a specific problem, restricting idea generation to 'real designers', refusing to consider multiple solutions, crafting a beautiful prototype too flimsy to actually use, assuming a rigorous process guarantees success, ignoring build cost, and blaming a person or the process when outcomes disappoint.

The first thing to develop is not a product but customers: progressively validate that you have found customers interested in a solution, and then that they will buy, use, and tell others about the solution you have in mind.

Apply build-measure-learn and minimize the time to get through the cycle, because spending a long time learning and designing makes you attached to solutions you never validated; a Lean Startup approach validates in days where a traditional design process takes weeks or months.

There is always some risk and uncertainty, so validated-learning strategies are useful in most contexts; dismissing a project as low-risk is famous last words, and you need not justify 'behaving like a startup' to use them.

Start by openly guessing: instead of pretending you are not guessing or forbidding it, use a mix of passion, experience, insight, and guessing, spending hours to a couple of days (never weeks or months) building simple prototypes and 'now' maps collaboratively with people who know the users.

After building shared understanding of users and the problem, guess at the solution using design thinking to consider multiple options but converge quickly on your best guess (or a couple), without agonizing, because you are probably wrong anyway.

Name your risky assumptions: write a bulleted list of the things you believe are true about your users and solution that, if false, would force a rethink — including technical feasibility risks — and identify the few biggest risks.
Design and build the smallest possible test to learn quickly, targeting your biggest risks — often something barely recognizable as a prototype.

To validate that a problem exists and that a solution idea resonates, you often need not build software: interview users and walk them through a simple design comic — a comic-style scenario showing real people solving the problem with your idea.
condition: when validating that the problem exists and the solution idea resonates

statement: Measure by running your test with real customers and users — scheduling interviews or doing customer intercepts (going where customers are and talking to them) — interviewing to confirm the problem, then showing the solution idea to get their response.

After a few test runs you get predictable results; roll what you learned back into your understanding of the users and their current work, rethink the solution and your assumptions, then design the next test.

Learning you were wrong after a couple of days is excellent news compared with learning it after weeks of building, so the biggest challenge is to celebrate what you learn rather than fear being wrong — failing to learn is frequently the biggest failure.

During discovery, stories are used faster and less formally than during delivery — aiming to build simple prototypes in hours, or code-and-data prototypes in days rather than weeks — because you are building to learn and expect most ideas to fail or need adjustment.

Use a story workshop recipe: announce ahead which stories you will work on and let people opt in; keep it to three to five people; include someone who understands users and the UI, one or two developers who know the codebase (feasibility), and a tester (who asks the tough 'what abouts'); dive deep into exactly who, how they use it, what it looks like, and how it behaves, and roughly how it will be built; then agree what you will check to confirm it is done and how you will demonstrate it.

A story workshop is not working when no one participates (one person dictates while others listen), when you focus only on acceptance criteria instead of telling the who/what/why story, or when you fail to consider both functional and technical options.
During a story workshop, speak in specific examples and 'split and thin' stories that are larger than a development cycle by breaking them up or removing unnecessary extras.

You can hold these story conversations during sprint or iteration planning if the team works well together and understands the product, but planning meetings are a common complaint where people agree just to end the torture, without real shared understanding.
condition: only when the team already collaborates well and understands its product

statement: Crowds do not collaborate: conversations get harder with too many people, especially uninterested ones, so let team members opt in (and invite complainers next time), and if everyone wants in, use a fishbowl pattern so people can drop in and out.

Replacing multi-page story-narrative documents with story elaboration around visual models that includes both the business and the delivery team, on a set grooming cadence, turns a flat, disengaged process into engaged real conversations, with the analyst acting as facilitator rather than intermediary.

Use a fishbowl collaboration pattern when more people want to join than a productive conversation allows: three to five people work at the whiteboard (the 'fish'), others observe silently, and an outsider may jump in only when an insider simultaneously jumps out, keeping the conversation small while others stay informed and learners get up to speed.

The list of smaller 'cupcake' stories a big story breaks into often looks just like its acceptance criteria, because discussing acceptance criteria reveals how to break the work into smaller parts you can build and inspect along the way.

Split stories with the Good-Better-Best game: list what would be just good enough (barely sufficient), then what would make it better, then what would make it fabulous, treating each as a separate smaller story.
Build the 'good enough' basics across the whole application first, before moving on to better and then best, which makes it safer to meet deadlines.

Prepare for development-cycle planning by choosing stories a cycle or two ahead with the core team, workshopping them ahead of time (digging into details, splitting large stories, considering options), and inviting the whole team.

Run development-cycle planning by starting with the cycle's big goal, reviewing stories just enough for the big picture, time-boxing the delivery team to plan on their own in small three-amigo-style groups while the product owner stays nearby to answer questions, accounting for holidays, and then agreeing together on a plan the team takes seriously.
If the planned work will not fit the development time-box, dial a story back from 'better' to just 'good enough' so it fits.

Use a story map during delivery to give the team visibility of the whole product or feature, because people make better tactical design and development decisions when they understand the context their decisions fit into.
Use the map as a visual progress dashboard — either removing completed detail stories so you see what is left, or marking completed ones — and scan it to decide what to focus on next.
Build a simple mini-map during a story workshop showing just the few steps of the feature and add acceptance criteria as stickies, because the visible flow makes the discussion move faster.

A big, transparent wall of sticky notes — organized left-to-right by week and top-to-bottom by priority, color-coded by activity — bridges the gap between developers and stakeholders who will not use the tracking tools, letting everyone see the work and participate in decisions.
Stakeholders often cannot accept incremental delivery ('why didn't you get it right the first time?') until they see the product improve week over week, which is what builds their trust.

A bad backlog strategy is breaking all the big stories down small enough to fit the next cycle, because you get buried in tiny stories flying in every direction and lose the big picture; instead break stories down progressively and just in time.

Break stories with a purpose at each stage — opportunity (who, what problems, strategy fit), discovery (valuable-usable-feasible into a minimal release backlog), development strategy (risk-driven, build to learn the most first), and next-cycle planning (exactly what to build plus confirmation) — rather than trying to have all four conversations at once.

To avoid a backlog of tiny stories, reassemble them: cluster related stories, list their titles as bullets on one card, and summarize them with a single new title, because unlike broken asteroids split stories can be put back together.

Clean up a deep backlog by getting stories onto cards, having people who know the system cluster similar ones (silently at first, by gut, with anyone free to move any card), then heading each cluster with a distilled, specific better name; the distillations become bigger stories whose bullets are the members, added back to the release or opportunity backlog.
Bundling also cleans up deep bug lists: group low-priority bugs with higher-priority bugs in the same area, since fixing the high-priority ones often makes the low-priority ones trivial to fix too.

Do not overdo mapping: when adding a feature to an existing product, map only a little before where the feature begins and a little beyond where it ends, not the whole product — if you do not need to discuss it, you do not need to map it.

Do not sweat the small stuff: for obvious small fixes, bugs, and improvements found after delivery, skip opportunity discussions and discovery and instead get them into the current release backlog and workshop them with the team to build quickly.

After a development cycle, hold a team product review and reflection first, limited to the people who worked together (product owner, product team, developers, and QA), because the team needs a safe place to honestly evaluate its work before widening the audience.
exception: it is acceptable to exclude business stakeholders from this first team-only review

statement: In the team product review, review three things: the product, the plan, and the process.

Review the product by bringing it up and trying all of it, subjectively grading user-experience quality, functional quality, and code quality (for example on a 1-to-5 scale) as a team to drive discussion, and writing stories to correct the quality issues you find.

Review the plan by deciding which stories are and are not done, totaling the done stories as your velocity and the started-but-incomplete ones as overhang (a large overhang signals a planning problem), and checking whether the discovery-time budget was used well.
Establish a shared team definition of 'done' — for example, that automated tests pass, manual testing is complete, and product owners or UI designers have reviewed it.
Review the process like a retrospective: discuss whether last cycle's changes worked (keep or kill them) and choose a few small changes to try next cycle, without taking on too much change at once.

After the team's own review, widen to a stakeholder product review open to anyone interested, with the whole team present, connecting what you built back to the bigger product picture because outsiders were not in the planning and will notice deferred work.

In a stakeholder review, cover both discovery work and delivery work, and treat reviewing discovery as critical, because the best time to get stakeholder feedback is before you have invested heavily in building.
The only thing that trumps an executive opinion is a cold, hard fact, so show real lessons learned from putting prototypes and software in front of customers and users.

Review delivery work with stakeholders at the minimum-viable-solution level rather than story-by-story, reminding them of the target customers and outcomes and explaining why an in-progress solution looks incomplete.

When stakeholders suggest off-target ideas, respectfully remind them of the target audience and the outcome you are focused on and why the suggestion, though possibly good, does not support that outcome.
The best-working product qualities are often the ones users never consciously notice, so treat those invisible qualities as important and worth getting right.

Calibrate 'enough' to the audience: enough for users is software that lets them reach a goal, enough for customers is a feature representing real value, and enough for stakeholders is progress they can see toward a business goal — the small parts that let the team learn are usually not enough to be relevant to other groups.

Plan to learn from each release rather than waiting for complaints (a lagging indicator): build usage metrics into the product, schedule time to observe users, and routinely discuss learnings as a team and turn them into stories, some for now and some for the opportunity backlog.
Software is never really done: you will not finish every story you imagine, but with an effective development strategy the software will be as good as it can be at release time.
Outcomes are never insured: despite all your validation, people often do not behave as predicted, so plan to keep learning and to make changes with each release.

The improvements you make after release are the most valuable, because the unpredictable things you observe once users adopt the product frequently yield the most insight, so budget time to measure and observe outcomes.

Use the map to evaluate release readiness: for each major user activity ask what grade you would give yourselves if you shipped now, producing a report card, and focus remaining time on the lowest-graded parts of the workflow, since shipping with As and Bs on time may beat straight As delivered late.
Run product development in fixed six-week cycles: long enough to build something meaningful end-to-end, yet short enough that the deadline is felt from the start so the time is used deliberately.

Base cycle decisions on whether the product will have moved forward by the end of the cycle rather than on micromanaging hours or days; avoid daily meetings and rethinking the roadmap every couple of weeks.
Shape a project before handing it over: a small senior group, working alongside the cycle, defines the solution's key elements before anyone considers the project ready to bet on.
Define projects at the right level of abstraction: concrete enough that the team knows what to do, yet abstract enough that they retain room to work out the interesting details themselves.
When scoping work, ask how much time an idea is worth (its appetite) instead of how long it will take (an estimate).

Hand a whole project to one small integrated team of designers and programmers that sets its own tasks, adjusts scope, and builds vertical slices one at a time, instead of having managers slice the work into tickets.

Team autonomy, senior shaping, and management load form a reinforcing loop: more autonomous teams free senior people to shape better projects, and better-shaped projects give teams clearer boundaries that increase autonomy.
Shape Up targets the risk of not shipping on time, not the risk of building the wrong thing.
exception: The risk of building the wrong thing (discovery) is deliberately out of scope and is addressed by other methods.

statement: Regain the ability to ship reliably before investing in improving the discovery process.
condition: when a team has lost its ability to ship on time

statement: Resolve open questions during shaping and do not commit a project to a time box while it still contains rabbit holes or tangled interdependencies.
Cap each bet at six weeks and, by default, refuse to extend a project that overruns (a 'circuit breaker'), so no concept ever consumes several times its original appetite before it is rethought.
exception: unless a deliberate, explicit decision is made to extend the bet

statement: Reduce building risk by integrating design and programming early: build one meaningful piece end-to-end first and then repeat, instead of assembling many disconnected parts late in the project.
Sequence the work from the most unknown and risky pieces toward the least worrisome, integrating as early as possible to learn what works and what does not.
Shaped work should sit at the right level of abstraction, neither too vague nor too concrete; product managers commonly err toward one of these two extremes.
Going straight to wireframes or high-fidelity mockups defines too much detail too early and leaves the designer no room for creativity.
The more specific and detailed a design is, the harder it becomes to estimate, because a precise interface can hide complexities and implementation details that were not visible in the mockup.
When scope is fixed rather than variable, over-specified work prevents the team from reconsidering a design decision that turns out to cost more than it is worth.
condition: when the scope is not variable

statement: Defining a project in only a few words is too abstract: team members cannot make trade-offs or know what to include or leave out.
Under-specified projects tend to grow out of control because nothing defines what is out of scope.
Under a fixed short appetite, deliberately build only the slice of a large feature that fits the appetite and serves a chosen use case, explicitly naming the trade-offs that are left out.
Leave shaped work rough and visibly unfinished so designers and programmers can apply their own judgement and discover the real trade-offs when they build.

Ensure shaped work is solved: all main elements of the solution exist at the macro level and connect together, and foreseeable open questions and rabbit holes are removed, even though it is not broken down into tasks.
Ensure shaped work is bounded: it indicates what not to do, carries a specific appetite, and requires limiting scope to fit the fixed time.
Roughness leaves room for the team while the solution and its boundaries act as guard rails that keep the team from building too much, wandering, or getting stuck.
Shaping is creative, integrative work that combines interface ideas, technical possibilities, and business priorities, performed by a generalist or a small collaboration of one or two people.
A shaper need not be a programmer but must be technically literate, able to judge what is possible and what is easy or hard to build.
Keep shaping a private, closed-door creative process and do not share work-in-progress with the wider team until a bet is committed, so unfinished shaping can be shelved or dropped.
Run shaping and building as two separate parallel tracks: during a cycle, teams build previously shaped work while shapers prepare what teams might build in a future cycle.
Shaping proceeds in four steps: set boundaries, rough out the elements, address risks and rabbit holes, and write the pitch.
Start shaping a raw idea by setting broad boundaries on the scope of the discussion before diving into possible solutions.
Explicitly decide how much time and attention an idea deserves before committing resources or debating possible solutions.

The appetite is a time budget for a standard team size, usually set as one of two sizes: a Small Batch (one designer and one or two programmers for one to two weeks, batched into a cycle) or a Big Batch (the same team for a full six weeks).
When scope is too big to fit six weeks, narrow the problem definition or break off a meaningful part that can itself be shaped to a six-week appetite.
An appetite is the opposite of an estimate: an estimate starts from a design and produces a number, whereas an appetite starts from a number and produces a design.
Treat time as fixed and scope as variable ('fixed time, variable scope'), using the appetite as a creative constraint on the design.
A fixed deadline forces explicit trade-offs among time, quality, and scope; without that pressure the trade-off is never made.
Apply fixed-time/variable-scope at every stage: the appetite constrains the shaped solution, and later the fixed time box pushes the team to distinguish core work from peripheral work.
There is no absolute best solution; a solution can only be judged good relative to how much time you want to spend and how important the problem is.
Make the default response to any new idea a soft 'maybe some day' that keeps options open, instead of an immediate yes or no or adding it to a backlog.
Saying yes to every incoming request produces an ever-growing pile of work.
Keep a poker face on unshaped ideas: neither shut them down nor show enthusiasm that sets expectations you may not be able to meet.
Narrow the understanding of the problem instead of taking a feature request at face value, because the real fix is often far smaller than the literal request.
Flip the question from 'What could we build?' to 'What is really going wrong?' and find where the user's current workflow specifically breaks down.
To surface the real use case, ask a requester when and in what situation they wanted the feature, rather than why they want it or what it should look like.
Narrow a need down to the specific pain it represents (for example, 'see free spaces') rather than reproducing everything a whole category of tool does.
Let the appetite govern how much research is worthwhile; if a problem is not critical and cannot yet be grasped, walk away and revisit it later.
Reject grab-bag efforts such as vague redesigns, refactorings, or '2.0' projects that are not driven by a specific problem or use case, and reframe them around a concrete problem.
A project kicked off without a clear definition of what 'done' looks like tends to become a mess; splitting it into smaller problem-driven projects with their own appetites is what recovers it.
Boundary-setting is complete only when three things are in hand: a raw idea, an appetite, and a narrowed problem definition.
When finding solution elements, move fast and explore many directions, working alone or with a single trusted partner of similar background rather than a crowd.
Avoid wireframes and specific visual layouts while finding elements, because they trap you in details and prevent broad exploration.

Use breadboarding to design flows at the right abstraction: write out places (navigable screens, dialogs, menus), affordances (buttons, fields, and interface copy the user acts on), and connection lines, using words rather than pictures.
Writing out flows as words and arrows provokes functional and interface questions early without the distraction of visual choices.
When an idea is fundamentally visual or spatial, use fat marker sketches (strokes so broad that adding detail is hard) instead of wireframes.
condition: when the two-dimensional arrangement of elements is the core problem

statement: Give the rough early design stage an explicit name and a deliberately coarse tool to avoid jumping ahead to the wrong fidelity before enough options have been surveyed.
The output of the find-elements step is a narrow, specific list of solution elements, far narrower than the original idea.
Avoid producing specific mockups during shaping, because any concrete mockup biases downstream work, especially when it comes from someone senior, as people treat every detail as direction.
Shaping output is not a specification but like the boundaries and rules of a game: specific enough to guide, yet leaving room for many later decisions.
After finding elements, stress-test and de-risk the concept by checking for holes and challenges that could prevent shipping within the appetite.
A single unaddressed hole can derail a fixed-time project (an unanticipated two-week problem burns a third of a six-week budget), and some problems turn out to have no apparent solution at all.
Do not assume a designer will simply 'figure it out'; validate during shaping that a viable approach actually exists before betting on the project.

Well-shaped work has a thin-tailed risk profile of independent, well-understood parts that assemble in known ways, whereas rabbit holes (technical unknowns, unsolved design problems, misunderstood interdependencies) stretch the tail to multiples of the appetite.

Hunt for rabbit holes by slowing down and walking a use case in slow motion to reveal gaps, and by questioning each solved part: does it need never-done-before technical work, does it assume parts fit together, does it assume a design solution you could not produce yourself, and is there a hard decision to settle in advance?
When a part hides a deep design problem, resolve it during shaping by dictating a simplifying trade-off rather than pushing a tangled knot of interdependencies to the team under deadline.
As a shaper, optimize for basic quality and risk reduction rather than the ultimate design: a compromised concept that keeps the valuable elements while cutting a big tail of risk is preferable.
Call out deliberate patches and simplifications explicitly in the pitch so nobody downstream is tripped up by them.
Explicitly declare specific use cases 'out of bounds' to keep a project within its appetite, because teams naturally try to cover every possible case.
Cut exciting-but-unnecessary parts from the core of the solution and flag them only as nice-to-haves, so everyone assumes the feature is valuable without them.

Before writing up a pitch, walk the shaped concept past technical experts to verify uncertain assumptions such as technical feasibility or whether usage data contradicts a belief about current behavior.
Frame an expert review as 'just an idea I am shaping, not committed yet' so experts give honest input rather than treating it as a decision already made.
Never ask merely whether something is possible; because almost anything can be built yet nothing comes for free, ask instead whether it is achievable within the appetite (for example, in six weeks).
In expert reviews, actively hunt for the risks and time bombs that could blow up the project once it is committed, not just for general opinions.
Keep the concept malleable ('keep the clay wet') by rebuilding it live on a whiteboard, presenting the worked-out concept first and only then inviting revisions and radical simplifications.
A pitch always contains five ingredients: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes, and no-gos.
Always present a problem together with its solution and never jump straight to what to build, because without a stated problem there is no test of fitness for judging whether a solution is good.
Define the problem as a single specific story showing why the status quo fails, giving a concrete baseline to test the solution's fitness against.

State the appetite in the pitch as part of the problem definition, both to head off unproductive 'there is always a better solution' debates and to make readers partners in finding a simple solution that fits the time.

Treat a problem without a solution as unshaped work and refuse to bet on it, because handing it to a team pushes research and exploration down to a level where skills, time limit, and risk profile are all misaligned.
Consider a project ready to bet on only when problem, appetite, and solution come together, so the fit between problem and solution can be scrutinized.

In the pitch, add just enough concreteness for a low-context reader to get the idea, but avoid wireframes or high-fidelity mockups that box in designers and derail discussion into color, proportion, or layout.
Increase visual detail only for a 'linchpin' element that everyone must see concretely, and add a disclaimer reminding designers of the latitude they still have.
List explicit no-gos in the pitch: functionality or use cases intentionally excluded to fit the appetite or keep the problem tractable.
Default to asynchronous communication and move to real-time discussion only when it is truly needed, so each person keeps as much self-directed, uninterrupted time as possible.
Post the pitch for stakeholders to read on their own time before the betting table, and use comments to poke holes or add missing information rather than to decide yes or no.
Do not maintain a backlog: a growing pile of tasks creates a false feeling of being behind and wastes time in constant grooming instead of advancing the timely work that matters now.
Really important ideas come back on their own, so something heard once and never again probably was not a real problem, while repeated demand naturally motivates shaping.
Before each cycle, hold a betting table that chooses among only a few well-shaped, risk-reduced pitches (recent or deliberately revived), with nothing else on the table.
If a pitch is not chosen, let it go with nothing to track; anyone who still cares re-tracks it independently and lobbies for it again later.
Replace a central backlog with decentralized lists that each person or department tracks in their own way, none of which is a direct input to the betting process.
Use regular but infrequent cross-department one-on-ones to cross-pollinate ideas about what to shape and work on next.
Two-week sprints are too short to finish anything meaningful and impose planning overhead and lost momentum that outweigh the output they produce.

Choose a cycle length long enough to finish a whole project yet short enough to see the end from the beginning so the deadline feels real; a too-distant deadline makes teams wander, and a fixed cycle also standardizes project size for shaping and scheduling.
Schedule roughly two weeks of cool-down with no assigned work after each cycle to breathe, meet, and plan, because the end of a cycle is the worst time to plan.
Standardize project teams as one designer with one or two programmers, joined later in the cycle by a QA person for integration testing.

A big-batch team spends a whole cycle on one project, while a small-batch team self-organizes several one-to-two-week projects to all ship before the cycle ends and does not schedule them individually.

Keep the betting table to a few senior decision-makers and short (an hour or two) with pitches studied beforehand; its output is a cycle plan that needs no second-step approval and that no one may interfere with afterward.
A bet has a defined payout: work is shaped into the time box so that something meaningful is finished, not merely to fill the time with tasks.
A bet is a commitment: give the team the entire, uninterrupted time to work exclusively on it, optimizing overall product progress rather than every individual hour.
A smart bet caps the downside: the most you can lose is the amount bet, so never let a project run to multiples of its original appetite.
Honor a bet by never interrupting or pulling the team away; requests for 'just a few hours' or 'just one day' still break the commitment.
Momentum is a second-order quantity, so interrupting someone costs not just the time taken but the momentum lost and the time to rebuild it: the wrong hour can kill a day, and a day can kill a week.
Absorb new issues by waiting at most until the next cycle and betting only one cycle ahead to keep options open.
exception: unless a genuine, rare crisis requires hitting the brakes immediately

statement: Treat a project that misses its cycle as a shaping failure: reframe the problem on the shaping track and re-review a new pitch at the betting table rather than pouring more time into a bad approach.
A hard deadline with a real chance of not shipping motivates teams to own their trade-offs and keep questioning how design and implementation decisions affect scope.
Bugs are not automatically more important than other work; what matters is their severity, all software has bugs, and trying to fix every bug means never shipping anything new.
Reserve dropping everything for true crises such as data loss, the app failing, or many customers seeing the wrong thing; most bugs can wait a cycle or longer and many need not be fixed at all.
Handle bugs without interrupting cycles via three routes: fix them during cool-down, pitch a large bug to compete for a bet at the betting table, or run an annual dedicated 'bug smash' cycle.

Give every cycle a clean slate: bet only one cycle at a time and never carry scraps of old work forward without first reshaping them as a new potential bet; for multi-cycle work, shape a specific target that is fully built and working at the end of the cycle while keeping the option to change course.
Set different cycle expectations depending on whether you are improving an existing product or building a new one, reflecting on where you are in the product's development arc.
Building a new product from scratch passes through three phases (R&D, production, and cleanup), each with different shaping and expectations, while still betting only one cycle at a time.
In R&D mode, since you cannot reliably shape the work in advance, bet time on spiking key pieces with much fuzzier shaping and learn what you want by building.

In R&D mode, staff the team with senior people who hold the product vision, because you cannot delegate what you do not yet understand and early architectural decisions define the holes that future features will fit into.
Do not expect to ship at the end of an R&D cycle; aim to spike and learn enough to commit to the load-bearing structure of main code and UI decisions.
Decide cycle by cycle whether to continue in R&D mode, because a cycle may reveal either that you are not ready or that the product is coming together.

Flip to production mode once the key architectural decisions are settled: shaping becomes deliberate again with clear shaping, betting, and building phases, and you can run multiple teams in parallel.
