Before a product is publicly available, define 'shipping' as merging into the main codebase and not expecting to touch it again, which lets you stay experimental and cut features from the final cut as long as the build team knows this up front.
condition: before the product is publicly available to customers

statement: In cleanup mode (the final phase before launch) drop the structure: do no shaping, keep no fixed team boundaries, have everyone help, and merge work continuously in the smallest possible bites.
Keep discipline in cleanup by verifying you are working on genuine must-haves rather than cold-feet delays, and cap cleanup at no more than two cycles.
Cleanup is when leadership makes final-cut decisions, and a smaller V1 surface area means fewer questions to answer, less to support, and less to maintain indefinitely.

For an experimental feature too risky to release directly, frame it like a production-mode bet on a new product: build a version just functional enough to use internally and do not ship it to customers without an additional cycle.
condition: when a feature is experimental and too risky to release directly to customers

statement: At the betting table, separate problem from solution and weigh problems against each other, because there are always more problems than time to solve them.
Treat a too-complicated or too-sweeping solution as a signal that the problem is not understood specifically enough, and look for a way to get 80% of the benefit from 20% of the change.

When a stakeholder resists an appetite, supply missing problem context, test whether the true objection is really the solution (for instance by asking how they would feel about a two-week version), or otherwise drop the idea or reshape a smaller one.
Interface elements carry an invisible cost of giving up screen real estate you cannot reuse later, so do not sell that real estate too cheaply to solve a single problem.
Avoid doing design work or debating technical solutions for more than a moment at the betting table, and pull the discussion back up to the high level.
Pass on a well-shaped, valuable project when the timing is wrong, for reasons such as recent similar work, dipping team morale, the need for a news splash, or overdue customer fixes.
As part of betting, assign specific people to roles on each team based on the expertise the project needs, the kind of work each person has been doing, and their availability.
Assign whole projects, not tasks: let no one act as a taskmaster or architect who splits the project into pieces, so the project stays whole and the team never loses the bigger picture.
Trust the team to define its own tasks and its own approach with full autonomy, bounded only by the pitch, rather than inventing a solution from scratch.
Projects turn out better when the team owns the whole, because nobody can predict up front what all the pieces need to fit together and the people doing the real work are best placed to adjust.
Assigning individual tasks lets each person execute a piece without feeling responsible for how the pieces fit, and planning everything up front blinds you to the reality discovered along the way.
Treat 'done' as deployed within the cycle, which forces testing and QA to happen inside the cycle and respects the circuit breaker.
Do not require thin-tailed follow-ups such as help documentation, marketing updates, or customer announcements within the cycle; handle them afterward during cool-down.
Kick off a project by posting the shaped concept (the original pitch or a distilled version) and holding a call so the team can ask questions the write-up does not answer.

Expect the first few days of a project to look like nothing is happening (no tasks checked, no deploys, even radio silence) as each person learns the existing system and finds the best starting point.

Respect the orientation phase: do not ask for status or visible progress too early, because that pushes necessary exploration underground, and instead empower people to openly say 'I am still figuring out how to start'.
If the orientation silence does not begin to break after about three days, treat that as a reasonable time to step in and check on the team.
Distinguish imagined tasks (assumed up front just by thinking) from discovered tasks (found by doing real work); the discovered tasks are the true bulk of a project and often the hardest.
Figure out what needs doing by starting real work, but pick something meaningful and central that is still small enough to finish end-to-end (working UI and working code) in a few days.

Do not build toward a master plan whose parts only come together at the 11th hour: many completed tasks with nothing to click on produce no felt progress, so lots can be done while nothing is really done.
Make something tangible and demoable early, within the first week or so, by integrating vertically on one small slice instead of chipping away at the horizontal layers.
Front-end and back-end (design and code) are the primary integration challenge, and design without a backend or a backend without UI stays hypothetical and cannot be judged.
Integrate the first slice on the most central piece of UI: the one that will appear in demo videos and that customers will use most.
Programmers should not sit idle waiting for design at the start of a project, because the pitch gives enough direction to begin back-end problems and foundational modeling decisions.
Programmers need only affordances (endpoints such as input elements, buttons, and places where stored data appears), not a pixel-perfect design, to start implementing.

Resolve questions of font, color, spacing, and layout only after the raw affordances are wired up; copywriting, basic affordances, and some wiring are enough to test a live version and answer whether it makes sense, is understandable, and does what you want.
Visual styling matters in the end product, not in the early stages; the biggest early uncertainties are whether the thing will work, whether it makes sense, and how hard it will be to implement.
First make it work, then make it beautiful: after the elements are hooked up, you can rearrange, restyle, and repaint work that already functions.

Back-end work need not be all-or-nothing; make it strategically patchy (a controller with no model, mock data, routes between unwired screens, or just the scaffolding a designer needs next) to unblock the next design or test step.

Use the cheapest thing that unblocks learning (for example, a hard-coded HTTPAuth password instead of full authentication) when the omitted work would not teach you anything about the problem you are solving.
Set up an iterative exchange between design and programming over a single piece of the product, taking turns to layer in affordances, code, and styling, rather than a single large hand-off.
Jump straight into the middle of the project where the interesting problem is and stub everything else to get there, rather than building login or setup screens first.

Choose the first thing to build by three criteria - core (other work is meaningless without it), small (finishable in a few days), and novel (never done before) - preferring the novel option when several candidates are core and small, because it eliminates the most uncertainty.

Organize work by the structure of the project (its independently finishable parts), not by person or role, because role-based lists produce tasks that do not add up to a finished part of the project early enough.
Break the overall scope of a project into separate scopes - integrated slices combining front-end and back-end that can be finished independently - and tackle them one at a time.

Capture concrete granular tasks first and factor them into scopes only after real work reveals how they relate; scopes are bigger than tasks but much smaller than the whole project and finishable in a few days or less.
Track scopes in practice as to-do lists, with one list per scope.
Scopes become the shared macro-level language of the project, used to discuss dependencies and to report status by pointing to finished pieces instead of defending individual outstanding tasks.
Treat scope mapping as discovery, not planning: walk the territory first, because well-drawn scopes reflect the real interdependencies of the problem rather than arbitrary tidy groupings.

Scopes, like tasks, must be discovered by doing real work, so accurate scopes usually appear only around the end of week one or start of week two, with early shuffling and renaming as the true boundaries become clear.

Scopes are right when you can see the whole project with nothing worrying hidden in the details, conversations flow because the scopes give the right language, and you always know which bucket a new task belongs in.

Redraw a scope when it is hard to tell how done it is (its tasks are unrelated, so factor something out), when its name is not unique to the project ('front-end' or 'bugs' grab-bags signal too little integration), or when it is too big to finish soon (break it up).
File bugs under a specific scope rather than a generic 'bugs' list, so you can tell whether that scope is actually done or still needs fixes.

For layer-cake work (a thin, evenly distributed back-end beneath the UI), integrate design and programming tasks in one scope and judge progress by UI surface area, a good default for information-system apps.

For icebergs (far more back-end than UI or vice versa), factor the UI into its own scope and split complex back-end into separate concerns and scopes, so work is finished and integrated in stages rather than at the 11th hour.
condition: when the UI is not interdependent with the back-end complexity

statement: Always question an iceberg's complexity before accepting it: is the complexity necessary and irreducible, is the fancy UI really needed, and is there a way to build the back-end with fewer interdependencies?
Keep a 'Chowder' list for loose tasks that fit no scope, but stay skeptical: once it grows past three to five items, a scope is probably hiding there.
Mark nice-to-haves with a leading tilde (~) so the team can continuously separate must-haves from nice-to-haves and cut the constantly growing scope.
To-do lists alone cannot show status: an empty list may mean the work is done or that tasks have not yet been discovered, and lists actually grow as the team makes progress.
Do not judge progress by counting tasks, because discovered work means the number of outstanding tasks can rise as well as fall.
Estimates do not show uncertainty - the same four-hour estimate means very different things for familiar versus never-done work - so numeric estimates mislead about a project's status.
Shift the focus of status reporting from what is done or not done to what is unknown versus what is solved.

Every piece of work has an uphill phase of figuring out the approach (full of uncertainty, unknowns, and problem-solving) and a downhill phase of execution (marked by certainty, seeing everything, and knowing what to do).
'Percent complete' and time estimates are meaningless during the uphill phase and become fair only at the top of the hill, once all the remaining steps are visible.
Plot each scope on the hill to show its status, letting the scopes supply the project's language and the hill supply the state (uphill versus downhill).

Make status self-serve: let the team who has full context position the scopes on the hill, and use the comparison of past states to see how work is moving - what is in motion and what is stuck - without interrupting the team with the status question.
People hide uncertainty because nobody wants to admit being stuck, which accumulates hidden risk, yet the moments when someone is stuck or going in circles hold the biggest risks and opportunities.

Use the hill chart to surface stuck work without anyone having to say it (a dot that does not move is effectively a raised hand) and keep the uphill/downhill conversation about the work rather than the person.

When a scope sits stuck on the hill, check whether it is simply badly drawn (several unrelated parts) and break it into smaller, independently movable scopes so progress shows accurately and more frequently.

Do the uphill work with your hands, not just your head: treat the first third uphill as 'I have thought about this', the second as 'I have validated my approach', and the final third as 'I have built enough to believe there are no other unknowns', since backsliding usually means a scope was declared solved from a mental theory.

Use the hill chart to sequence work by pushing the scariest, most uncertain scopes uphill first, asking which could be whipped together despite their unknowns and which might prove harder than expected.
Get the critical unknown scopes over the top of the hill early and leave the routine 'screw-tightening' work for last.

Work expands to fill the available time, so tackle novel, risky work first (such as a geocoder) rather than easily refinable work (such as an email template), so nasty surprises do not surface at the end of the cycle.

Sequence problem-solving like a journalist's inverted pyramid: solve the most important, most-unknown problems first and leave the most routine or least worrisome for last, aiming to end the cycle with only nice-to-haves lingering.
Shipping on time means shipping something imperfect, because there is always more work than time.
Direct pride in the work at the right target: aiming for an ideal, perfect design is unreachable, yet you also must not lower your standards.
Shift the point of comparison from the ideal down to the baseline - the current reality for customers without the feature - to decide when the work is good enough.
Judge good-enough by asking how customers solve the problem today and whether the current work already beats that frustrating workaround.
'Better than what they have now' beats 'never good enough'; framing the decision as customer value rather than personal perfection motivates making the calls.
Let the circuit breaker force trade-offs: before accepting a 'wouldn't it be better if...' or a newly found edge case, first ask 'is there time for this?'
Expect teams to actively make trade-offs and question scope rather than cram to finish tasks, questioning any new work before accepting it as necessary.
Scope grows naturally and scope creep is nobody's fault, because projects are opaque at the macro scale and you only discover the complexities and possible improvements once you are down in the work.
Every project is full of scope you do not need: not every part must be equally prominent, fast, or polished, and not every use case is equally common, critical, or aligned with the target market.
Instead of fighting to prevent scope from growing, equip teams with the tools, authority, and responsibility to keep cutting it back.
Cutting scope does not leave holes in the product; making choices makes the product better at some things than others and differentiates it in competitive space.
Variable scope is not about sacrificing quality - stay extremely picky about quality - but about asking which things actually move the needle for the core use cases.

'Hammer' scope (a stronger act than merely cutting) by asking of each new item: is it a must-have, could we ship without it, what happens if we don't, is it new or pre-existing, how likely is the case, which customers see it (core or edge), what is its actual impact, and how aligned is it with the intended audience?

Capture must-haves as tasks without which a scope is not done, and mark nice-to-haves with a leading tilde as do-if-time items that usually never get built - the act of marking them is the scope hammering.
Place QA at the end of the cycle to hunt edge cases outside the core, because designers and programmers own the basic quality of their own work and programmers write their own tests.
Treat QA as a level-up, not a gate that every piece of work must pass through, and do not depend on QA to ship quality features.
Treat QA-discovered issues as nice-to-haves by default, collecting them on a separate list and dragging only the ones triaged as must-haves onto the scope they affect.
Treat code review like QA: not a required check-point that blocks shipping, but a 'makes it better' teaching opportunity to use when there is time.

Extend a project past its deadline only rarely, and only when the outstanding tasks are true must-haves that survived every scope-hammering attempt and the remaining work is all downhill with no unsolved problems or open questions.
condition: only when the remaining tasks are true must-haves and all remaining work is downhill

statement: Treat any uphill work left at the end of a cycle as a signal of a shaping oversight or hole; because unknowns are too risky to bet on, put the troubled project back into shaping rather than extend it.

For most projects, stay disciplined and hold the appetite: the two-week cool-down usually absorbs a handful of leftover must-haves, and routinely spilling into cool-down points to a shaping or team-performance problem.

Expect shipping to generate new work (feature requests, bugs, and sometimes intense pushback on workflow or visual changes); stay cool, avoid knee-jerk reactions, give it a few days to die down, and remember why you made the change.
Do not commit to changes in response to incoming feedback; treat it as raw ideas handled with a gentle 'no' to keep a clean slate, because saying yes takes away future freedom like taking on debt.
Remember that what you shipped was a bet for one cycle, so more work on that area requires a new bet - let new requests and bugs compete with everything else at the next betting table.

Treat customer feedback as unshaped raw input to the Set Boundaries step; if a request is truly important, make it a top shaping priority next cycle (betting other work for the teams to build) and schedule the shaped version later.
When adopting Shape Up, separate its basic truths (which are universal) from its specific practices (which are scale-dependent).

It takes real work to figure out the right work (shaping), and if you do not make trade-offs up front by shaping, the universe forces you into them later in a rush against deadlines, technical limits, and resource constraints.
Whatever the exact time frame, be deliberate about what you bet on and cap the downside with a circuit breaker.
Separate the knowns from the unknowns so you can order the work sensibly and keep capacity in reserve for the unknowns, with or without a hill chart.

A tiny team of two or three people can drop most of the structure (no fixed six-week cycles, cool-down, formal pitches, or betting table) and instead have the same people alternate shaping and building fluidly with variable bet sizes, staying deliberate about which hat and phase they are in.
condition: when the team is only two or three people

statement: As headcount grows, the earlier fluidity flips from an asset to a liability and ad-hoc coordination breaks down, which is when it makes sense to adopt six-week cycles, cool-downs, and a formal betting table.
condition: after the team grows beyond a handful of people

statement: With more builders available, someone must carve out more time to figure out what to build, whether a founder shaping more than building or an employee elevated from in-cycle work to out-of-cycle shaping.
Protect the core product team from interruptions at scale by assigning lower-level infrastructure, operations, and support-side technical work to separate dedicated teams.

Adopt Shape Up incrementally with a single six-week experiment: shape one project conservatively, guarantee one designer and two programmers uninterrupted time, present it as a pitch, hand over task discovery to the team, and encourage them to Get One Piece Done.
Prove success on one team and one commitment first to gain the credibility needed to convert the wider organization to the method.

Alternatively enter through shaping (better-shaped work opens the team to longer cycles and deliberate betting) or through cycles (six-week cycles remove sprint-planning overhead and let programmers build momentum).
Fix shipping first: build the muscle of finishing and shipping before improving research or discovery, because the best customer insight is worthless if you cannot turn it into a shipped project.

Judge success at the macro level - whether you will feel good having shipped the project after the cycle - rather than micromanaging whether every hour or day was optimally used or whether someone sat idle briefly.

Lean UX applies Lean principles to remove waste from the UX design process: produce only the design artifacts genuinely needed to move the team's learning forward, rather than heavily documented handoffs.

Lean UX harmonizes the whole cross-functional system (designers, developers, product managers, QA engineers, marketers) through transparent collaboration that brings non-designers into the design process.

Rather than relying on a single hero designer to divine the best solution from one point of view, Lean UX uses rapid experimentation and measurement to learn how well ideas actually meet the team's goals.
In Lean UX the designer's role evolves toward design facilitation, taking on a new set of responsibilities beyond producing artifacts.
Lean UX rests on three foundations: Lean Startup, design thinking, and Agile development philosophy.
Agile development refocuses software work on value by delivering working software to customers quickly and adjusting regularly to new learning.
Design thinking is a solution-focused approach to problem solving that iterates collaboratively through ideation, prototyping, implementation, and learning.

Lean UX breaks down the barriers that isolate software designers from business needs and from implementation, bringing business and technology partners into ongoing collaboration on the best solutions.
Teams should get out of the deliverables business and refocus effort on delighting customers rather than on producing hand-off documents.
Building a pixel-perfect specification is not a reliable way to make a meaningful difference to a real product; detailed spec deliverables are frequently celebrated and then never acted upon.

An interaction-design team spent months and a six-figure fee producing a pixel-perfect ecommerce-redesign specification deck; the client praised it but six months later nothing on the site had changed.

Handing engineering a fixed, complete up-front specification is a failure mode because the spec cannot adapt when it proves unworkable, when market conditions change, or when concepts that worked in the lab lack commercial appeal.
condition: when design work is delivered as a fixed, complete specification handed off to engineering

statement: A company that funded a multi-year 'view of the future' study commercialized none of its recommendations a decade later and blamed its engineers and managers rather than the big-design-up-front approach.
Lean UX is fundamentally a mindset, not merely a collection of tactics and techniques.
Lean UX applies to both green-field (brand-new) products and established products, but the challenges differ by context.
condition: green-field projects face continual change with little time for up-front planning, while established products must build on existing platforms while growing revenue and brand value

statement: Practising Lean UX by sharing rough, unfinished work depends on a high-functioning, supportive team that accepts it will not get the design right the first time and iterates together.
condition: requires a supportive, high-functioning team

statement: Reframe design conversations away from features and documents toward objective, measurable business goals.
Designers can no longer work in isolation; effective Lean UX requires daily, continuous engagement with the whole product team.
Continuous team engagement lets a team strip away heavy deliverables in favour of techniques that build shared understanding with teammates.

Design thinking asserts that any part of a business can be tackled with design methods, which licenses designers to work beyond their usual boundaries and invites non-designers to apply design methods to their own problems.

Lean UX applies Agile's values to product design by favouring individuals and interactions over processes and tools and working software over comprehensive documentation: engage the whole team, exchange ideas freely, and build working software sooner so competing solutions can be assessed for market fit and viability.

Lean UX applies Agile's values to product design by favouring customer collaboration over contract negotiation and responding to change over following a plan: collaboration builds shared understanding and consensus, and the team assumes its initial designs are wrong and adjusts through repeated testing against market input.
Lean Startup's build-measure-learn feedback loop minimizes project risk by getting teams to build and learn quickly, shipping Minimum Viable Products early to start learning as soon as possible.
Treat each design as a hypothesis, a proposed business solution, and validate it as efficiently as possible using customer feedback before evolving it.
An MVP is the least you can build to put a hypothesis to the test, and it does not have to be code: it can be a rough stand-in for the eventual experience.

Lean UX is the discipline of surfacing a product's true nature sooner through cross-functional collaboration that de-emphasizes heavy documentation in favour of a shared, first-hand grasp of the real product experience.

Staff Lean UX teams with all relevant disciplines (software engineering, product management, interaction and visual design, content strategy, marketing, and QA) collaborating continuously from day one to the end of the engagement, which collapses the gated-handoff waterfall process.
Keep teams small (no more than about ten core people), dedicated to a single project, and colocated in one place, to maximize communication, focus, and camaraderie.
condition: core team of no more than ~10 people, dedicated to one project, and colocated

statement: Measure progress by explicitly defined business outcomes rather than by outputs (features and services), because a feature's efficacy is largely speculation until it is live in the market.
Assign a team a business problem to solve rather than a fixed set of features to implement, because doing so shows trust and drives deeper ownership of the solution.
Treat anything in the team's process that does not contribute to improved outcomes as waste, and remove it so the team can move faster and stay focused.

Use small batch sizes: create only the design necessary to move the team forward and avoid building a large inventory of untested, unimplemented design ideas, which forces waiting, idles teammates, and produces unused assets.

Practise continuous discovery: engage customers throughout the design and development process via regularly scheduled qualitative and quantitative research that involves the entire team, building shared empathy and reducing later debriefs.

Get out of the building (GOOB): resolve debates about user needs with real customers in the marketplace rather than in internal meeting rooms, giving customers a chance to react to ideas much sooner than traditional practice.

Build shared understanding as the team's core currency, because the more the team collectively understands what it is doing and why, the less it must depend on secondhand reports and detailed documents.

Avoid staffing ego-driven rockstars, gurus, and ninjas, because individuals who do not share their ideas or the spotlight break down the team cohesion and collaboration that shared understanding depends on.

Externalize work by getting it out of individuals' heads and computers into public view (whiteboards, artifact walls, printouts, sticky notes), creating an ambient flow of information and letting every team member, even the quiet ones, participate.

Value making over analysis: creating the first version of an idea is more valuable than debating its merits in a conference room, because the hardest questions are answered by customers in the field, not internally.
Favour learning first and scaling second, because scaling an unproven idea across the entire user base wastes time and resources if it turns out not to work.

Give teams permission to fail, providing a safe technical and cultural environment to experiment, because most experimental ideas fail and a culture of safe experimentation breeds creativity, innovation, and greater mastery of skills.

In a ceramics-class experiment, the group graded on the total quantity of pots they produced ended up making higher-quality pots than the group graded on a single perfect pot, because rapid iteration and repeated failure let them learn faster.

Get out of the deliverables business: refocus stakeholder conversations from which artifact is being produced to which outcome is being achieved, because documents do not solve customer problems, good products do.
Day to day, a Lean UX team works together, iteratively, and in parallel with minimal handoffs and deliverables, keeping its attention on working software and signals from the market.
A shared living style guide of premade components lets front-end developers begin building in parallel without waiting for the designer to finish detailing the design.
condition: when the team maintains a living style guide of reusable premade components

statement: Frame work as changing something in the world (an outcome) rather than producing a deliverable: start with assumptions instead of requirements, create and test hypotheses, and measure whether the desired outcomes were achieved.
Use a hypothesis statement as a project's starting point to shift the conversation from outputs (for example, 'create a single sign-on feature') to outcomes (for example, 'increase new sign-ups').

A hypothesis statement expresses assumptions in testable form and comprises five elements (assumptions, hypotheses, outcomes, personas, and features), where outcomes are the market signal (often quantitative, sometimes qualitative) sought to validate or invalidate the hypotheses.
Begin the Lean UX process by explicitly declaring the team's assumptions, because every project rests on assumptions that teams usually ignore or, worse, treat as facts.

Declare assumptions as a group exercise with all disciplines and any relevant subject-matter experts present (for example, a call-center representative for a customer-complaint problem), to create a common starting point and surface both divergent opinions and a broad set of possible solutions.

Before an assumptions exercise, prepare inputs in advance: analytics on how the current product is used, usability findings on why customers act, the history of past fix attempts, the business stakeholder's analysis of impact, and competitive analyses.
Start the assumptions exercise from a problem statement, because it gives the team a clear focus and defines the constraints that group work needs as guardrails to stay grounded and aligned.

Use a problem-statement template with three parts: what the product was designed to achieve, the observed gap and its adverse business effect, and an explicit 'how might we improve X so customers are more successful based on [measurable criteria]' request that does not dictate a specific solution.
Teams starting from scratch may not have a clear problem statement; they can still use the business assumptions worksheet but should expect reaching consensus on some questions to take longer.
exception: teams starting from scratch may lack a clear problem statement

statement: Use a business assumptions worksheet to facilitate the assumptions discussion, answering the questions as a team either through open discussion or a structured brainstorm/affinity-mapping exercise, and make sure everyone gets a chance to contribute.

The goal of the assumptions worksheet is to collect statements of what the team thinks might be true; full agreement is not required, and where there is strong disagreement the team should capture the differing perspectives.
exception: the team need not reach agreement on every answer; capture divergent perspectives on points of strong disagreement

statement: The business-assumptions portion of the worksheet surfaces beliefs about customer needs, the solution, initial customers, the number-one value the customer wants, additional benefits, the primary acquisition channel, how the business makes money, the main competition, the basis for beating it, the biggest product risk and its mitigation, and any other assumptions that would cause failure if proven false.

The user-assumptions portion of the worksheet asks who the user is, where the product fits in their work or life, what problems it solves, when and how it is used, which features matter, and how it should look and behave.

Adapt the worksheet questions to your situation: early in a product's life spend more time on business assumptions, and for a mature product focus on user assumptions, while still casting a broad net across all dimensions.
condition: early-stage products weight business assumptions; mature products weight user assumptions

statement: Declare assumptions at the start of work specifically to identify project risks, then determine which assumptions are riskiest so the team can work on those first.

Lean UX is an exercise in ruthless prioritization: since you cannot test every assumption, prioritize the ones to test by their level of risk (how bad it would be to be wrong) and how little the team understands them, testing the highest-risk, most-unknown assumptions first.
Keep a backlog of the assumptions that do not make the first cut so the team can return to test them if and when it makes sense, rather than discarding them permanently.

Transform each prioritized assumption into a testable hypothesis statement of the form: 'We believe [this statement is true]. We will know we are right or wrong when we see [qualitative and/or quantitative feedback or KPI change].'
Expressing assumptions as hypotheses removes much of the subjective and political conversation from decision-making and reorients the team toward market feedback and toward users and customers.

When a hypothesis is too large to test in one go, split it into narrower subhypotheses using a template such as: we believe [this feature or experience] for [this persona] will produce [this outcome], and we will know we are right when we observe [a market signal, quantitative measure, or qualitative insight].

Success criteria should not be all numbers: include qualitative feedback such as delight, recommendations, and social sharing alongside quantitative measures, because reducing every design decision to measurable factors can take the soul out of products.

Capture a benchmark of the current state of your success metrics before writing hypotheses, because without a prior benchmark the metrics are meaningless and the team will not know what it is targeting.
Assemble hypothesis statements from three kinds of raw material: the outcomes you are trying to create, definitions of the personas you are serving, and the set of features you believe might work.

Be specific about outcomes and break high-level outcomes (such as increasing signups or usage) into smaller predictive behaviours (more site visitors, higher email click-through, more items in the cart), sometimes via a team brainstorm.

In Lean UX, reverse the traditional persona order of operations: start with assumption-based personas and then do research to validate them, instead of treating personas as the untouchable output of lengthy, expensive research studies.

Create proto-personas, a best guess of who is using the product and why, in a few hours sketched on paper with the whole team contributing, then refine them as ongoing research reveals how accurate the initial guesses were.

A team building a Community-Supported-Agriculture app assumed its cooks were mostly women and spent about an hour creating a persona named Susan, but field research revealed most cooks were young men, so they revised the persona to Timothy and stopped wasting time designing for the wrong audience.

Sketch each proto-persona on a folded four-quadrant sheet holding a rough sketch with name and role, behaviour-predicting demographic information, the user's needs and pain points, and potential feature or solution ideas.
Create personas through a team brainstorm, then narrow to an initial set of three or four target personas, differentiating them by needs and roles rather than by demographics.
In Lean UX, features are only a means to serve business, customer, and user needs, so avoid the common trap of beginning from a feature idea and then reasoning backward to justify it.

Brainstorm candidate features as a team, with each member writing ideas on sticky notes with a thick marker, then posting them to the wall and arranging them into themes, looking for features that will drive customer behaviour in the desired direction.

Organize the raw material into testable hypotheses, splitting any hypothesis in which one feature drives more than one outcome so each statement refers to a single outcome, and keeping ideas specific enough to create meaningful tests.

Collaborative design brings designers and non-designers together in co-creation to yield ideas bigger and better than any individual's, but it is not design-by-committee: it increases the team's ownership by giving all opinions a hearing much earlier in the process.

Across a project's full arc, collaborative design outperforms hero-based design (parachuting a designer in to produce something beautiful and then depart), because working together lifts the whole team's design IQ, broadens the pool of ideas, and builds ownership and shared understanding.

Collaborative design remains a designer-led activity: it is the designer's responsibility both to call the sessions and to facilitate them, whether a one-on-one whiteboard session with a developer or a full-team Design Studio.
Produce low-fidelity sketches and wireframes in collaborative sessions, because low fidelity keeps the work malleable and makes it much easier to pivot when tests reveal the approach is not working.

Promote conversation as the primary means of communication among team members (in line with Agile's 'individuals and interactions over processes and tools'), because it unites the team around a shared vision and brings cross-disciplinary insight to the project far earlier than a traditional design cycle.

Have design conversations early and often so team members can start their own work sooner: for example, engineers can begin required back-end infrastructure while the design is still being refined, and parallel software-development and design paths are the fastest route to an actual experience.

A designer struggling to lay out a data-heavy dashboard grabbed a whiteboard with the lead developer, co-sketched back and forth for about two hours, converged on a layout that was both usable and feasible within their two-week sprint, and then built the first version without waiting to document it.

Use a Design Studio (also called a Design Charrette) to bring a cross-functional team into one space to visualize potential solutions to a design problem, which breaks down organizational silos and builds the trust needed to move toward more frequent, informal collaboration.

Treat the Design Studio ritual as adjustable rather than fixed: the specific steps are not the goal, so run more or less formal versions as the situation and timing warrant, aiming to solve problems with colleagues and clients.
exception: run more or less formal Design Studios as the situation and timing warrant

statement: A Design Studio follows five steps: problem definition and constraints, individual idea generation (diverge), presentation and critique, iterate and refine (emerge), and team idea generation (converge).
A Design Studio works best for a team of five to eight people; when there are more people, create multiple teams and have them compare output at the end.
condition: teams of five to eight; split into multiple teams when larger

statement: In the individual idea-generation step, give each person a six-box (6-up) template and a few minutes to sketch six low-fidelity solutions as visual articulations rather than written words, reassuring the team that anyone who can draw a circle, square, and triangle can sketch an interface.

In presentation and critique, give each participant about three minutes to present while stating the persona and pain point addressed, and require critique that clarifies the presenter's intentions (for example 'How does this address the persona's problem?') rather than vague dislikes, ensuring every member both presents and receives critique.

In the iterate-and-refine step, have each participant use the critique they received to develop their six ideas into a single, more evolved big idea on one sheet, then repeat the present-and-critique cycle.

After individual sketching and critique, have the team converge on the single idea with the biggest chance of success, sketching its components and workflow on a large easel pad or whiteboard; this converged idea becomes the basis for creating an MVP and running experiments.

Reaching consensus on a converged design requires compromise: have the team prioritize and pare back features, and use a 'parking lot' to capture good ideas that do not make the cut so it is easier to let them go.
Use the artifacts produced in a Design Studio to create the refined wireframes, prototypes, and early code that drive the team toward proving their hypotheses.

A style guide (pattern library) is a living collection of all of a product's customer-facing components across interactive, visual, and copy elements; the rule of thumb is that if it is made of pixels, it belongs in the style guide.

Style guides create efficiency by providing a repository of ready-to-go, approved interface components, so developers can start building core UI without waiting for a designer and the team stops debating mundane elements like label or button placement.

Style guides also free interaction and visual designers from recreating experiences that already exist, letting them focus on novel design challenges, and they streamline approval and review cycles so reviews focus on the core product challenge.

Treat the style guide as a maintained living process rather than a static artifact: dedicate people and time to keeping it current, and lower the friction of using it so that following the guide is easier than bypassing it, keeping compliance effortless.

There are two approaches to building a style guide: 'big bang', where the team takes a fixed block of time away from projects to document all UI elements at once (fast to produce but the team learns nothing new meanwhile), and 'slow drip', where an element is added whenever one is created or changed (keeps the project moving but is rarely completed).
Choose the big-bang style-guide approach for a young or relatively simple product and the slow-drip approach for a legacy or complex product.
condition: young/simple product favours big bang; legacy/complex product favours slow drip

statement: Facing roughly 500 developers per designer, GE's UX team could not scale design by hiring more designers or by reviewing every project (which turned the UX Center of Excellence into a bottleneck), so it built the Industrial Internet Design System to empower about 8,000 engineers with templates, guidelines, assets, and code snippets.

After GE introduced the Industrial Internet Design System, average project lifecycles shortened by as much as six months with estimated resource savings in the millions per year, and teams could reach a clickable version of an experience in days instead of months and validate it before heavy back-end integration.

Empowering developers with reusable templates, guidelines, assets, and code snippets lets teams create good user experiences themselves without waiting for design assistance or approval, which is how design scales in a very large organization.

For each interaction-design element in the style guide, provide three data points: what it looks like (minimum and maximum sizes, vertical and horizontal constraints, styling), where it is usually placed on screen (and any exceptions), and when it should be used rather than an alternative element.

Also include visual-design elements (color palette with hex values and per-state colors, logos, headers, footers, grid structures, typography) and codified copywriting styles (brand tone, allowed and forbidden words, grammar, and button and navigation language), documented with the same what/where/when detail.
A successful style guide has three characteristics: it is accessible, it is continually improved (a living document), and it is actionable.

Make the style guide accessible: easily found via a memorable URL everyone knows, easily distributed so teams can reach it anywhere including mobile, easy to search, and easy to use, because if it is not usable it will quickly go unused.
Keep the style guide continually improved as a living document, malleable enough to easily add updates as the product and customers evolve and as designers create new elements.

Use a wiki for the style guide because wikis are familiar to developers, keep revision histories that let you roll back UI changes, and track who changed what with commenting that captures decisions and rationale and speeds onboarding of new team members.

Make the style guide actionable, functioning as a 'widget factory' that produces any interface element on demand: offer each element for download not just as code but also as graphical and wireframe assets, so every designer always has a full palette for prototyping.

Create a style guide in two parts: first build a table of contents that structures it into sections (interaction design, visual design, copywriting, branding guidelines, accessibility, and any other high-level buckets), then populate the content via the big-bang or slow-drip approach.

Assign an owner or curator responsible for keeping the style guide current by reaching out to content creators so elements are entered as they are created; because the editor role is thankless, rotate it regularly, for example every three months.
condition: rotate the style-guide curator role roughly every three months

statement: The style guide must serve developers, not just designers: house code snippets so developers have a one-stop shop for design direction plus foundational code that gets them to an experience far faster.

A live style guide uses the same code the application uses, which makes it much closer to self-maintaining because changes to the site's HTML and CSS appear in the guide, but it adds infrastructure and process burden and still needs someone to curate it and resolve conflicts.
condition: live style guides trade extra infrastructure and process burden for near-self-maintenance and still require curation

statement: Physical distance is one of the biggest challenges to strong collaboration and makes techniques like Design Studio harder, but tools such as video calls, shared Google Docs, wikis, and a camera phone can make cross-time-zone collaboration effective.

A distributed team split between New York and Vancouver ran a remote Design Studio by connecting each conference room through a location-specific group video account, using a shared Google Docs spreadsheet for affinity mapping, and setting up dual monitors so each room could see both the sketches and their remote teammates.

For remote affinity mapping, have each person write ideas in their own labeled column, read them aloud so the whole distributed team is aware of them, then copy each idea into a matching theme on a second sheet, creating or renaming themes as needed until ideas are sorted into groups.

To run a remote Design Studio, mimic the co-located version as closely as possible: distribute paper and pens to each location, keep a persistent group video connection, and share photographed sketches so every member can present, receive critique, and converge on one idea together.

Use MVPs to test assumptions about whether a tactic will achieve the desired outcome while minimizing the work invested in unproven ideas, so the team can focus its limited resources sooner on the best solutions; this is an important way Lean UX minimizes waste.

An MVP is the smallest thing you can create to determine the validity of a hypothesis; you run experiments with it, and the experiment outcomes tell you whether the direction should be pursued, refined, or abandoned.

The term MVP is used in two different ways, so clarify which you intend: an MVP built primarily to learn something (not concerned with delivering value yet) versus a small version of a product or feature built to start delivering value to the market quickly (from which you can also learn if it is designed and deployed correctly).

A company weighing an expensive monthly newsletter first tested demand with an MVP that was merely a signup form on its existing high-traffic site, which delivered no customer value yet but let the team learn quickly whether to proceed, deferring any work on the actual newsletter until a GO/NO-GO decision.

When planning an MVP, first decide what you are trying to learn among three basic questions: is there a need for the solution, is there value in the solution and features offered, and is the solution usable.

The need question is probably best answered with traditional design research, while value and usability questions are well served by an MVP: a value question favours a learning-optimized MVP, and a usability question favours emphasizing value delivery so you can release the product and observe users in realistic contexts.
condition: need -> traditional research; value -> learning-optimized MVP; usability -> value-delivery MVP

statement: To maximize learning from an MVP: be clear and concise by distilling the idea to its core value proposition, prioritize ruthlessly and let the best ideas prove themselves, stay agile in a medium that is easy to update, measure behaviour rather than opinion because behaviour trumps opinion, and use a call-to-action because opting in or signing up signals genuine interest.

To deliver value with an MVP: make it functional enough to integrate with the rest of the application for a realistic usage scenario, integrate it with existing analytics so performance is measured within real product workflows, and keep it consistent with the current style guide and brand to minimize novelty bias.
Regardless of its focus, build the smallest MVP possible and treat it as a tool for learning that you will iterate on, modify, or may throw away entirely.
In many cases an MVP involves no code at all, relying instead on the UX designer's existing tools such as sketching, prototyping, copywriting, and visual design.

One of the most effective ways to create an MVP is to prototype the experience: a clickable or tappable approximation that simulates using the product, built with as little effort as possible, which makes the choice of prototyping tool important.
Choose a prototyping tool based on who will interact with it, what you hope to learn, and how much time you have to create it.

Specify the intended audience for a prototype so you can build the smallest prototype that generates meaningful feedback: engineers on your own team can ignore unaffected areas like global navigation, whereas stakeholders less familiar with the product need higher fidelity to grasp the concept.
condition: tailor prototype fidelity to the audience: lower for informed engineers, higher for less-familiar stakeholders

statement: Keep a fairly broad prototyping toolkit and range of methods so you can meet the differing fidelity needs of disparate audiences.

Paper prototypes (paper, pens, tape) let you simulate an experience quickly and cheaply with no digital investment, giving an immediate sense of what is present or missing and how the workflow coalesces, and are especially helpful for touch interfaces; their limits are that iteration and duplication become tedious, the simulation is artificial because real input devices are not used, and feedback is confined to high-level structure and flow.

Clickable wireframes add fidelity so participants use real digital input, giving better insight at the level of the click, tap, or gesture, and reveal workflow length, major obstacles to task completion, and the findability of core elements while reusing existing assets; their limits are that savvy users recognize an unfinished product and that labeling and copy draw more attention than normal.

Many tools exist for low-fidelity clickable wireframes (for example Balsamiq, Visio, OmniGraffle, PowerPoint or Keynote, and mobile tools like POP), and no single list is comprehensive, so trial several (most offer free trials) to see which fits how your team works.

Mid- and high-fidelity prototypes carry near-final detail in interaction, visual, and content design, let you test visual and brand elements and UI interactions, and often allow pixel-perfect simulation with working forms, menus, buttons, and minor animations; their limits are that interactivity is still more constrained than native, users usually cannot interact with real data, and building and keeping them in sync with the product can be time-consuming and duplicative.

Coded prototypes offer the highest fidelity, being nearly indistinguishable from the final product until their scope limits are reached, since they live in the native environment with real interactive elements and real input devices; their risks are that the team can get bogged down debating finer points, working code is slow to build, it is tempting to perfect the code before release, and iterating takes a lot of time.

There are two levels of coded prototype: hand-coded prototypes that look and function like the product but handle no real-time data, and live-data prototypes that connect to real-time data, process user input, can be deployed to real customers for analytical insight, and can support A/B testing.
Do not prototype the entire product; simulate only the most important part of the experience for the customer and the business by focusing on the core workflows that illustrate your MVP.

Concentrating a prototype on its primary workflows gives the team a helpful, temporary narrowing of focus, letting them examine one slice of the experience and judge whether it is valid and effective.

Test the prototyped MVP broadly, first with teammates, stakeholders, other teams, and colleagues, then with customers and potential customers, because more exposure yields more insight into its validity and also shows stakeholders that progress is being made.

An established startup considering opening its exclusive subscription community to a broader market framed the plan as a hypothesis, built five Balsamiq wireframes into a clickable prototype in a week (showing current customers twice), tested it on iPads at a conference, and in eight business days total gathered feedback showing the plan needed further differentiation to succeed.

Prototyping is not the only path to an MVP: sometimes an MVP that does not simulate your product but tests something related to it is better, and building a prototype is occasionally unnecessary and can even be harmful.

When creating a non-prototype MVP, keep the mantra 'you can always go leaner' and plan it by asking four questions: what am I trying to learn, what main market signals validate the hypothesis, what proxy signals can indicate the main signal, and what is the fastest way to find this information.
Email can serve as a non-prototype MVP because recipients' open, click-through, and task-completion rates all indicate whether an idea holds value.
Use Google AdWords as a cheap experiment: monitor which searches and messages resonate with your audience and measure click-throughs to gauge how much interest there is in your proposed language.

Use a landing page, a facade of your service carrying one specific, obvious call-to-action (Sign-up, Buy Now, or Share-With-A-Friend), to validate an idea, counting each user who completes the action as validation of the product idea.

Use a 'button to nowhere': add a button that touts new functionality but only measures how often it is clicked, treat each click as a signal of desire for that feature, and give the user an explanation of why it is not working while capturing an email address or other feedback.
Designing MVP tests is a creative process, and the best approach is often a mashup of several methods, so use the listed techniques as inspiration rather than a fixed menu.

Cheryl Yeoh validated CityPockets with a Concierge MVP: a front-end-only site where each signup received a unique email address to forward coupons to, which she entered into a database by hand, using an arbitrary threshold of 500 emails a day as the signal that demand justified building the real back end.
At its core the Lean UX approach means designing no more than necessary, delivering it rapidly, and staying in close enough contact with customers to learn from real feedback quickly.
Validate your MVPs with lightweight, continuous, and collaborative research rather than outsourcing research to a specialized team or running it only at the beginning or end of a project.
Make research continuous by building bite-sized research activities into every sprint instead of running a costly, disruptive big-bang research process.

Make research collaborative by distributing research activities and responsibilities across the whole team, because eliminating the handoff between researchers and team members increases the quality of learning and builds a rich shared understanding.

Use collaborative discovery, in which the whole team gets out of the building to test ideas with customers, to multiply the number of customer-insight inputs and let everyone see how the hypotheses are testing; do not outsource it, because outsourcing wastes time, squanders team-building, and filters information through deliverables, handoffs, and interpretation.
If you have a trained researcher, include them on the team as a coach who helps the team plan and execute research, rather than outsourcing the research work to that person.
condition: a researcher is available; use them as a coach, not an outsourced doer

statement: Run collaborative discovery in the field with a defined sequence: as a team review your questions, assumptions, hypotheses, and MVPs and decide what to learn and whom to speak to, create a shared interview guide, split into mixed-discipline interview pairs each armed with the MVP, and send them out to meet customers.

In each discovery interview, have one member interview while the other takes notes, start with questions, conversation, and observation, demonstrate the MVP later in the session, collect notes as the customer reacts, switch roles so the note-taker can ask follow-ups, and end by asking the customer for referrals to others.

Prepare an interview guide as a notebook cheat sheet of questions and topics, structured as a sequential funnel: first identify whether the person is in your target audience, then confirm your problem hypotheses for that segment, and show any prototype or mockup last to avoid limiting the conversation to your own vision of the solution.

A PayPal team of two designers, a researcher, four developers, and a product manager ran collaborative discovery at shopping malls with an Axure prototype in mixed pairs, swapping interviewer and note-taker roles after an hour; reading notes back revealed patterns that proved and disproved assumptions, they adjusted the prototype and returned to the field, and the next sprint began with a shared baseline of clarity.

Build a regular cadence of customer involvement, because regularly scheduled customer conversations minimize the time between hypothesis creation, experiment design, and user feedback and remove pressure from decision-making by keeping the team never more than a few days from meaningful market data.
Use a weekly '3-12-1' lab rhythm, three users seen by 12 noon once a week, to keep the whole team involved in continuous research by bringing customers into the building.

Structure the 3-12-1 research week as: Monday recruit and plan (outsource recruiting if possible because it is time-consuming), Tuesday and Wednesday refine the MVP or prototype until it tells at least one complete story and write the moderator's test script, Thursday test with no more than an hour per customer while the whole team takes notes and watches, and review findings immediately, and Friday decide whether hypotheses were validated and what to do next.

You no longer need a dedicated usability lab to test: a quiet space in the office, a computer with a network connection and a webcam, and desktop recording and broadcasting software (such as Morae, Silverback, or GoToMeeting) are enough.

Broadcasting test sessions to team members and stakeholders who cannot be present spreads understanding of your customers deep into the organization and has an enormous positive impact on collaboration.

The whole team should watch usability tests, because when the entire team observes and reacts in real time you need fewer subsequent debriefings and everyone learns firsthand where efforts are succeeding and failing.

Offload the time-intensive work of recruiting, scheduling, and confirming participants to a third-party recruiter (roughly $75 to $150 per participant) who also handles screening and the replacement of no-shows on testing day.

Meetup iterated toward a 'minimally viable process' for testing: only the moderator sits with the user while the rest of the team watches a video feed from another room (a full room of observers made participants uneasy), product managers guide moderators over instant messaging instead of fixed scripts, the team debriefs immediately, recruiting was brought in-house, and testing scaled up to nearly every day to minimize the time from concept to customer feedback.

Meetup built its own mobile usability testing rig for $28 rather than waiting for expensive equipment, and by 2012 ran about 600 test sessions a year for roughly $30,000 with full video and notes coverage, approximately the cost of a single outsourced usability study.
Make sense of research data as a team rather than handing synthesis over to specialists, working as hard as you can to interpret the findings collectively.

Hold a review session as soon as possible after research (the same day if you can): have everyone read their findings aloud, transcribe the notes onto index cards or sticky notes, and sort them into themes, because this reading, grouping, and discussing builds shared understanding and reveals the next steps for the MVP.
When feedback is contradictory, look for patterns in the data, since patterns represent multiple instances worth exploring, and treat anything that does not fall into a pattern as likely an outlier.
Do not ignore outliers or try to serve them in your solution; instead park them in a backlog, because as weekly research continues you may later find other data that turns an outlier into a pattern.

When you are unsure whether feedback from one channel is valid, verify it against other channels (such as customer-support emails or customers both inside and outside your office); if the signal does not corroborate, your sample may have been skewed.

Because Lean UX research is continuous and sees only a few users each week, some questions may stay open across several weeks, but this cadence lets interesting patterns and gradual shifts in customer attitudes reveal themselves over time.

Regular weekly sessions at TheLadders revealed job seekers' strong initial disdain for SMS in 2008 softening into acceptance by 2011, a trend the team could only recognize because it sampled the same audience week after week.

Ask a regular set of level-setting questions in every research session to capture the audience's 'vital signs' regardless of what else you are testing, because signals that seem anecdotal in one session become powerful when aggregated over time.

Adopt a 'test everything' policy in which whatever is ready on testing day goes in front of users, which frees the team from rushing toward testing-day deadlines and yields insight at every stage of design and development, provided you set proper expectations for the kind of feedback each artifact can generate.

Feedback on sketches validates the value of a concept but yields no tactical step-by-step process feedback, design-element insight, meaningful copy feedback, or usability learning, whereas static wireframes let you assess information hierarchy, layout, taxonomy, navigation, and information architecture and begin testing copy, with only the first trickles of workflow feedback.

High-fidelity non-clickable visual mockups yield tactical feedback on branding, aesthetics, visual hierarchy, element grouping, call-to-action clarity, and color palette but cannot elicit natural reactions to clicks (so you must ask what users expect and validate it against your planned experience); clickable mockups let users see the actual results of their clicks and teach a lot about product structure but cannot test data interactions such as search; and live coded prototypes are the best test experience, replicating design, behaviour, and workflow with real or convincingly simulated data so feedback is real and directly applicable.

After launch, customers constantly give feedback about themselves, the market, and the competition from every corner of the organization, so seek out and harness these sources of customer intelligence to drive ongoing product design and research.

Harness customer-service agents, who talk to more customers daily than you will over a whole project, by asking what they hear, holding regular monthly trend meetings, tapping their product knowledge in design sessions and reviews, and embedding your hypotheses into their call scripts as one of the cheapest ways to test an idea.

A tech company's UX team held a standing monthly meeting where support reps reported the top ten customer complaints, used it to prioritize work and to measure efficacy (an issue that did not recede on the list meant the solution had not worked), and found the reps then proactively shared feedback, creating a continuous feedback loop.

Set up onsite feedback mechanisms such as email forms, customer-support forums, and third-party community sites, and repurpose them for research by counting inbound emails per site section, suggesting hypotheses in discussions, and soliciting hard-to-find test participants, remembering that these channels reflect your most active and engaged customers.

Use search logs as clear indicators of what customers are seeking and whether they find it, since repeated queries with slight variations reveal a findability challenge, and validate a planned feature by launching a test page and watching whether continued searching shows the content is not meeting users' needs.

Use site-usage analytics, especially funnel analyses, to see how customers use the site, where they drop off, and how they work around the product, and to measure whether a publicly launched experiment shifted usage toward your defined outcome, which these tools answer without bias.

Once your hypotheses have evolved into working code, use A/B (or A/B/n) testing by releasing the new experience to a small subset of users and comparing your success criteria against a control cohort, keeping the changes small enough that any behavioural change can be attributed directly to them.
condition: hypotheses have evolved into working code

statement: If an A/B variant does not move the needle, you are left with an audience of customers you can engage directly to understand why their behaviour did not change.
Taken together, the process techniques form one complete Lean UX loop, and the aim is to run through that loop as frequently as possible, sharpening the team's thinking on each pass.

At TheLadders a developer-driven Waterfall-to-Agile transition would have failed without including UX, and it was the UX team's own venting-retrospective diagram of pain points (such as 'not enough time for gold-medal work' and 'no time to iterate') that triggered the dialog leading to successful cross-functional collaboration.

Scrum, the most popular form of Agile, promotes time-boxed cycles, team self-organization, and high accountability: a sprint is a single team cycle (most teams use two weeks) whose goal is to deliver working software, and a stand-up is a daily short meeting at which each member states what they are doing and what is blocking them.
A user story is the smallest unit of work framed as a benefit to the end user, usually following the pattern: as a given type of user, I want to do something, so that a stated benefit results.

The backlog, a prioritized list of user stories, is Agile's most powerful project-management tool, and it is through actively grooming the backlog that the team manages its daily workload, refocuses on incoming knowledge, and stays agile.

Treat your process as being as iterative as your product by running a retrospective at the end of each sprint to honestly review what went well, what went poorly, and how to improve the process next sprint.

In the staggered-sprints model (also called Cycle 0 or Sprint Zero), design activity runs one sprint ahead of development; its authors always intended strong designer-developer collaboration during both sprints, but many teams misread it and communicate by handoff, creating a mini-waterfall.

Staggered sprints suit teams whose environment cannot release frequently (packaged or embedded software, or where continuous deployment is difficult), where the premium on getting the design right is higher; but in such low-market-feedback environments Lean UX may not be a great fit, and staggered sprints work best only as a transition rather than an end state.
condition: development environments that cannot release frequently, such as packaged or embedded software
exception: in such low-market-feedback environments Lean UX may not fit well; staggered sprints are best only as a transition

statement: Avoid making staggered sprints permanent, because it becomes easy for the different disciplines never to work on the same thing at the same time, which loses cross-functional collaboration and shared understanding, forces reliance on documentation and handoffs, and wastes effort on design docs and on designs whose infeasibility is discovered only at handoff.
Use Scrum's many meetings as mileposts during the sprint to build a blended Lean UX and Agile process where the whole team focuses on the same work at the same time.

Tie a series of sprints together under one umbrella called a theme, and kick off each theme with brainstorming and validation exercises (from an afternoon to a week, scaled to the theme's scope) that get the whole team sketching and ideating together and create a backlog of ideas to test.
Before each new sprint begins, run a shorter brainstorming session so the team can use its latest insight to create the backlog for the next sprint.

Bring the kickoff session's artifacts (sticky notes, sketches, wireframes, paper prototypes) into the iteration planning meeting and use them to write user stories together and then evaluate and prioritize those stories, because the shared understanding from co-creating the artifacts is what lets the team extract stories from them.

Plan user validation sessions every single week so the team is never more than five business days from customer validation while ideas still have time to react before the sprint ends, using the artifacts from ideation sessions as the base material for the tests.
Test raw, low-fidelity ideas for value first (do people want to use the product?), and once desire is established, use subsequent higher-fidelity artifacts to reveal whether the solution is usable.

Designers need protected creative time, which concurrent two-week design-and-development cycles rarely provide; some Agile methods are more flexible (for example Kanban's single-piece flow drops the two-week batch), but you can still deliberately make time for creative work within a Scrum sprint.

For Lean UX to work within Agile, the entire team must participate in all activities (stand-ups, retrospectives, iteration planning meetings, and brainstorms), because without a discipline's participation its concerns and needs are not reflected in the project plans.

Cross-functional participation enables effective backlog prioritization: for example, a designer present at planning can flag a design-heavy story so the team sequences a less design-dependent story first and buys the designer lead time, whereas an absent designer only surfaces the problem at the next stand-up when the story stalls.

Sparse meeting participation also erodes shared understanding, because teams make decisions in meetings and, even when ninety percent of a meeting is irrelevant to you, the relevant ten percent saves hours of downstream explanation of what was decided and why.
Participating in the team's meetings is how you negotiate for the time you need to do your work, and this is as true for UX designers as for everyone else on the team.

On the one-month Knowsy iPad game, the designer kept her practice collaborative, visual, lightweight, and iterative: she sketched a rough game flow on paper together with the front-end developer, used probing 'what happens in this case?' questions to turn who-is-right arguments into joint problem-solving, built a paper prototype the team play-tested (after which everyone grasped the concept and offered complementary ideas), and only raised fidelity to a clickable prototype once the shared vision was in place.

A shared product vision empowers independent work, and you can recognize its absence when the team argues about which features matter or what to do first, feels it is not moving fast enough, or keeps going back over the same issues.

Collaborate with teammates in real time and sketch ideas out as fast as reasonable at the lowest sensible fidelity, raising the fidelity of design artifacts only after the team grasps and commits to the concept.

When you must collaborate remotely with a development team that is less available, expect to produce heavier deliverables, but the basic principle of iterating your way up to higher fidelity still applies.
condition: working remotely with a development team that is less available to collaborate

statement: Management and stakeholder check-ins are one of the biggest obstacles to team momentum, because outcome-focused teams responsively plan only small batches (at most an iteration or two ahead), which dissatisfies managers who want to bless a long project plan; counter this with proactive communication.

A team launched a radical workflow change to a product with thousands of paying customers without alerting anyone in the organization, and within an hour the VP of Customer Service confronted them because call-center reps had no troubleshooting script for the unannounced change.

Proactively tell your product owners and executives how the project is going, what you have tried and learned, and what you will try next, keeping the conversation focused on outcomes and how you are trending toward the goal rather than on feature sets.

Ensure that dependent departments such as customer service, marketing, and operations are aware of upcoming changes that can affect their work, and give them plenty of time to update their own workflows.

Lean UX is not only a mindset and a process but also a management method, so getting the most benefit from it requires organizational change, and because every organization is different each must find the right solution through close collaboration with colleagues.

Move the organization to gauge success by progress toward specific outcomes rather than by features shipped; setting those outcomes is a leadership responsibility, and teams need the authority to choose for themselves the features likely to produce the outcomes the business needs.

Shift the conversation with leadership from features to outcomes at every level: product managers and owners determine which business metrics need the most attention and then discuss outcomes with their own managers, so the shift propagates to the highest levels of the organization.

Do away with product roadmaps and redefine success criteria, replacing them with backlogs of hypotheses the team wants to test and prioritizes by risk, feasibility, and potential success, and retrain managers to give teams the latitude to experiment.

Adopt a mantra of 'competencies over roles': every team member delivers on a core competency but may also contribute secondary competencies, so let colleagues contribute in any discipline where they have expertise and interest, because job-description gatekeeping is deeply anticollaborative and leaves talent unused.

Silos are the death of collaborative teams, because discouraging cross-functional input lets people retreat into their own discipline, which makes cross-discipline conversation wane and grows mistrust, finger-pointing, and cover-your-ass behaviour.

UX designers must add facilitation as a core competency by opening up the design process so the team, not the individual, owns the product design, and by taking a leadership role facilitating group activities such as Design Studio.
Hiring designers merely to produce wireframes, specs, and site maps for a waterfall 'design phase' limits their effectiveness by narrowing their scope and reinforces a siloed team model.

Single-discipline collaboration produces single-faceted ideas and forces disciplines to explain their work to one another through heavy documentation, whereas cross-functional collaboration puts everyone on the same page and the same level, with no single discipline dictating to the others.

Robert Dailey's 1978 study of R&D teams linked a team's problem-solving productivity to four predictors (task certainty, task interdependence, team size, and team cohesiveness), supporting the practice of breaking down discipline-based boundaries to keep teams cohesive.

Keep teams small, because larger groups are less efficient and, less obviously, a smaller team must work on smaller problems, which makes it easier to maintain the discipline needed to produce MVPs; a useful rule is the 'two-pizza team' (if it needs more than two pizzas to feed, it is too big).

Break down physical barriers to collaboration by co-locating teams in open, visible, accessible workspaces with wall space for putting up work, and seat people in cross-functional groupings rather than discipline clusters, since even a single cubicle wall can hinder conversation.

Augment open workspaces with breakout rooms and generous whiteboard surface, and when co-location is not possible give teams video conferencing, smart boards, and occasional plane tickets for in-person meetings, because one or two in-person meetings a year noticeably improves team morale.
condition: when co-location is not possible, provide remote-collaboration tools plus occasional in-person meetings
