statement: Beautiful, glossy design deliverables can drive bad corporate decisions by biasing judgment through their persuasive aesthetics, and it is misguided to base awards, hiring, and compensation on the beauty of deliverables rather than on the outcomes of the work.

No lone design hero can be credited with the success of the experience, the business, and the team, so Lean UX depends on broad collaboration; framing each design as a hypothesis undercuts heroism because a designer must anticipate that many ideas will fail under testing, and the one thing held sacred is customer insight.

At AOL, a developer who grew tired of waiting and started implementing browser ideas before the designer's mockups and specifications were complete let the team see the actual product experience much sooner and iterate toward more usable and feasible designs, which led the team to relax its Big-Design-Up-Front requirements.

Eliminate Big Design Up Front: do not require complete mockups, specifications, and flow diagrams before implementation can begin, because building early gives the team a real glimpse of the product experience and speeds iteration toward usable, feasible designs.

Put speed first and aesthetics second in early work: do not waste time debating which artifact to create or polishing it to perfection, but use whatever artifact takes the least time to create and communicate, treating early artifacts as transient (get it done, get it out, discuss, move on).

Reserve visual polish for the visual-design refinement stage, where fit and finish genuinely contribute to brand, emotional experience, and professionalism, because obsessing over the presentation of early artifacts like wireframes, sitemaps, and workflow diagrams is a waste of time and makes the team less willing to rework its ideas.

Organizations should promote the ability to think fast and build shared understanding alongside (not instead of) aesthetics, and should seek out and reward problem-solvers who can illustrate the path they took from idea to validated learning to experience.

Embrace UX debt the way teams treat technical debt (it is not iterative if you only do it once): commit to continuously improving the user interface by writing backlog stories that capture the gap between where the experience is and where you want it to be and advocating for them, because framing rework as debt gets it prioritized.

Applying Lean UX in an interactive agency is especially hard because the basic agency business model has clients pay for deliverables rather than outcomes, the culture of hero design is strong (elevating individuals to roles like Executive Creative Director), and project-phase processes encourage deliverables and departmental silos.

The hardest agency obstacle is the client's habit of handing work off and expecting to see finished results only when they are ready, which reduces collaboration to biased, unproductive critique driven by personal bias, politics, and cover-your-ass behaviour.
To make Lean UX work in an agency, everyone in the engagement must maximize two factors: increasing collaboration between client and agency, and shifting the focus from outputs to outcomes.

Move agency engagements away from fixed-scope, deliverable-based contracts toward time-and-materials or, more radically, outcome-based contracts, which free the team to iterate toward a specified goal; clients give up the illusion of control that a deliverables contract offers but gain the freedom to pursue meaningful, high-quality solutions defined by outcomes rather than feature lists.

Increase client-agency collaboration by pulling clients into the process earlier and more frequently, constructing check-ins around less formal milestones, and arranging collaborative work sessions so both sides benefit from the shared insight and feedback.

Do not treat software development partners as outsiders brought in at the end of a design phase; development partners must participate throughout the life of the project as active collaborators, and software development should start as early as possible so the team works side by side.

Outsourcing part of the work to a third-party development vendor makes the Lean UX process more likely to break down because the contractual relationship resists the flexibility Lean UX requires, so structure such engagements on a time-and-materials basis and plan for the change that learning will inevitably cause.
condition: when part of the work is outsourced to a third-party development vendor

statement: Where an organization has strict documentation standards for internal or regulatory compliance, do not try to circumvent them, because doing so inevitably leads to rework, delays, and dissatisfaction with your performance.
condition: the organization has strict documentation standards for compliance

statement: In compliance-heavy environments, 'lead with conversation and trail with documentation': run the Lean UX practices (conversation, collaborative problem solving, sketching, experimentation) early in the lifecycle, then, as hypotheses are proven and design directions solidify, transition back to the required documentation standard and use those documents for their intended purpose of capturing decision history and informing future teams, without letting them prevent the right product decisions.

When managers feel threatened by proposals to work in a new way, ask forgiveness rather than permission: try out ideas and prove their value through quantifiable successes such as time and money saved or a more successful release, using those achievements to make your case.
condition: managers feel threatened by the proposed new way of working

statement: If leadership still does not see the value of working this way and the organization continues down a path of 'blind design,' it may be time to consider alternative employment.

Abandoning the product roadmap removes a key tool the business uses to coordinate the activity of teams, so the freedom Lean UX gives a team to pursue its own agenda comes with a responsibility to communicate that agenda.

Constantly reach out to members of the organization who are not currently involved in your work so they know what is coming and you learn what they are planning, because customer-service managers, marketers, parallel business units, and sales teams all do their jobs better when informed and become far less resistant to the changes your designs make.

Two lessons make validation cycles smoother: other departments are always affected by your work and are ignored at your peril, and customers should be made aware of significant upcoming changes and allowed to opt out at least temporarily.

At Hobsons, a UX director overcame 'we cannot do Lean UX because we are not a startup' resistance in an enterprise steeped in business analysis, technical specs, and waterfall development by bringing in an outside coach to reinforce the internal message and introducing a system that helped teams internalize the discovery-phase steps, getting the full team in sync and speaking the same language within a year.

Bringing in an outside coach can help a Lean UX transition by using an external voice to reinforce what is being said internally, and making the change a little bit fun reduces people's resentment about having to change old habits.
Lean UX techniques are not only for startups; they can be applied successfully in enterprise organizations as well.

Lean UX is the evolution of product design that blends the best interaction-design techniques with the scientific method (combining Lean Startup, Agile software development, and design thinking) to take the bloat and uncertainty out of product design and push it toward an objectively grounded result that is easy to use, beautiful, and measurably successful.

A set of 18 general, empirically validated design guidelines for human-AI interaction, synthesized from over 150 collected recommendations, gives practitioners a reusable resource for designing and evaluating AI-infused systems.
The 18 human-AI interaction guidelines are organized by the interaction phase in which they typically apply, into four groups: Initially, During interaction, When wrong, and Over time.
Initially, make the AI system's capabilities clear so the user understands what the system can and cannot do (Guideline 1).
Initially, make clear how well the system performs its functions so the user understands how often the AI may make mistakes (Guideline 2).
Time when the AI system acts or interrupts based on the user's current task and environment (Guideline 3).
condition: based on the user's current task and environment

statement: Show information that is contextually relevant to the user's current task and environment (Guideline 4).
Match relevant social norms so the experience is delivered in a way users expect given their social and cultural context (Guideline 5).
condition: given the user's social and cultural context

statement: Mitigate social biases so the AI system's language and behaviors do not reinforce undesirable or unfair stereotypes and biases (Guideline 6).
Support efficient invocation so it is easy for the user to invoke or request the AI system's services when needed (Guideline 7).
condition: when the user needs the service

statement: Support efficient dismissal so it is easy for the user to dismiss or ignore undesired AI system services (Guideline 8).
Support efficient correction so it is easy for the user to edit, refine, or recover when the AI system is wrong (Guideline 9).
condition: when the AI system is wrong

statement: When uncertain about the user's goals, scope the AI system's services by disambiguating or gracefully degrading rather than acting confidently (Guideline 10).
condition: when the system is uncertain about the user's goals

statement: Make clear why the system did what it did by enabling the user to access an explanation of the AI system's behavior (Guideline 11).
Remember recent interactions by maintaining short-term memory and letting the user make efficient references to that memory (Guideline 12).
Learn from user behavior by personalizing the user's experience based on their actions over time (Guideline 13).
condition: over time as the user acts

statement: Update and adapt cautiously by limiting disruptive changes when updating and adapting the AI system's behaviors (Guideline 14).
condition: when updating or adapting the system's behavior

statement: Encourage granular feedback by enabling the user to indicate their preferences during regular interaction with the AI system (Guideline 15).
Convey the consequences of user actions by immediately updating or conveying how the user's actions will affect the AI system's future behavior (Guideline 16).
Provide global controls that let the user customize what the AI system monitors and how it behaves at a global level (Guideline 17).
Notify users about changes by informing the user when the AI system adds or updates its capabilities (Guideline 18).
Phrase each design guideline as a short, verb-first rule of action of roughly 3-10 words with no conjunctions, so a designer can unambiguously judge whether an interface applies or violates it.
Accompany each design guideline with a one-sentence description that qualifies or clarifies potential ambiguities.
Split a compound guideline containing conjunctions into separate single-action guidelines so each can be independently validated as applied or violated.
When building a guideline set, discard candidate concepts that are too vague to design for directly, too specific to a single AI scenario, or not AI-specific.

Exclude guidance that cannot be observed or designed for at the user-interface level, even when it matters at the AI-modeling level (e.g., balancing exploration and exploitation, or being especially conservative early on).
condition: when the guidance is intended to be applied and evaluated at the interface level

statement: The 18 guidelines were developed and validated through a four-phase process: consolidating over 150 recommendations, an internal modified heuristic evaluation, a user study with design practitioners, and an expert evaluation.
In the user study, 49 HCI practitioners tested the guidelines against 20 popular AI-infused products spanning a range of interaction scenarios, verifying the guidelines' broad relevance.
Because AI inferences are typically made under uncertainty and commonly produce false positives and false negatives, AI-infused systems can exhibit unpredictable behaviors.
AI-infused systems can violate traditional usability principles such as consistency and error prevention because their behavior is probabilistic and changes through learning over time.
Inconsistent and unpredictable AI behavior can erode users' confidence and lead them to abandon the technology.

AI explanations are most valuable in complex, high-risk scenarios such as sensor-based ubiquitous computing or medical and financial decision support, and may be less important in low-cost scenarios such as search or music and movie recommenders.
condition: in complex, high-risk decision scenarios
exception: low-cost scenarios such as search or media recommenders

statement: Build safeguards such as verification steps or controlled levels of autonomy into intelligent systems to help prevent unwanted adaptations or actions.
Manage user expectations so that unpredictable adaptive agents do not mislead or frustrate users during interaction.
Decide whether to act on an AI inference or wait for user input by weighing the expected costs, benefits, and uncertainties of automating under uncertainty.
Eight of the 18 guidelines correspond to principles from Horvitz's earlier work on mixed-initiative user interfaces.

To validate a set of design guidelines, run a heuristic-evaluation-style study: assign each evaluator an AI-driven feature they are familiar with and ask them to find both applications and violations of each guideline.

For each guideline, first have evaluators judge whether it applies to the assigned feature or is out of scope; when it applies, collect concrete examples rated on a 5-point 'clearly violated' to 'clearly applied' scale with a written explanation of each rating.
Separately rate the wording clarity of each guideline on a 5-point 'very confusing' to 'very clear' scale to identify guidelines that need rephrasing.
Before an evaluation, familiarize evaluators with the guidelines by giving at least one application example and one violation example for each guideline.

Select evaluation targets using a maximum-variance sampling strategy over popular AI-infused products that cover a wide range of scenarios, choosing a prominent AI-driven feature to evaluate per product.
Recruit evaluators screened for at least one year of HCI/UX experience and familiarity with discount usability methods such as heuristic evaluation or cognitive walkthrough.
Assign roughly 2-3 evaluators per product and ensure each product is assessed by evaluators with a range of experience rather than only inexperienced ones.
condition: when evaluators have both usability experience and familiarity with the product being tested

statement: Before counting guideline examples, clean the data: remove duplicate application/violation instances, reclassify 'does not apply' responses that actually describe a violation as violations, and remove 'does not apply' responses that merely mean the evaluator could not find an example.
Obtain reliable counts with a two-pass review in which one team member flags each adjustment case and a second verifies it, discarding instances where the two reviewers disagree.
Across 20 products, participants identified 785 examples of the 18 guidelines after adjustments: 313 applications, 277 violations, 89 neutral ratings, and 106 'does not apply' responses.

Participants found at least one application or violation of every guideline in every product category tested, providing broad evidence that the 18 guidelines are relevant across common AI-infused systems.

Product categories relying on interaction modalities beyond graphical UI and text (image, sensor, or voice interaction) accumulated more 'does not apply' responses and fewer total applications or violations.
condition: for products whose interaction is primarily image-, sensor-, or voice-based rather than GUI and text

statement: Interpret guideline-audit counts as follows: total applications plus violations indicates a guideline's overall relevance; a large excess of applications over violations indicates it is widely implemented; a large excess of violations over applications indicates it is relevant but under-implemented and thus a design opportunity; and many 'does not apply' responses flag scope or observability issues.

Absence of observed instances of a guideline can reflect observability limits rather than irrelevance, because some guidelines (such as scoping services when in doubt or updating cautiously) are hard to detect within a single session or without knowledge of the underlying AI.
condition: within a single short session or without knowledge of the underlying algorithm

statement: Timing services based on context is more relevant for products that take proactive (push) actions without explicit user requests and less relevant for purely pull-based interactions where the user explicitly requests each service.
condition: for proactive or push-style products
exception: pull-only interactions where the user explicitly requests each service

statement: Explanations of AI behavior are sometimes undesirable for financial or business reasons; for example, explaining a search engine's ranking could worsen adversarial gaming by content authors.
exception: when an explanation would enable adversarial gaming or otherwise harm the business

statement: Recognizing whether a system matches social norms or reinforces biases is hard for designers reasoning only from their own social context, so a diverse set of evaluators is needed to surface issues invisible to majority-group members.
Designers may need specific training or dedicated tools (for example, GenderMag for identifying gender bias in interfaces) to recognize social norms and biases in AI systems.
Flag a guideline as needing clarification when confusion is systematic, defined as four or more instances confused with another guideline or multiple participants making similar clarity complaints.
condition: when confusion between guidelines is systematic

statement: Reduce confusion between related guidelines by wording them in parallel language that emphasizes the intended distinction, such as what the system can do versus how well it does it versus why it did something.

When wording guidelines, keep 'current context' (the user's current task and environment) distinct from 'personalization' (preferences learned over time) to avoid conflating contextual relevance with learning from behavior.
When wording guidelines, distinguish maintaining short-term memory of recent interactions from learning user behavior over the longer term.
When wording guidelines, distinguish instance-level (local) feedback given during a specific interaction from global customization of the system's behavior across all instances.
Expert review by UX/HCI practitioners familiar with discount usability methods is an effective way to identify guideline wording and clarity problems.
After revision, experts preferred the revised guideline wording for nearly all guidelines, although distinguishing what the system can do from how well it does it remained somewhat difficult.

The 18 guidelines were iteratively refined across four phases by a team of 11 researchers and were applied or reviewed by about 60 additional designers and usability practitioners across 10 product categories, evidencing broad relevance.
The guidelines lend themselves well to usability-inspection methods such as heuristic evaluation and are intended for evaluating both existing products and emerging design ideas.

There is a tradeoff between generality and specialization: a set of general guidelines may not adequately address all types of AI-infused systems, so additional or specialized guidelines can be necessary.
Some guidelines do not directly apply to AI systems that lack graphical user interfaces, such as voice assistants and activity trackers, which may require additional guidelines.
condition: for AI systems that lack a graphical user interface

statement: High-risk or highly regulated domains, such as semi-autonomous vehicles, robot-assisted surgery, and financial systems, may require specialized guidelines beyond the 18 general ones.
condition: in high-risk or highly regulated domains

statement: Designers and model developers should collaborate to apply the guidelines; for example, given an AI model's expected performance, designers can choose designs that reduce costs while optimizing user benefit, such as offering multiple options until the model is accurate enough to act proactively on the user's behalf.
condition: given the AI model's expected performance level

statement: The 18 guidelines only begin to address fairness and ethics: a system can satisfy all of them and still affect people's lives consequentially, so designers must deliberately evaluate broader societal impacts beyond matching social norms and mitigating bias.

Applying several guidelines together can create interactions and trade-offs; for example, a complex or deep model can make it hard to both convey the consequences of user actions and actively learn from user behavior at the same time.
condition: when the system uses a complex or deep model

statement: The 18 guidelines are offered as a shared, reusable resource that designers can apply to build more human-centric AI-infused systems and that researchers can further develop and refine.

After revision, experts judged the previously confusable pairs of guidelines to be different in meaning and mostly easy to distinguish, with the pair 'what the system can do' versus 'how well it does what it can do' remaining the hardest to tell apart.
To teach or document a design guideline, illustrate it with concrete examples of both its application and its violation drawn from real products, while anonymizing the specific product names.
Human-computer interaction is best advanced by elegantly coupling automated services (interface agents) with direct manipulation, rather than treating the two approaches as competing alternatives.

Designers should avoid two symmetric failure modes: building complex reasoning machinery to compensate for fundamentally poor designs or metaphors, and restricting an interface to direct manipulation when automated reasoning would add significant power or efficiency.
Computers are frequently uncertain about a user's goals and current focus of attention.
Automation should deliver genuine added value beyond what the user could already accomplish through direct manipulation alone.
Systems should explicitly represent and reason about their uncertainty regarding the user's goals and focus of attention instead of assuming those are known.
Systems should account for the user's attentional state when timing services and alerts, deferring action to moments when it will be less distracting.
Systems should infer the ideal action by weighing the context-dependent costs, benefits, and uncertainties of acting under uncertainty about the user's goals and attention.
When uncertain about the user's intentions, a system should be able to engage in an efficient clarifying dialog, weighing the cost of needlessly bothering the user.
condition: the system is uncertain about the user's intentions

statement: Systems should provide efficient means for users to directly invoke and to terminate automated services.
Designs should minimize the cost of poor guesses about action and timing, for example through appropriate time-outs and natural gestures for rejecting an offered service.
Under uncertainty, a system should gracefully scale the precision or scope of its service to match the current level of uncertainty, preferring to do less but do it correctly.
condition: under uncertainty about the user's goals

statement: Agents should be designed on the assumption that users will often want to complete or refine an agent's analysis, and should provide mechanisms for efficient agent-user collaboration to do so.
Agents should exhibit socially appropriate default behaviors and courtesies consistent with expectations of a benevolent assistant.
Systems should maintain a working memory of recent interactions so users can make efficient, natural references to objects and services from their shared short-term context.
Automated services should continue to learn from observing the user in order to become better at serving that user's goals and needs over time.

Automated assistance can be layered as a service over an existing direct-manipulation application by detecting a newly focused item, inferring the task it implies, and pre-filling the relevant fields for the user to review, edit, and save.

When a system cannot confidently identify a precise parameter such as an exact date and time, it should degrade its goal to the most relevant coarser scope (for example a day, week, or month) and present that, rather than committing to a precise but likely-wrong guess.
condition: the system cannot confidently identify the precise value

statement: Even when an automated guess is wrong, placing the user in an approximately correct starting state still adds value by reducing the number of interactions and the navigation effort otherwise required.

A system can infer the probability that the user currently holds a given goal from observable evidence (such as the header, subject, and body of the message in focus) using a probabilistic classifier trained by watching the user work.

Given the inferred goal probability together with an assessment of expected costs and benefits, a system should select among three responses: do nothing, engage the user in a dialog, or perform the service.
Autonomous action should be taken only when the agent believes it will yield greater expected utility for the user than inaction.

The expected utility of acting versus not acting is derived from four outcome utilities defined over the joint of whether the user actually has the goal and whether the system takes the action, each mapped onto a zero-to-one utility scale.
Plotting expected utility against the probability that the user has the goal yields two lines, one for acting and one for not acting, that intersect at a threshold probability p*.
The optimal policy is to take the action when the inferred goal probability exceeds the threshold p* and to refrain when it is below p*.
The threshold probability p* can be computed for any four outcome utilities by setting the expected-utility expressions for action and inaction equal and solving for the goal probability.
At run time a system need only compare the inferred goal probability against the precomputed threshold to decide whether to invoke a service, without recomputing expected utilities.

The action threshold is context-dependent and should shift with the outcome utilities: raise it when the cost of unwanted action grows (for example as the user's focus on another task deepens), and lower it when that cost falls (for example when more screen real estate is available) or when the cost of failing to act rises (for example when the user is more rushed).

Asking the user a clarifying question can be treated as an additional action within the same expected-utility framework, with its own outcome utilities for the cases where the user does or does not have the goal.

Typically the utility of initiating dialog when the user does not have the goal exceeds the utility of acting when the goal is not desired, while simply performing a genuinely desired action is worth more than asking about it first.

Introducing dialog as a third option produces two decision thresholds, one separating inaction from dialog and one separating dialog from action, that jointly index whether to do nothing, ask, or act as a function of the inferred goal probability.

A system need not perform explicit expected-value computations: designers or users can assess the action thresholds directly, and such directly assessed thresholds still imply an underlying expected-utility model.
A system should supply sensible default utilities and thresholds while allowing users to specify their own outcome utilities or to set directly the two key thresholds that control dialog and action.
Timing involves a genuine trade-off: acting before the user is ready is distracting, yet delaying service diminishes the value of automation, so service timing must balance the two.
The value of services and alerts can be enhanced by building and applying models of the temporal pattern of the user's attention.

An empirical user study found a nonlinear, sigmoid-shaped relationship between the size of the message being reviewed and how long users prefer to dwell before accepting automated service, and such timing preferences can be fit from observed user data as a function of an observable task feature.
Timing information can be used in two ways: fold time dependence into the outcome utilities, or use it separately to defer service until the user is likely ready to receive it.
A system can ship with a pretrained probabilistic user model and a pretrained timing model while being deliberately designed to keep improving from ongoing user interaction.

Training labels can be derived implicitly from user behavior: a reviewed message is recorded as schedule-relevant when the user invokes a calendaring or scheduling action within a predetermined time horizon after it.
condition: the calendaring or scheduling action is invoked within a predetermined time horizon after the message

statement: Continual learning collects observed behavioral signals, namely implicit relevance labels and the dwell time before the user invokes scheduling, and periodically uses them to incrementally refine both the probabilistic user model and the attention or timing model.
Users should be able to specify a policy or training schedule that governs when the system incrementally refines its learned models.
The purpose of continual learning is to improve both which service to offer (relevance predictions) and when to offer it (timing estimates).

Design systems for both high human control and high computer automation rather than trading one off against the other; this joint goal is the central aim of Human-Centered AI and drives higher human performance and wider adoption.
Human-Centered AI is a two-dimensional framework that treats level of automation/autonomy and level of human control as independent axes, replacing the one-dimensional Sheridan-Verplank scale.
The prevailing one-dimensional automation model (Sheridan and Verplank's ten levels) misleadingly implies that increasing automation must reduce human control.
Systems that pursue high autonomy with inadequate human control tend to increase the operator's monitoring burden and can degrade overall performance (the autonomy paradox).
condition: when a system pursues high autonomy while leaving humans to supervise it

statement: Excessive autonomy has produced high-profile failures, including a Patriot missile system downing friendly aircraft and the Boeing 737 MAX crashes.

Achieve reliability through technical practices: audit trails and failure/near-miss analysis tools, accepted benchmark tests for verification and validation, continuous review of data quality and bias, and design that builds stakeholder confidence.

Achieve safety through open management that builds a culture of safety: visible leadership commitment, channels to report problems, internal review of failures and near misses, and public reporting of failures.

Achieve trust through respected independent oversight structures (capable firms, professional standards bodies, government regulators, certifiers, auditors, and insurers) that review design, operation, and maintenance.
Hold designs to the standard of being trustworthy, not merely trusted, because a system that users trust may not actually be trustworthy.
Do not design computers as teammates, collaborators, or partners; design them to support human activity by reducing workload, raising performance, and ensuring safety.

Match design rigor to an application's consequence tier: low-stakes consumer/professional tools (e.g., recommenders), consequential systems (medical, legal, financial) with substantial benefits and harms, and life-critical systems whose actions are rapid and often irreversible.

In consequential (middle-tier) applications there is often time for a human to reflect on, consult about, or probe an algorithm's recommendation, and adequate logs let managers repair damage after the fact.
condition: middle-tier consequential applications where actions are not instantaneous or irreversible

statement: Even for low-consequence automation such as recommenders, spell-checking, and query completion, design to preserve user control, avoid disruptive behavior, and limit malicious manipulation.
Recommender systems can be manipulated by malicious actors to shift buying habits, election outcomes, and public attitudes, so improving user control both raises satisfaction and reduces misuse.
Google Flu Trends succeeded initially but failed within two years because its designers did not anticipate changes in search algorithms, user behavior, and social context.
Guard against algorithmic hubris, the overconfident belief that one can build foolproof autonomous systems.

The two-dimensional framework yields four quadrants: upper-right is the Reliable, Safe, and Trustworthy target (high control and high automation); lower-right is high automation with low control for rapid-action, well-understood tasks; upper-left is high control with low automation for human mastery; lower-left is simple devices.
For well-understood, predictable tasks in standardized contexts, favor high automation with low human control (the lower-right quadrant).
condition: tasks that are well understood, predictable, and used in standardized contexts

statement: For poorly-understood, complex tasks with varying contexts of use, target high human control together with high automation (the upper-right quadrant).
condition: tasks that are poorly understood, complex, or used in varying contexts

statement: Reserve full computer control for cases where action must be faster than a human could intervene (e.g., airbags, anti-lock brakes, pacemakers, defibrillators, defensive weapons), and then require extremely careful design, extensive testing, and monitoring at scale.
condition: rapid-action tasks where there is no time for human intervention and failure is very costly

statement: Reserve full human mastery with low automation for tasks where the value is in the doing itself (building competence, self-efficacy, and creative exploration), such as cycling, piano, or baking.
condition: tasks where users seek mastery, self-efficacy, or creative exploration and the goal is in the doing

statement: Avoid the two design danger zones of excessive automation and excessive human control.

The Boeing 737 MAX MCAS illustrates excessive automation: a single angle-of-attack sensor as a single point of failure, plus designer overconfidence that led to leaving MCAS undocumented and pilots untrained to override it.
Make automation perceptible and documented to users, because imperceptible AI is not ethical AI.
Naming or marketing automation beyond its actual capability (for example calling driver assistance 'Autopilot') encourages users to lower their vigilance and over-trust the system, increasing risk.
condition: when a system's name or marketing implies more capability than it actually delivers

statement: Treat many so-called human errors as design failures, since excessive human control that permits deadly mistakes is a design problem to be engineered against.

Prevent mistakes from excessive human control with interlocks and guards, such as breathalyzer ignition interlocks, Positive Train Control speed limits, aviation reverse-thruster strain-gauge interlocks, and self-cleaning-oven door locks.
exception: interlocks must be well designed, because poorly designed ones (e.g., over-frequent automatic door locking) become annoying

statement: Generalize physical interlocks in software as range checking that constrains an algorithm's inputs to permissible values and its outputs to acceptable ones.

Reach Reliable, Safe, and Trustworthy designs by incrementally refining proven automations (anti-lock brakes, then cruise control, lane-keeping, and collision avoidance) rather than leaping directly to full autonomy.

Full self-driving autonomy within the next decade is likely overstated; a cautious, human-centered, incremental approach improves safety while handling edge cases such as snow, unusual vehicles, vandalism, construction zones, and emergency responders.

Patient-Controlled Analgesia demonstrates an RST design: let patients trigger their own doses, but use sensors and machine learning to set safe amounts, enforce lockout periods and total-dose limits, explain the limits, and add a central station that monitors many devices.
condition: life-critical dosing where patient control must be bounded to prevent overdose

statement: Dissolve the old AI-versus-intelligence-augmentation debate by integrating AI algorithms with user-interface design so the system amplifies, augments, enhances, and empowers people.
Treat the choice between automation and augmentation as a false dichotomy; well-designed systems combine both to simplify and improve outcomes.

Major industry and academic guideline sets converge on user understanding and control, including Microsoft's 18 human-AI interaction guidelines, Endsley's 20 human-autonomy guidelines, and Apple's Human Interface Guidelines that put people, not apps, in control.
Do not design a system to endear itself to users or to form a full emotional bond with them.
Use automated assistance for routine tasks rather than higher-level cognitive functions, and provide automation transparency.
Aim for designs that are comprehensible, predictable, and controllable, because these properties raise user self-efficacy and produce Reliable, Safe, and Trustworthy systems.

Apply the Prometheus Principles as a core set of six interface design rules for human control over automation: consistent interfaces, continuous visual display, reversible incremental actions, informative feedback, progress indicators, and completion reports.
Provide consistent interfaces so users can form, express, and revise their intent.
Continuously display the objects and actions of interest so users can see current state.
Make user actions rapid, incremental, and reversible.
Give informative feedback that acknowledges each user action.
Show progress indicators that communicate the status of ongoing operations.
Provide completion reports that confirm an action was accomplished.
Expect interface decisions based on these principles to involve tradeoffs with no default right answer, so invest in careful study, creative design, and rigorous testing.
Continuously monitor deployed designs with domain experts to detect problems and refine them.
Let users express intent through visual interfaces and give informative feedback about machine state, progress, and completion.
exception: auditory and haptic interfaces are preferable in some situations and for users with disabilities

statement: The elevator interface exemplifies RST design: it confirms recognized intent with lit buttons, shows progress with a floor display, and signals completion with a tone, while triply-redundant safety systems, door-obstruction detectors, and multi-car coordination operate automatically.
Retain manual override controls for authorized humans even in highly automated systems (for example, firefighter and moving-crew overrides in elevators).

The smartphone camera exemplifies simultaneous high control and high automation: a live preview and manual overrides such as touch-to-focus coexist with automatic aperture, focus, high-dynamic-range, and hand-shake compensation.
Guide design choices by the consequences and reversibility of the mistakes a system can make.
There is currently no objective measure of levels of human control and automation tied to specific tasks; developing such measures is an important open research direction.
Let human responsibility for mistakes drive design advances such as detailed audit trails and consistent machine-state feedback, which enable rapid retraining of users and redesign of systems.
Design against two persistent automation risks: de-skilling that erodes the human skills needed when automation fails, and degraded vigilance when human actions become infrequent.
condition: systems that automate enough to reduce how often operators act or practice skills

statement: A human-centered RST system is reliable through sound technical practices, safe through open management that builds a safety culture, and trustworthy through well-designed independent oversight, and it improves rapidly because monitoring failures and near misses feeds creative improvement.
Human-centered AI should combine intelligent algorithms with human-centered design so that AI systems are judged by their effects on people as well as technical performance.
AI development should shift from a narrow focus on machine autonomy toward a balanced focus on users, stakeholders, user experience, and human performance.
A central aim of HCAI design is to increase the chance that technology empowers people rather than replacing them.
HCAI systems should preserve meaningful human control while serving human values such as rights, justice, dignity, self-efficacy, creativity, responsibility, and social connection.
AI-enabled products and services should be designed around concrete human and societal benefits such as care, sustainable communities, and environmental restoration.
The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals can serve as a value framework for aligning interface and AI design with social, educational, health, environmental, and equity outcomes.
A one-dimensional automation scale is a weak model for HCAI because it treats machine autonomy and human control as a zero-sum tradeoff.
Design analysis for automated systems should treat human control and computer automation as two independent dimensions.
High levels of automation can be compatible with high levels of human control when designers assign users meaningful choices over goals, timing, framing, and action initiation.
condition: when designers assign users meaningful choices over goals, timing, framing, and action initiation

statement: Designers should identify when human mastery, computer control, or a balanced high-control/high-automation arrangement is appropriate for the application context.
condition: when selecting an automation strategy for a specific application

statement: Designers should prevent configurations where excessive user control or excessive automation creates unsafe, confusing, or undesirable outcomes.
condition: when either side of the control-automation balance creates operational risk

statement: The HCAI control-versus-automation framework applies to ordinary consumer devices and to life-critical systems, so designers should not reserve it only for abstract AI software.
AI research and development should combine the scientific goal of understanding intelligence with the innovation goal of producing useful applications for people.

Metaphor choices such as agent versus supertool, teammate versus teleoperation, assured versus supervised autonomy, and social robot versus active appliance shape design expectations and should be selected deliberately.
condition: when framing an AI system for development, communication, or policy

statement: Researchers, developers, business leaders, and policymakers need coordinated design language to move public and organizational expectations toward human-centered AI.
A stronger HCAI emphasis is expected by the source to reduce exaggerated AI fears and raise confidence that people can use AI systems for daily work and creative exploration.
Interfaces for automated systems should show users the current state of the machine and what the system is likely to do over near, medium, and longer time horizons.
Users are better positioned to control automated systems when they can preview possible outcomes or receive equivalent accessible alternatives before committing to an action.
condition: when an automated system can present forecasted outcomes before action

statement: Automated systems should let users compare alternatives, choose one, deliberately start execution, and then monitor the action as it unfolds.
Accessible alternatives to visual previews are required when visual-only interfaces would exclude users with visual impairments.
condition: when previews are provided visually
exception: visual-only preview is insufficient for users who need a nonvisual interface

statement: The preview-choice-execution-monitoring interaction pattern should be applied beyond cameras and navigation to high-consequence domains such as robotics, drones, trading, navigation, and medical devices.
condition: when automated actions have material safety, financial, operational, or health consequences

statement: Governance structures are needed to convert high-level AI ethics commitments into practical organizational and technical action.
Reliable HCAI systems should be built on established software engineering practices.
A safety culture for HCAI requires management practices that make safety an organizational responsibility rather than only a technical property.
Trustworthy HCAI certification should include independent oversight and, where appropriate, government regulation.
condition: where certification or public accountability is needed

statement: HCAI governance should operate across multiple layers: technical reliability, organizational safety culture, external review, and public regulation.
HCAI principles must be refined through practice, adapted to industry needs, and revisited as technologies and use contexts change.
condition: as innovations emerge or industry context differs

statement: HCAI work should address misuse and harm risks including misinformation, cybercrime, political oppression, online bias, hatred, and bullying.
Future AI systems should emphasize supertools and active appliances that amplify human abilities while retaining human control.
AI services should pair engaging user experiences with embedded AI capabilities to support tasks and services that users actually want.
Human-centered AI systems should be designed to amplify human abilities while preserving human control, rather than replacing people with autonomous machine behavior.

Putting people at the center of AI design should prioritize self-efficacy, creativity, clear responsibility, and social participation, while also surfacing concerns such as privacy, security, environmental protection, social justice, and human rights.
A human-centered AI framing treats algorithms and AI components as supporting elements around human goals, not as the primary center of system design.
Design discussions for AI products and services should shift language, imagery, and metaphors toward human empowerment instead of machine autonomy or human-like machine agency.
The distinction between automation and autonomy is not reliably sharp enough to support separate design treatment when automated systems increasingly incorporate AI-like adaptive features.
Human-centered AI design should measure success through user needs, user experience, human performance, explainability, and meaningful human control rather than only algorithmic capability.
Centering humans in design does not require mimicking human form or behavior; it requires systems that serve human needs through comprehensible, predictable, and controllable interfaces.
Bio-inspired design ideas can be useful starting points only when designers also compare them with non-human-like alternatives and evaluate performance across options.
condition: When bio-inspired concepts are considered as design inputs.

statement: Designing computers or robots to resemble people can prevent designers from exploiting machine strengths such as algorithms, sensors, dense displays, and powerful effectors.
Robots are more likely to succeed when they use machine-distinctive capabilities as tool-like or tele-operated systems under human supervisory control through well-designed interfaces.
Computers used in human group work should provide information and execute tasks under human control rather than imitate the reciprocal social behaviors of human teammates.
Legal and moral responsibility for machine and robot design remains with humans, so system designs should not encourage users to assign responsibility to machines.

Human-like speech interaction is appropriate for some applications when users cannot conveniently use their hands or eyes, but high-capacity visual interfaces are often better for persistent, detailed, or spatial information.
condition: When interaction modality is being chosen for an AI-enabled system.
exception: Do not prefer speech when ambient noise, information density, persistence, or spatial comparison make visual display more effective.

statement: Humanizing robots can lead users toward emotional over-attachment, false expectations about robot responsibility, and mistaken beliefs about appropriate robot use.
Interactive visual interfaces that present abundant information in compact, spatially stable layouts help users maintain situational awareness, interpret status, plan, act, and monitor performance.
condition: When users must supervise dynamic, information-rich systems.

statement: Recommendations, alerts, alarms, and highlights should be placed predictably and modestly so users can notice time-sensitive information without losing control of attention.
condition: When designing dashboards or supervisory control interfaces.

statement: Users should be able to tailor window layouts, sort orders, and highlighted features to their work needs, and share useful configurations with colleagues.
condition: When an interface supports repeated expert work or collaborative operations.

statement: Co-locating operators can improve mutual monitoring, assistance seeking, and rapid collaboration in time-sensitive control-room work.
condition: When users respond to fast-moving events that benefit from shared awareness.

statement: Human control and computer automation should be modeled as separate design dimensions, because high automation and high human control can coexist.
Designers should search for designs that combine high automation with high human control instead of assuming automation necessarily reduces human agency.
Some applications need high automation with limited direct human timing control, such as rapid safety devices or embedded medical systems.
condition: When human reaction time or continuous intervention is impractical.

statement: Some applications need high human control with limited automation, such as skilled creative or physical activities where human judgment is the main value.
condition: When the user’s embodied skill, creative judgment, or direct control is central to the task.

statement: Design processes should include interlocks or other constraints that mitigate both excessive automation and excessive human control.
condition: When failures could arise from either unchecked automated action or unchecked human action.

statement: AI application design can go wrong when lessons from human-emulation research are directly transferred into systems meant to provide useful services.
Useful AI applications should often favor comprehensible, predictable, and controllable designs over intelligent, autonomous, or human-like presentation.
condition: When the design goal is practical user empowerment rather than AI science or human-emulation research.

statement: Human-centered AI designs should combine the useful parts of intelligent agents, simulated teammates, autonomous systems, and humanoid robots with powerful tools, tele-operation, supervisory control, and appliance-like reliability.
For rescue robotics and similar field systems, continuous multimodal visual or sensor displays can be more effective than speech-like status reports.
condition: When users need ongoing awareness of location, hazards, obstacles, and possible routes.

statement: Public-facing AI imagery should emphasize user interfaces, appliances, and tele-operated devices when the intended message is human control and human responsibility.
condition: When communicating or branding human-centered technologies.

statement: Exploratory interactive visual interfaces may be a stronger path to machine-learning adoption and stakeholder comprehension than relying mainly on post-hoc explanations of automated decisions.
condition: When stakeholders need to understand, inspect, or work with machine-learning behavior.

statement: Bridging ethical AI principles into practice requires governance structures that operate at team, organization, and industry levels.

HCAI teams should use audit trails, software engineering workflows, verification and validation testing, bias testing, and explainable user interfaces to improve reliability and support inquiry or redress.
condition: When developing HCAI products or services as a software team.

statement: Organizations building HCAI systems should create a safety culture through leadership commitment, safety-oriented hiring and training, failure and near-miss reporting, internal review boards, and alignment with industry practices.
condition: When managing an organization that builds or deploys HCAI systems.

statement: Industry-wide trust in HCAI can be strengthened through independent oversight mechanisms such as regulation, external audits, insurance accountability, civil-society participation, and professional standards.
condition: When HCAI systems affect an industry or public stakeholders beyond one organization.

statement: Responsible AI principles are useful starting points, but practical HCAI requires realistic management processes that translate ethics into operational practice.
HCAI systems should support self-efficacy, creativity, clear responsibility, and social participation as foundations for privacy, security, fairness, reliability, safety, and trustworthiness goals.
Human-centered design thinking reframes AI by placing humans at the center of systems design rather than treating AI methods as the center of attention.
Progress toward HCAI is slowed by entrenched beliefs among researchers, developers, journalists, and policy makers that AI systems should be understood through human-like abilities.

Technology development must be paired with behavioral change when HCAI work is intended to contribute to broad societal goals such as health, poverty reduction, hunger reduction, or environmental protection.
condition: When AI-enabled technologies are designed to support broad social-development goals.

statement: Well-designed technologies can support social goals such as quality education, gender equality, peace, and social justice when they are aligned with human-centered development objectives.
condition: When technology design is aligned with human-centered development objectives.
